The increasing use of machine-learning (ML) enabled systems in critical tasks fuels the quest for novel verification and validation techniques yet grounded in accepted system assurance principles. In traditional system development, model-based techniques have been widely adopted, where the central premise is that abstract models of the required system provide a sound basis for judging its implementation. We posit an analogous approach for ML systems using an ML technique that extracts from the high-dimensional training data implicitly describing the required system, a low-dimensional underlying structure--a manifold. It is then harnessed for a range of quality assurance tasks such as test adequacy measurement, test input generation, and runtime monitoring of the target ML system. The approach is built on variational autoencoder, an unsupervised method for learning a pair of mutually near-inverse functions between a given high-dimensional dataset and a low-dimensional representation. Preliminary experiments establish that the proposed manifold-based approach, for test adequacy drives diversity in test data, for test generation yields fault-revealing yet realistic test cases, and for runtime monitoring provides an independent means to assess trustability of the target system's output.

Recent work on adversarial attack and defense suggests that PGD is a universal $l_\infty$ first-order attack, and PGD adversarial training can significantly improve network robustness against a wide range of first-order $l_\infty$-bounded attacks, represented as the state-of-the-art defense method. However, an obvious weakness of PGD adversarial training is its highly-computational cost in generating adversarial samples, making it computationally infeasible for large and high-resolution real datasets such as the ImageNet dataset. In addition, recent work also has suggested a simple "close-form" solution to a robust model on MNIST. Therefore, a natural question raised is that is PGD adversarial training really necessary for robust defense? In this paper, we give a negative answer by proposing a training paradigm that is comparable to PGD adversarial training on several standard datasets, while only using noisy-natural samples. Specifically, we reformulate the min-max objective in PGD adversarial training by a problem to minimize the original network loss plus $l_1$ norms of its gradients w.r.t. the inputs. For the $l_1$-norm loss, we propose a computationally-feasible solution by embedding a differentiable soft-quantization layer after the network input layer. We show formally that the soft-quantization layer trained with noisy-natural samples is an alternative approach to minimizing the $l_1$-gradient norms

Adversarial imitation learning has become a popular framework for imitation in continuous control. Over the years, several variations of its components were proposed to enhance the performance of the learned policies as well as the sample complexity of the algorithm. In practice, these choices are rarely tested all together in rigorous empirical studies. It is therefore difficult to discuss and understand what choices, among the high-level algorithmic options as well as low-level implementation details, matter. To tackle this issue, we implement more than 50 of these choices in a generic adversarial imitation learning framework and investigate their impacts in a large-scale study (>500k trained agents) with both synthetic and human-generated demonstrations. While many of our findings confirm common practices, some of them are surprising or even contradict prior work. In particular, our results suggest that artificial demonstrations are not a good proxy for human data and that the very common practice of evaluating imitation algorithms only with synthetic demonstrations may lead to algorithms which perform poorly in the more realistic scenarios with human demonstrations.

Federated learning (FL) is a promising solution to enable many AI applications, where sensitive datasets from distributed clients are needed for collaboratively training a global model. FL allows the clients to participate in the training phase, governed by a central server, without sharing their local data. One of the main challenges of FL is the communication overhead, where the model updates of the participating clients are sent to the central server at each global training round. Over-the-air computation (AirComp) has been recently proposed to alleviate the communication bottleneck where the model updates are sent simultaneously over the multiple-access channel. However, simple averaging of the model updates via AirComp makes the learning process vulnerable to random or intended modifications of the local model updates of some Byzantine clients. In this paper, we propose a transmission and aggregation framework to reduce the effect of such attacks while preserving the benefits of AirComp for FL. For the proposed robust approach, the central server divides the participating clients randomly into groups and allocates a transmission time slot for each group. The updates of the different groups are then aggregated using a robust aggregation technique. We extend our approach to handle the case of non-i.i.d.

This paper considers stochastic optimization problems for a large class of objective functions, including convex and continuous submodular. Stochastic proximal gradient methods have been widely used to solve such problems; however, their applicability remains limited when the problem dimension is large and the projection onto a convex set is costly. Instead, stochastic conditional gradient methods are proposed as an alternative solution relying on (i) Approximating gradients via a simple averaging technique requiring a single stochastic gradient evaluation per iteration; (ii) Solving a linear program to compute the descent/ascent direction. The averaging technique reduces the noise of gradient approximations as time progresses, and replacing projection step in proximal methods by a linear program lowers the computational complexity of each iteration. We show that under convexity and smoothness assumptions, our proposed method converges to the optimal objective function value at a sublinear rate of $O(1/t^{1/3})$. Further, for a monotone and continuous DR-submodular function and subject to a general convex body constraint, we prove that our proposed method achieves a $((1-1/e)OPT-\eps)$ guarantee with $O(1/\eps^3)$ stochastic gradient computations. This guarantee matches the known hardness results and closes the gap between deterministic and stochastic continuous submodular maximization. Additionally, we obtain $((1/e)OPT -\eps)$ guarantee after using

Prescriptive process monitoring approaches leverage historical data to prescribe runtime interventions that will likely prevent negative case outcomes or improve a process's performance. A centerpiece of a prescriptive process monitoring method is its intervention policy: a decision function determining if and when to trigger an intervention on an ongoing case. Previous proposals in this field rely on intervention policies that consider only the current state of a given case. These approaches do not consider the tradeoff between triggering an intervention in the current state, given the level of uncertainty of the underlying predictive models, versus delaying the intervention to a later state. Moreover, they assume that a resource is always available to perform an intervention (infinite capacity). This paper addresses these gaps by introducing a prescriptive process monitoring method that filters and ranks ongoing cases based on prediction scores, prediction uncertainty, and causal effect of the intervention, and triggers interventions to maximize a gain function, considering the available resources. The proposal is evaluated using a real-life event log. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing baselines regarding total gain.

Offline handwritten mathematical expression recognition is a challenging task, because handwritten mathematical expressions mainly have two problems in the process of recognition. On one hand, it is how to correctly recognize different mathematical symbols. On the other hand, it is how to correctly recognize the two-dimensional structure existing in mathematical expressions. Inspired by recent work in deep learning, a new neural network model that combines a Multi-Scale convolutional neural network (CNN) with an Attention recurrent neural network (RNN) is proposed to identify two-dimensional handwritten mathematical expressions as one-dimensional LaTeX sequences. As a result, the model proposed in the present work has achieved a WER error of 25.715% and ExpRate of 28.216%.

Co-evolving time series appears in a multitude of applications such as environmental monitoring, financial analysis, and smart transportation. This paper aims to address the following challenges, including (C1) how to incorporate explicit relationship networks of the time series; (C2) how to model the implicit relationship of the temporal dynamics. We propose a novel model called Network of Tensor Time Series, which is comprised of two modules, including Tensor Graph Convolutional Network (TGCN) and Tensor Recurrent Neural Network (TRNN). TGCN tackles the first challenge by generalizing Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) for flat graphs to tensor graphs, which captures the synergy between multiple graphs associated with the tensors. TRNN leverages tensor decomposition to model the implicit relationships among co-evolving time series. The experimental results on five real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

Crowd-sourcing has become a popular means of acquiring labeled data for a wide variety of tasks where humans are more accurate than computers, e.g., labeling images, matching objects, or analyzing sentiment. However, relying solely on the crowd is often impractical even for data sets with thousands of items, due to time and cost constraints of acquiring human input (which cost pennies and minutes per label). In this paper, we propose algorithms for integrating machine learning into crowd-sourced databases, with the goal of allowing crowd-sourcing applications to scale, i.e., to handle larger datasets at lower costs. The key observation is that, in many of the above tasks, humans and machine learning algorithms can be complementary, as humans are often more accurate but slow and expensive, while algorithms are usually less accurate, but faster and cheaper. Based on this observation, we present two new active learning algorithms to combine humans and algorithms together in a crowd-sourced database. Our algorithms are based on the theory of non-parametric bootstrap, which makes our results applicable to a broad class of machine learning models. Our results, on three real-life datasets collected with Amazon's Mechanical Turk, and on 15 well-known UCI data sets, show that our methods
AI: This work introduces $\epsilon$-Consistent Mixup ($\epsilon$mu), a novel data-driven regularization method that integrates Mixup’s linear interpolation with directional consistency regularization through an adaptive balancing mechanism. By learning this optimal combination, $\epsilon$mu enforces a more adaptable structural relationship in the feature space, leading to improved semi-supervised classification performance on SVHN and CIFAR10—particularly in low-label scenarios. Comparative experiments between $\epsilon$mu and Mixup demonstrate its advantages, revealing that $\epsilon$mu generates more reliable synthetic labels and higher-confidence predictions than standard Mixup, offering insights into its superior efficacy.

Autoencoders play a valuable role in high-energy physics for identifying anomalies, especially when analyzing jets—collimated particle showers from collisions like those at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. In this work, we investigate graph-based autoencoders that process jets as "particle clouds," allowing them to capture the relationships between particles within a jet. Furthermore, we introduce a differentiable approximation of the energy mover’s distance using a graph neural network, which can serve as a reconstruction loss function in autoencoder models.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have framed compelling modern challenges within the traditional framework of tree search—notably exemplified by the game of Go. Intriguingly, the state space behind these sequential decision-making problems frequently exhibits a richer underlying structure that surpasses what a simple tree can represent.  

This work introduces a probabilistic approach designed to uncover and leverage the latent structure within a search space, enabling information sharing across the search tree. Our technique combines approximate inference in jointly Gaussian models for the explored regions of the problem with an abstraction method for unexplored regions, which dynamically reduces complexity as needed.  

Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms existing non-probabilistic alternatives in both Tic-Tac-Toe and a feature selection application.

Ticks are responsible for spreading numerous bacterial, viral, and parasitic infections worldwide. Over the past ten years, tick-borne illnesses have surged dramatically, with Lyme disease cases in the U.S. alone reaching an estimated 300,000 annually. This rise underscores the urgent need for advancements in identifying and diagnosing these diseases.  

This study aims to enhance the methodology of Burlina et al. by employing multiple convolutional neural network models to identify tick-borne skin lesions. To diversify training data and improve detection accuracy, we sourced images from Google in seven different languages. The final dataset consisted of 6,080 images, trained across various architectures including ResNet 34, ResNet 50, VGG 19, and DenseNet 121. Our best-performing model, using DenseNet 121, achieved an accuracy of 80.72%.

Deep neural networks play a crucial role in numerous computer vision applications, yet their effectiveness relies heavily on extensive labeled datasets for supervised learning. This paper examines and evaluates various existing methods designed to enhance model performance without the need for gathering more manually annotated real-world data. These approaches primarily focus on either augmenting available datasets through label-preserving transformations or generating artificial training data through synthetic means.

Voice-based diagnosis and treatment evaluation for Parkinson's disease hold significant importance, yet the few-shot learning challenge remains substantial. While deep learning excels at automated feature extraction, it struggles with limited training samples. The conventional approach involves prior knowledge-based feature extraction followed by dimensionality reduction for classification. However, this method presents two key limitations: 1) Existing approaches fail to explore structural relationships among speech features to reconstruct higher-quality representations, and 2) Inter-sample structural patterns remain unexplored, preventing the generation of improved data samples.  

To address these issues, this paper proposes a deep double-side learning ensemble model that simultaneously performs in-depth reconstruction of both speech features and samples. For feature reconstruction, we develop an embedded deep stacked group sparse auto-encoder to perform nonlinear feature transformation, producing enhanced high-level features that are subsequently combined with original speech features through L1-regularized feature selection. For sample reconstruction, we introduce a novel deep sample learning algorithm to optimize data quality. These innovations are implemented using an existing Parkinson's disease speech feature dataset.

We examine the challenges of identity and closeness testing for discrete populations using random samples. Our objective is to design efficient testing methods while ensuring Differential Privacy for the population's individuals. We present a solution that produces private testers with strong sample efficiency for both problems. Theoretically, we demonstrate that differentially private identity and closeness testers can achieve sample complexity comparable to non-private methods. We also evaluate our algorithms empirically using synthetic data. The experimental results indicate that our private testers maintain low type I and type II errors while requiring sample sizes that grow sublinearly with the domain size of the underlying distributions.

Cities worldwide are now tracking parking spaces to help drivers find available spots more easily, and initial outcomes show real potential. Yet these methods face limitations due to the expensive sensors required for accurate monitoring across entire urban areas. This study explores how parking data from sensor-equipped zones can be expanded to areas without sensors. By assessing neighborhood similarities using geographic information systems, we examine how occupancy rates from monitored parking zones can be applied to unmonitored areas.

Measuring document similarity allows for effective summarization and analysis of extensive text collections. Traditional distance metrics between documents either fail to capture semantic word relationships or face scalability challenges. To address this, we propose hierarchical optimal transport as a document meta-distance, representing documents as distributions over topics, which in turn are modeled as distributions over words. By solving an optimal transport problem in the more compact topic space, we compute similarity scores efficiently. We establish conditions under which this approach forms a valid distance metric and explore its connection to word mover's distance. When tested for k-NN classification, our method demonstrates improved interpretability and scalability while achieving competitive performance with existing approaches at significantly lower computational cost.

Speaker diarization, the process of identifying speech segments from specific speakers, has become increasingly important for human-centered applications like video conferencing and human-computer interaction systems. This paper presents a novel self-supervised approach to speaker diarization that learns audio-video synchronization while eliminating the need for extensive labeled data. Our method advances prior work through two innovative loss functions: the dynamic triplet loss and multinomial loss. Experimental evaluation on a real-world human-computer interaction system demonstrates significant performance improvements, with our optimal model achieving an 8% F1-score boost and reduced diarization error rate. Additionally, we contribute a new large-scale Chinese audio-video dataset to address the current lack of such resources for Mandarin speech processing.

The development of network-centric Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) presents intricate software engineering challenges in design and validation. This paper introduces an innovative model-driven approach, leveraging domain-specific modeling methodologies within the software engineering paradigm. We specifically examine Machine Learning (ML) as a key subset of AI and advocate for offloading data analytics and ML processing to the IoT edge.  

By distributing ML workloads across edge devices, we enhance service quality—improving availability, performance, and resilience to varying network conditions—while ensuring privacy, security, and sustainability. Our approach enables the deployment of ML models on resource-constrained edge devices, including embedded microcontrollers with limited memory (measured in Kilobytes) and ultra-low power consumption (in milliwatts), a field known as TinyML.  

Additionally, we demonstrate the role of multi-layered software models—platform-independent and platform-specific abstractions—in streamlining the development lifecycle. To validate our methodology, we present a case study focusing on predictive maintenance for a networked hydraulics system, incorporating diverse sensors and actuators.

Despite significant advancements in maternal healthcare, high rates of maternal and perinatal mortality persist in low- and middle-income countries. While fetal ultrasound is a critical element of antenatal care, its widespread use has been hindered by a lack of properly trained medical professionals. To address this gap, we created and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of estimating gestational age (GA) and detecting fetal malpresentation from "blind sweep" ultrasound videos captured by minimally trained operators. We also tackled implementation challenges specific to low-resource settings. By employing a streamlined sweep protocol enhanced with real-time AI guidance on scan quality, we showed that our models perform effectively when used by novice operators with affordable ultrasound devices featuring integrated on-device AI. The GA estimation model matched the accuracy of conventional fetal biometry measurements with only two sweeps, while the fetal malpresentation detection model maintained high AUC-ROC scores across different operators and devices. These AI solutions could enhance the diagnostic capabilities of minimally trained ultrasound operators in resource-constrained environments.

This paper advocates for a declarative approach as the foundation for data-intensive machine learning systems. Rather than developing specialized systems for each machine learning task or manually implementing optimizations, we propose using recursive queries to implement diverse machine learning systems. This method leverages database query optimization to generate efficient execution plans, which can then run on a unified data-parallel query processing engine.  

To demonstrate this concept, we examine two machine learning programming models—Pregel and Iterative Map-Reduce-Update—and illustrate their implementation in Datalog. We show how these models can be adapted for specific tasks and compiled into optimized execution plans. Experimental results from a large-scale cluster using real-world data confirm that this declarative approach delivers strong performance while improving flexibility and simplifying programming.

Data poisoning attacks seek to corrupt a model's training data to manipulate the resulting output. We investigate differential privacy as a defense against these attacks. Our findings demonstrate that models trained with differential privacy can resist poisoning when the attacker alters only a limited portion of the data, but this resilience weakens as the number of poisoned samples increases. To validate this, we develop attack strategies specifically for objective and output perturbation learners—two common differential privacy methods in machine learning. Experimental results confirm that our attacks succeed when adversaries can inject a significant volume of corrupted training samples.

When sampling from a probability measure supported on a submanifold in Euclidean space, a neighborhood graph can be constructed to approximate the submanifold. This graph’s Laplacian is widely employed in machine learning techniques such as semi-supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and clustering.  

This paper investigates the pointwise convergence of three commonly studied graph Laplacians as the sample size grows and the neighborhood size shrinks to zero. For a uniform measure on the submanifold, all three Laplacians converge to the same limit, differing only by constant factors. However, when the measure is non-uniform, only the random walk graph Laplacian converges to the weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator.

We present a novel approach using two-scale loss functions designed for gradient descent optimization in classification tasks with deep neural networks. This versatile method can be integrated across diverse machine learning architectures, including both deep neural networks and support vector machines. The two-scale loss functions prioritize training on misclassified examples within the dataset, enhancing model performance. When evaluated on standard deep networks with MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets, properly configured two-scale loss functions demonstrate improved performance metrics compared to conventional cross-entropy loss.

We reexamine regret lower bounds for multi-armed bandit problems, deriving non-asymptotic, distribution-dependent bounds through simple proofs that rely solely on fundamental properties of Kullback-Leibler divergences. Our results reveal that regret initially grows in an almost linear fashion, with the well-known logarithmic regret rate emerging only in later stages. The analysis distills the core information-theoretic reasoning, eliminating unnecessary complexities to present these insights clearly and concisely.

Reparameterizing variational autoencoders with continuous random variables effectively reduces gradient estimate variance. For discrete cases, reparameterization can be achieved using the Gumbel-Max trick, though this introduces a non-differentiable objective due to the argmax operation. Unlike previous approaches that employ softmax relaxations, we propose direct optimization through loss minimization. This method readily applies to structured discrete latent variable models where argmax computations are feasible. Empirical results confirm the effectiveness of direct loss minimization in variational autoencoders with both structured and unstructured discrete latent variables.

This study evaluates a diverse range of machine learning models designed to predict both diagnosed and undiagnosed diabetes using eight years of NHANES data. Model performance is optimized and assessed using Brier Scores, followed by a comparison of the most influential variables in the top-performing algorithms. A linear-kernel Support Vector Machine achieved the highest predictive accuracy for diabetes detection, demonstrating a Brier score of 0.0654 and an AUROC of 0.9235 on test data. For undiagnosed diabetes prediction, elastic net regression proved most effective, yielding a Brier score of 0.0294 and an AUROC of 0.9439. Analysis reveals consistent key predictors across both models, including blood osmolality, family history, concentrations of specific biochemical compounds, and hypertension status. Notably, ethnic or genetic factors emerged as particularly strong predictors in models identifying undiagnosed diabetes cases.

Federated learning (FL) stands as a prominent distributed machine learning framework, prized for its advantages in preserving data privacy and optimizing communication efficiency. While full client participation is often impractical due to resource limitations, prior research has explored partial participation FL algorithms that actively select or sample a subset of clients to approximate the performance of full participation.  

This paper examines an understudied passive partial client participation scenario, where dropout—driven by external factors rather than algorithmic choice—leads to incomplete involvement. We frame FL with client dropout as a specific instance of a broader class of FL challenges where clients may submit substitute local updates, which could be approximate.  

Building on our convergence analysis, we introduce *FL-FDMS*, a novel algorithm that dynamically identifies “friends” (clients with similar data distributions) and employs their local updates as substitutes for dropped-out clients. This approach minimizes substitution errors and enhances convergence. Additionally, FL-FDMS integrates a complexity reduction mechanism, ensuring both theoretical rigor and practical applicability. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate FL-FDMS’s superior performance in managing client dropout in FL.

As data centers and computing systems experience surging energy demands, integrating energy efficiency into algorithm design—particularly scheduling—has become essential. Machine learning offers a practical solution by forecasting system loads using historical data and other factors. Yet this approach’s success hinges on prediction accuracy, often falling short of optimal when forecasts are unreliable. Conversely, traditional online algorithms provide worst-case guarantees but may perform too conservatively for many real-world inputs.  

In line with the emerging field of machine learning-augmented algorithms, this paper bridges the gap for the classic online speed-scaling problem with deadlines. We introduce a new prediction framework and develop algorithms that: (i) achieve provably low energy consumption with accurate predictions, (ii) remain resilient to poor predictions, and (iii) exhibit smooth degradation in performance as prediction errors grow.

Recent research has investigated the capabilities of large-scale Transformer-based pre-trained models, particularly Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), in natural language processing. However, this advancement has sparked concerns regarding financial expenses and environmental impact due to carbon emissions. Consequently, compressing PLMs such as BERT while maintaining performance for faster inference and cost-effective deployment has garnered significant interest. This study focuses on achieving higher compression ratios for PLMs, with tensor decomposition emerging as a promising yet understudied approach. We introduce two decomposition and reconstruction techniques to enhance both the efficiency and effectiveness of compression. Our compressed BERT model, retaining only **1/7** of the parameters in Transformer layers, performs comparably—and occasionally slightly better—than the original BERT on the GLUE benchmark. A highly compact variant delivers **96.7%** of BERT-base's performance with just **1/48** of the encoder parameters (fewer than **2M** parameters, excluding embeddings) and achieves a **2.7×** speedup in inference. To demonstrate the compatibility of our method with existing compression techniques like knowledge distillation, we also evaluate its application on a distilled BERT model.

Optimizing matrix rank under affine constraints is a common challenge across various fields, including signal processing and machine learning. While nuclear norm serves as a convex relaxation technique—capable of exact rank recovery under specific theoretical conditions—its practical performance often falls short for real-world applications. To achieve more accurate results than nuclear norm methods, this paper introduces a Logarithm-Determinant-based rank approximation.  

We specifically apply this approximation to subspace clustering, presenting a flexible framework capable of handling diverse error and noise types. Additionally, we develop an efficient optimization strategy with theoretical convergence guarantees to stationary points. Experimental evaluations on face clustering and motion segmentation tasks demonstrate superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art subspace clustering approaches.

We present two testable hypotheses regarding generalization error expectations in concept drift learning scenarios. The first suggests that optimal forgetting rates for minimizing generalization error rise with increasing drift rates—and conversely, decline with slower drift. The second proposes that as a learner's forgetting rate grows, the optimal bias/variance trade-off shifts toward lower variance, and vice versa.  

These hypotheses introduce the notion of a *sweet path*—a trajectory through the three-dimensional space of drift rates, forgetting rates, and bias/variance profiles where generalization error is minimized. On this path, gradual drift aligns with slower forgetting and lower bias, while rapid drift pairs with fast forgetting and lower variance.  

Empirical results support the existence of this sweet path. Additionally, we show that simple learners, when equipped with well-chosen forgetting rates and bias/variance profiles, perform comparably to state-of-the-art incremental learners on real-world concept drift problems.

We present Coarse-Grained Nonlinear Dynamics—a versatile and efficient method for parameterizing nonlinear system dynamics using the Volterra series expansion. These models use a quasilinear number of parameters relative to the system's memory length, regardless of the truncation order of the Volterra expansion. This achieves a superpolynomial reduction in parameter count as the order increases. The efficiency stems from coarse-graining sections of the dynamics that depend on the product of widely separated input samples, akin to the fast multipole method’s coarse-graining for $\mathcal{O}(n)$ n-body simulations.  

This streamlined parameterization facilitates regularization, enabling Coarse-Grained Nonlinear System Identification—a technique that accurately identifies nonlinear dynamic models with minimal experimental data. We validate the method’s effectiveness through a synthetic example and a real-world application, successfully modeling the voltage-to-luminosity dynamics of a tungsten filament using less than a second of experimental data.

Training neural networks on adversarially perturbed inputs—known as adversarial training—has been extensively researched as a technique to enhance model robustness against potential attacks during inference. However, this increased robustness is achieved at a cost: it typically reduces overall model accuracy and performance. Recent studies in robot learning applications have revealed that adversarial training creates an unbalanced trade-off, often resulting in an overall performance decline when assessing full robotic system capabilities.  

This study re-examines the robustness-accuracy trade-off in robot learning by investigating whether advancements in robust training techniques and theoretical insights—when combined with adversarial training—can make the approach viable for real-world robotic applications. We conduct evaluations across diverse robotic tasks, including autonomous driving in high-fidelity simulated environments designed for sim-to-real transfer and mobile robot gesture recognition. Our findings indicate that while modern robust training methods yield marginal relative improvements, the detrimental effects of adversarial training still outweigh the benefits by a significant margin. We conclude that more substantial breakthroughs in robust learning methods are needed before they can be effectively applied to practical robot learning scenarios.

Adversarial learning has become a key approach for countering the vulnerability of existing methods to adversarial perturbations. However, most current defense strategies are designed to protect against only one specific type of adversarial perturbation (e.g., $\ell_\infty$-attack). This limitation renders them ineffective in safety-critical scenarios where attackers may employ varied adversarial strategies. Additionally, training models to handle multiple perturbations simultaneously imposes a substantial computational burden.  

To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework that explicitly learns to generate noise, enhancing model robustness against diverse adversarial attacks. The core of this framework is the Meta Noise Generator (MNG), which produces optimal noise to perturb input samples stochastically, thereby reducing error across multiple adversarial perturbations. By leveraging MNG-generated samples, we train models while maintaining label consistency under various attack types.  

Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts robustness across multiple datasets and a wide range of adversarial perturbations, consistently outperforming baseline methods with minimal computational overhead.

Improving the interpretability of deep neural networks (DNNs) depends on assessing their ability to perform symbolic computation. A key aspect of symbolic reasoning is variable binding—the process of connecting an input value to an abstract variable stored in the system’s internal memory. While previous research has explored the computational capabilities of DNNs, it has not conclusively determined whether these models utilize variable binding in their internal operations. We suggest this gap exists because of a fundamental limitation in how earlier experiments were structured.  

This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of variable binding in state-of-the-art Transformer models, specifically BERT and RoBERTa. Our experimental design ensures that the model must apply a learned rule across entirely distinct subsets of the input vocabulary, preventing reliance on simple associative pattern matching. The findings reveal a stark contrast between classification and sequence-to-sequence tasks: BERT and RoBERTa successfully learn to copy or reverse strings even when tested with task-specific vocabularies that differ from their training data. However, both models fail completely to generalize across vocabularies in analogous classification tasks. This suggests that Transformers’ strong performance in sequence modeling may be due to their heavy reliance on the input as an external "memory" rather than true internal symbolic operations involving variable binding.

Visual Question Answering (VQA) continues to draw significant research attention due to its valuable applications, including support for visually impaired individuals and image retrieval. This study investigates scene graph-based approaches for VQA, focusing on the challenging GQA dataset that features complex questions demanding counting skills, compositional understanding, and sophisticated reasoning—along with extensive scene graph annotations. We adapt image-question models for scene graph integration, assess various scene graph generation methods for novel images, introduce a novel training strategy combining human-annotated and machine-generated scene graphs, and develop late fusion frameworks capable of processing multiple visual representations. Our comprehensive analysis establishes the first in-depth examination of scene graph applications in VQA systems.

The widespread use of monitoring devices in urban traffic flow systems leads to high maintenance and operational costs. A solution is needed to minimize the number of deployed devices without compromising data accuracy or granularity. This paper introduces a method for estimating real-time, detailed crowd flows across a city using coarse-grained data. The approach addresses two key challenges: spatial relationships between coarse and fine-grained urban flows, and the complexities of external influences.  

To solve these challenges, we propose UrbanFM, a model with two core components: 1) an inference network that generates fine-grained flow distributions from coarse inputs, leveraging a feature extraction module and a novel distribution-based upsampling technique; and 2) a fusion subnet that enhances performance by integrating external factors. While UrbanFM excels in small-scale upsampling, it struggles with higher scaling ratios due to its single-pass upsampling approach.  

To overcome this limitation, we introduce UrbanPy, a cascading model that progressively refines urban flow predictions by breaking the task into multiple subtasks. This enhanced architecture delivers superior results for large-scale flow inference compared to UrbanFM.

Eligibility traces in reinforcement learning serve as a mechanism to balance bias and variance, frequently accelerating training by efficiently propagating information across multiple time-steps in one update. Our study explores the application of eligibility traces alongside recurrent neural networks within the Atari domain. Through experimentation, we demonstrate the advantages of combining these techniques in certain Atari games while also emphasizing the critical role of optimization methods in the training process.

Language Identification (LI) serves as a critical initial component in many speech processing applications. As voice-enabled assistants become increasingly prevalent, speech-based LI has grown into a prominent area of research. Two primary approaches exist for language identification: an implicit method that relies solely on speech input without transcripts, and an explicit method that utilizes corresponding textual data. This study focuses on the implicit approach due to the unavailability of transcriptive information.  

The paper evaluates current models and introduces a novel attention-based architecture for language identification, using log-Mel spectrogram images as input features. Additionally, it explores the potential of raw waveform data as an effective input for neural network-based LI systems.  

For model training and assessment, six languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Russian, and Italian) were classified with 95.4% accuracy, while a subset of four languages (English, French, German, Spanish) achieved 96.3% accuracy using the VoxForge dataset. The proposed method is scalable and can be extended to support additional languages.

This paper presents novel approaches for addressing two key challenges in time series (TS) analysis through quantum computing: reconstruction and classification. We frame the TS reconstruction task as an unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, solvable by both quantum annealers and gate-model quantum computers. Our approach involves discretizing the TS and transforming the reconstruction into a set cover problem, enabling a one-versus-all reconstruction strategy. Building upon the reconstruction solution, we demonstrate its extension to semi-supervised TS classification. Our results suggest the method performs competitively with existing semi-supervised and unsupervised classification approaches while requiring less data than classical techniques.

We examine the challenge of jointly encoding structured data, such as natural language, for transmission over noisy channels. Conventionally, this involves compressing the text via source coding before applying channel coding to ensure robustness during transmission. While this method is optimal for minimizing end-to-end distortion with sufficiently long block lengths over discrete memoryless channels, its effectiveness diminishes with finite document lengths and constrained encoding sizes. In such cases, we demonstrate that a deep learning-based encoder-decoder framework can achieve lower word error rates. Unlike traditional approaches that focus solely on minimizing bit error rates through separate source and channel coding, our method prioritizes preserving semantic meaning. It does so by embedding sentences in a semantic space—where similar meanings are mapped closer together—before performing joint source and channel coding on these embeddings.

I develop neural machine translation models for English-Hungarian and Hungarian-English language pairs using the Hunglish2 corpus. The key focus of this research involves assessing various data augmentation approaches during NMT model training. I introduce five structure-aware augmentation techniques that leverage dependency parse trees to guide word selection for blanking or replacement, rather than using random selection.  

The thesis begins with an extensive literature review covering neural networks, sequential modeling, neural machine translation, dependency parsing, and data augmentation. Following a thorough exploratory analysis and preprocessing of the Hunglish2 corpus, I conduct experiments with the proposed augmentation methods. The top-performing model for Hungarian-English translation achieves a BLEU score of 33.9, while the best English-Hungarian model reaches 28.6 BLEU.

Neural network integer quantization involves approximating high-precision computations in standard neural networks using lower integer precision. This technique is crucial for optimizing machine learning (ML) systems, as it decreases memory usage and often speeds up processing. In this study, we introduce an integer-only quantization approach for Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks—a backbone of many operational ML applications. Our method maintains accuracy, supports efficient post-training quantization, and executes rapidly by employing 8-bit integer weights and predominantly 8-bit activations. Additionally, it is adaptable to diverse hardware platforms by utilizing instruction sets in standard CPUs and compatible neural accelerators.

Automated design synthesis could transform contemporary engineering practices, expanding access to precisely optimized and tailored products in diverse industries. Applying generative machine learning to engineering design may unlock this potential, making it a critical area of research. This paper examines current applications of deep generative models (DGMs) in engineering design. These models use deep neural networks to analyze datasets and generate novel designs. Recent advances in DGMs—including feedforward neural networks (NNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), and select deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches—have demonstrated significant promise in areas such as structural optimization, materials innovation, and geometric synthesis. Since 2016, the adoption of DGMs in engineering design has surged, and with further growth expected, this review highlights recent progress to aid researchers exploring DGMs for design. The discussion organizes key developments, covering algorithms, datasets, representation techniques, and real-world applications. Specifically, we examine influential studies that have introduced novel DGM methodologies, effectively utilized DGMs in design-related fields, or contributed to DGM advancement through datasets and supporting tools.

Although natural language processing systems excel at numerous tasks, they remain vulnerable to minor adversarial input modifications. Current defense strategies fall into two categories: (i) heuristic approaches that prove ineffective against sophisticated attacks or (ii) methods offering guaranteed protection against worst-case scenarios, though incompatible with advanced architectures like BERT. We present robust encodings (RobEn)—a straightforward framework that ensures provable robustness without architectural compromises. At its core, RobEn employs an encoding function that transforms sentences into a compact, discrete encoding space. By implementing these encodings as a system bottleneck, models achieve certified robustness through standard training while maintaining cross-task compatibility. We establish two key criteria for robust encoding functions: perturbations must yield a limited set of encodings (stability), and encoded models must preserve performance (fidelity). Applying RobEn to defend against diverse adversarial typos, our BERT-based implementation achieves 71.3% average robust accuracy across six GLUE tasks, significantly outperforming prior typo-correction methods that achieved only 35.3% accuracy against basic greedy attacks.

This paper explores the application of machine learning techniques in reservoir history matching by incorporating 4D seismic data into the inversion process. A novel integrated approach is introduced for reconstructing petrophysical properties in a synthetic reservoir using a modified Ensemble Smoother with Multiple Data Assimilation (ES-MDA). The permeability field is parameterized through an unsupervised learning method combining K-means clustering with Singular Value Decomposition (K-SVD), alongside the Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) technique—a common choice for sparsity-promoting regularization. Additionally, seismic attributes, specifically acoustic impedance, are parameterized using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT).  

By merging machine learning, sparsity regularization, seismic imaging, and history matching, this framework aims to efficiently tackle the ill-posed nature of production data inversion with ES-MDA. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these sparse representations of petrophysical properties and seismic attributes lead to improved production data matches compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, this approach enhances the accuracy of waterfront progression quantification, showcasing its superiority over conventional techniques that lack similar parameterization strategies.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a groundbreaking field with the potential to revolutionize deep learning, much like Convolutional Neural Networks did in 2012. Despite significant advancements and notable performance gains across various tasks, evaluating and comparing different NAS methods remains a major challenge. Although many algorithms are tested on common datasets, there is no unified experimental framework, and the limited use of ablation studies makes it difficult to determine why certain approaches outperform others.  

Our first contribution is a comprehensive benchmark of eight NAS methods across five datasets. To ensure fair comparison despite differing search spaces, we introduce a novel metric: a method's relative improvement over the performance of an average randomly sampled architecture. This approach eliminates biases from handcrafted search spaces or specialized training protocols. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that numerous NAS techniques struggle to surpass the baseline performance of randomly sampled architectures by a meaningful margin.  

To delve deeper, we conduct additional experiments using the widely adopted DARTS search space, dissecting the impact of individual components in the NAS pipeline. Our analysis uncovers two critical insights: (i) evaluation protocol optimizations—often underestimated—play a dominant role in...

Although randomized clinical trials typically have sufficient sample sizes to accurately estimate average treatment effects, they often lack the statistical power needed to assess treatment-covariate interactions, which are essential for advancing data-driven precision medicine. Real-world observational data could help address this limitation. A standard trial-based approach involves fitting separate regression models for each treatment arm to predict outcomes, then calculating treatment effects by comparing these predictions. However, in observational studies, this method risks generating false treatment-covariate interactions if the regression models are misspecified.  

Focusing on the need to model relapse counts in multiple sclerosis patients—where the ratio of relapse rates provides a clinically meaningful measure of treatment effect—we propose estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as the ratio of expected potential outcomes. We develop a doubly robust estimator for this CATE within a semiparametric framework that accounts for treatment-covariate interactions. Additionally, we introduce a validation procedure to assess the estimator's accuracy on independent samples. Through simulations, we evaluate the finite-sample performance of our methods and demonstrate their advantages in real-world applications by analyzing treatment effects.

**Code Smell** refers to surface-level indicators of underlying issues in software development, much like how a bad odor signals something amiss. These signs often point to deeper problems in the code, recognizable by experienced developers who follow good coding practices. Research suggests that code with such smells is more likely to undergo frequent changes during the software development lifecycle.  

This paper introduces prediction models for eight types of code smells, leveraging features extracted from source code. To address class imbalance, we employed data sampling techniques, while feature selection methods helped identify the most relevant attributes. Unlike prior studies, which primarily used Naive Bayes and Random Forest, our work explores the application of deep learning for code smell prediction. We trained **576 distinct deep learning models** using the collected datasets and extracted features.  

Our findings demonstrate that models using **Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE)**-generated data achieved superior performance, with notable improvements in accuracy and AUC—some models reaching **88.47% accuracy**, up from previous benchmarks.

We explore $Q$-learning with knowledge transfer, leveraging samples from a target reinforcement learning (RL) task as well as related source tasks. Our work introduces transfer learning algorithms for both batch and online $Q$-learning, incorporating offline source data. The proposed approach includes a re-targeting step that facilitates vertical information propagation across multiple RL steps, complementing the traditional horizontal knowledge transfer seen in supervised learning. We provide the first theoretical analysis of transfer learning in RL, demonstrating accelerated convergence in offline transfer settings and a reduced regret bound for offline-to-online transfer under specific similarity conditions. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the algorithm and support our theoretical findings.

Measuring physical activity energy expenditure (PAEE) can enhance health monitoring, encouraging healthy aging by motivating behavioral changes linked to personal health benefits in older adults. While wearable accelerometers have been developed to track PAEE, existing methods primarily target younger populations. However, since older adults have distinct energy needs and activity patterns, current models may not accurately estimate PAEE for this demographic. Recognizing that past activities impact current PAEE, we introduce a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach, which excels at analyzing sequential data.  

To train the RNN for older adults, we utilized the GOTOV dataset, which includes 34 healthy participants aged 60 and above (average age 65) performing 16 different activities. Accelerometers were placed on the wrist and ankle, while indirect calorimetry measured energy expenditure. After optimization, we developed a model architecture featuring a 3-layer GRU-based RNN combined with a feedforward network that integrates both accelerometer data and participant-level information. This study explores advanced applications of GRU-based RNNs to improve accuracy in estimating PAEE for elderly populations.

Symmetry transformations give rise to invariances often characterized by deep latent variable models. While these invariances appear in complex domains like chemical space, their underlying symmetry transformations often lack analytical formulations. We introduce a model that learns symmetry transformations using two latent subspaces: one encoding the target information and the other preserving the invariant features.  

Our method leverages the deep information bottleneck framework enhanced by a continuous mutual information regularizer. Unlike existing approaches, we specifically address the challenge of reducing mutual information in continuous domains. This is achieved through mutual information estimation based on correlation matrices combined with a bijective variable transformation.  

Experiments across synthetic and molecular datasets show that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

Gaussian processes have emerged as a powerful method for safety-critical applications, leveraging the posterior variance to directly estimate model error and quantify risk. While existing approaches for such settings rely on the assumption of known kernel hyperparameters—an unrealistic requirement in practice—this work addresses the challenge by developing robust Gaussian process uniform error bounds for scenarios where hyperparameters are unknown.  

Our method constructs a confidence region within the hyperparameter space, providing a probabilistic upper bound on the model error for a Gaussian process with any hyperparameters. Unlike prior work, we do not assume prior knowledge of hyperparameter bounds—instead, our approach derives these bounds from data in an intuitive manner.  

Furthermore, we apply this technique to establish performance guarantees for a class of learning-based control problems. Experimental results demonstrate that our bound significantly outperforms both standard and fully Bayesian Gaussian processes.

We introduce the first learning-based visual odometry (VO) approach capable of generalizing across multiple datasets and real-world environments while surpassing traditional geometry-based methods in complex scenes. Our method leverages TartanAir, a comprehensive SLAM dataset offering extensive synthetic data from diverse and challenging scenarios. To enhance cross-dataset generalization, we implement an up-to-scale loss function and integrate camera intrinsic parameters directly into the model architecture. Empirical results demonstrate that TartanVO—trained exclusively on synthetic data without any fine-tuning—successfully adapts to real-world benchmarks including KITTI and EuRoC, outperforming conventional geometry-based techniques particularly in demanding trajectories. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/castacks/tartanvo.

We examine sequential online decision-making scenarios where an agent navigates the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Introducing a class of Bayesian optimistic policies—which generalizes Thompson sampling for stochastic multi-armed bandits—we present a novel regret analysis demonstrating that any algorithm generating policies within this optimistic framework achieves $\tilde O(\sqrt{AT})$ Bayesian regret for problems with $A$ actions over $T$ time steps.  

Our regret bounds extend to bilinear saddle-point problems, encompassing zero-sum matrix games and constrained bandits as specific cases. Notably, we identify scenarios where Thompson sampling fails to produce optimistic policies, leading to linear regret. To address this, we formulate policy optimization as a convex problem, yielding the Variational Bayesian Optimistic Sampling (VBOS) algorithm. This approach accommodates arbitrary posterior distributions—imposing no requirements like log-concavity, unimodality, or smoothness—while offering practical advantages: tunable exploration-exploitation balance, regularization support, constraint integration, and linear policy parameterization. The variational perspective further enables flexible algorithmic design while maintaining theoretical guarantees.

Modern deep learning models excel in performance when trained on extensive, well-structured datasets. Yet, their predictive accuracy declines notably when learning new classes incrementally, primarily because they tend to lose previously acquired knowledge—a challenge known as catastrophic forgetting. In contrast, Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) can preserve past knowledge by modeling the input space through constrained k-means clustering.  

To address this limitation, we introduce a biologically inspired algorithm called the Dendritic-Self-Organizing Map (DendSOM). This architecture comprises a single SOM layer that extracts patterns from distinct regions of the input space, along with a set of hit matrices—one for each SOM—that estimate the association between units and class labels. The best-matching unit for an input pattern is determined using the maximum cosine similarity rule, while class inference relies on point-wise mutual information.  

Unlike supervised approaches, DendSOM performs unsupervised feature extraction, as it does not require labels for targeted weight updates. Evaluations on benchmark datasets, including Split-MNIST and Split-CIFAR-10, demonstrate that DendSOM surpasses both classical SOMs and leading continual learning methods. Our findings suggest that integrating neuronal dynamics into SOMs could provide an effective solution to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

This research investigates the denoising of piecewise smooth graph signals characterized by varying smoothness levels across different regions of a graph. The signals may have vector-valued node attributes. We generalize the graph trend filtering framework to handle vector-valued signals by introducing a family of non-convex regularizers, which outperform existing convex approaches in signal recovery. Through an oracle inequality, we derive the statistical error rates for first-order stationary points of our non-convex method across arbitrary graph structures. Additionally, we develop an ADMM-based optimization algorithm with guaranteed convergence. Experimental validation includes denoising, support recovery, event detection, and semi-supervised classification tasks on both simulated and real-world datasets.
