Paul spin blockade (PSB) serves as a valuable tool for initializing and reading spin qubits, even at higher temperatures, though its detection can be challenging. We introduce a machine learning method designed to automatically recognize PSB through charge transport measurements. To address limited experimental PSB data, the algorithm is trained using simulated data and validated across devices. Our method is tested on a silicon field-effect transistor, achieving 96% accuracy across various test devices, demonstrating resilience to device variations. This technique is anticipated to be adaptable for use with diverse quantum dot device architectures.

This study examines fairness challenges in unsupervised outlier detection. Conventional detection algorithms, lacking explicit fairness considerations, may inadvertently perpetuate statistical biases present in the data, leading to potential social implications. To address this issue and produce equitable outlier candidates, we introduce Deep Clustering-based Fair Outlier Detection (DCFOD), which learns optimal representations for utility performance while ensuring these representations remain invariant across sensitive attribute subgroups. Recognizing the interdependent relationship between clustering and outlier identification, we employ deep clustering to reveal underlying cluster patterns and detect deviations from these structures. Simultaneously, adversarial training eliminates sensitive attribute patterns to ensure fairness. Our technical contribution includes an instance-weighted representation learning approach that strengthens the integration of deep clustering and outlier detection, where an adaptive weighting mechanism prioritizes probable inliers while reducing outlier interference. Extensive evaluations across eight datasets against 17 baseline methods demonstrate that DCFOD consistently outperforms alternatives in both detection accuracy and fairness metrics across multiple definitions of fairness.

This letter presents our initial research on applying deep neural networks (DNN) to wireless communication scenario identification in multi-path fading channels. We evaluate six channel scenarios based on the COST 207 model, achieving 100% identification accuracy at signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) above 20dB and an average accuracy of 88.4% across the 0dB to 40dB SNR range. The proposed method has been validated under realistic, fast time-varying conditions that closely emulate real-world multi-path fading channels, demonstrating its practical applicability for scenario identification.

Noisy labels pose a persistent challenge in machine learning, undermining a classifier’s generalization by causing overfitting to incorrect annotations. Current approaches to handling noisy labels primarily involve adapting the classifier during training, but these methods have limitations. First, they cannot be applied to pre-trained models without additional access to the training process. Second, simultaneously training a classifier while mitigating the adverse effects of noisy labels remains inherently difficult.  

We propose *Noisy Prediction Calibration (NPC)*, a novel post-processing framework for learning with noisy labels. By estimating a new type of transition matrix through a generative model, NPC adjusts the noisy predictions of a pre-trained classifier to better approximate true labels without requiring retraining. We demonstrate that NPC is theoretically consistent with transition-matrix-based methods while offering a more precise estimation of true labels, even when detached from classifier training.  

Additionally, NPC is versatile, applicable to any classifier trained with noisy label methods—provided predictions and training instances are available. Empirical results show that NPC consistently enhances classification performance across baseline models on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Code is available at [https://github.com/BaeHeeSun/NPC](https://github.com/BaeHeeSun/NPC).

This paper investigates shape fitting problems, $\epsilon$-coresets, and total sensitivity, with a particular focus on $(j,k)$-projective clustering problems. These include $k$-median/$k$-means clustering, $k$-line clustering, $j$-subspace approximation, and the integer $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem. We establish upper bounds for total sensitivity in these problems and leverage these bounds to construct $\epsilon$-coresets. By employing a dimension-reduction approach, we simplify prior results on total sensitivity for $k$-median/$k$-means clustering while deriving positively-weighted $\epsilon$-coresets for various $(j,k)$-projective clustering variants. Additionally, we generalize existing findings on $\epsilon$-coresets for the integer $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem from fixed dimensions to high-dimensional spaces.

The rise of big data and breakthroughs in pre-trained models (such as BERT and XLNET) have transformed the accuracy and capabilities of modern natural language processing—from text classification to generation. As a result, businesses now deploy these models through machine learning as a service (MLaaS), offering fine-tuned BERT-based models via APIs. However, these APIs come with significant security and privacy risks.  

Previous research has exposed security flaws in BERT-based APIs—particularly adversarial attacks using extracted model replicas. Yet, privacy leaks stemming from these extracted models remain underexplored. Additionally, due to the complexity of BERT-based APIs, fine-tuned models are prone to overlearning, but the extent of sensitive information they may leak is unclear.  

This study addresses these gaps by introducing a practical model extraction attack, enabling adversaries to steal a BERT-based API (the target model) with only a limited number of queries. We also propose an effective attribute inference attack capable of uncovering sensitive attributes from the training data used in BERT-based APIs. Our comprehensive experiments...

Imitation learning allows for high-fidelity, vision-based policy training in detailed, photorealistic environments. Yet, many of these approaches still depend on conventional discrete-time neural models, struggling with domain generalization due to their inability to capture causal interactions between agents and their surroundings.  

In this work, we introduce a theoretical and experimental framework for learning causal representations using continuous-time neural networks, emphasizing their advantages over discrete-time alternatives. We assess our approach through drone visual-control tasks, testing capabilities across multiple challenges—including short- and long-term navigation, as well as tracking static and dynamic objects in photorealistic settings.  

Our findings show that causal continuous-time deep models excel in robust navigation scenarios where even sophisticated recurrent models fall short. These networks effectively learn intricate causal control representations directly from raw visual data and successfully generalize across a range of tasks using imitation learning.

A key goal of artificial intelligence is to develop learning algorithms that operate on versatile computational systems like the human brain. The Neural Turing Machine (NTM) represents significant progress toward achieving such a system. This paper presents a systematic review of NTMs, beginning with an overview of machine learning, neural networks, and Turing machines through mind-maps and taxonomy. The study then examines NTMs in depth—covering their fundamental concepts, architecture, different variants, applied tasks, and comparative analyses. The discussion concludes by addressing current challenges and proposing potential future research directions.

The transferability of adversarial attacks between models—from a surrogate to a victim model—has raised significant concerns in the machine learning (ML) community. Successfully evading black-box models highlights the alarming ease with which such attacks can be executed. 

In this work, we identify a key limitation in current research on transfer attacks: attackers are often assumed to have access to the exact same training data as the victim, an unrealistic advantage. We conduct the first study examining adversarial transferability under more practical, imperfect conditions, where the attacker lacks query access to the victim model and there are varying degrees of overlap in either the training data or the classes learned by each model. This scenario is highly relevant to real-world applications, such as medical diagnosis and malware detection, where data disparities are common.

Our findings reveal that attack success rates under this new threat model do not follow expected correlations with data or class overlap and instead vary significantly depending on the dataset. This unpredictability complicates both attack strategy and defense mechanisms, underscoring the need for deeper research into model robustness and security. To address this challenge, we introduce a masked variant of Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) that accounts for class disparity, providing a more realistic framework for evaluating and mitigating adversarial transfer risks.

The rise of powerful, affordable IoT systems has made edge computing—processing data near its source—an increasingly practical solution. Beyond reducing the costs of network infrastructure, edge computing minimizes edge-cloud latency, a crucial advantage for mission-critical applications. This paper demonstrates the feasibility and evaluates the performance of image classification on IoT devices.  

We examine the impact of key factors on energy consumption, including dataset size, image resolution, algorithm type, algorithm phase, and device hardware. Our findings reveal a strong, positive linear correlation between energy consumption and three variables: model complexity, image resolution, and dataset size.  

To enable energy consumption prediction for edge-based image classification, we assess three machine learning algorithms trained on experimental data. We analyze the performance and trade-offs of linear regression, Gaussian process, and random forest models, validating our results. The random forest model proves superior, achieving R-squared scores of 0.95 and 0.79 in two separate validations, outperforming the other two methods.

Knitting offers an effective method for creating intricate three-dimensional surfaces due to the inherent adaptability of interlooped yarns and advancements in manufacturing that enable precise control over local stitch patterns. Since yarn-level modeling is impractical for large-scale knitted membranes, a two-scale homogenization approach is adopted—representing the membrane as a Kirchhoff-Love shell on the macroscale and as Euler-Bernoulli rods on the microscale. Both the shell and rod governing equations are discretized using cubic B-spline basis functions, with homogenization focusing solely on the membrane's in-plane response. Solving the nonlinear microscale problem is computationally expensive due to substantial deformations and contact constraints, making traditional online homogenization methods unfeasible. Instead, a pre-trained Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model maps macroscale deformations to macroscale stresses. During offline training, the GPR model learns from a diverse range of deformation states, generated through uniform or Sobol sampling, by solving the microscale problem repeatedly. The trained GPR model effectively captures the nonlinearities and anisotropies of the microscale, serving as an efficient material model for membrane behavior.

Classifying data with partial separability poses significant challenges, since only certain portions of the data contain meaningful information for discrimination. The remaining portions provide no useful distinction for classification tasks. Traditional approaches, which assume that the entire labeled dataset serves as an informative unit for classification, prove inadequate in such cases. As a result, conventional classification methods often fail under these conditions.  

This study introduces a framework specifically designed to classify partially separable datasets that resist standard classification techniques. The proposed algorithm employs an iterative clustering method to identify separable subgroups within the data. These detected subgroups are then leveraged in the classification process. When applied to an autism screening dataset, the method successfully distinguished children with autism from typically developing children—achieving what other methods could not.

Human decision-making behavior varies widely. In many gaming scenarios, people generally fail to maximize their payoffs, and individual players continue to exhibit inconsistent strategies even after repeated rounds of play. For example, in iterated prisoner’s dilemma games, humans often do not optimize their average rewards and instead display a wide range of cooperative behaviors. The underlying reasons for this failure to maximize outcomes remain unclear.  

This study demonstrates that the interplay between shifting choice probabilities toward previously rewarding actions and adapting to an opponent’s strategy can explain both systematic deviations from rationality and the observed diversity in decision-making. Using the prisoner’s dilemma as a key example, we examine how choice probabilities evolve when playing against opponents with varying levels of extortion or generosity.  

Even a basic model of human learning can account for an unexpectedly broad spectrum of decision behaviors. It explains why cooperation declines against extortionist strategies while increasing when facing generous opponents. Additionally, the model captures the wide distribution of individual choices among players and accurately predicts how cooperation rates shift over successive rounds. Our findings suggest that fundamental aspects of human decision dynamics arise from adaptive learning in strategic interactions.

Many deep reinforcement learning methods incorporate inductive biases that shape both the agent's goals and how it interacts with its environment. These biases can manifest as specialized domain expertise or carefully optimized hyperparameters. Typically, algorithms face a trade-off between broad applicability and specialized performance when employing such biases—stronger biases may accelerate learning, while weaker biases could produce more versatile solutions. This balance is crucial since developing appropriate biases demands significant effort, whether through acquiring domain-specific knowledge or meticulous hyperparameter tuning.  

In this study, we revisit common domain-specific elements in deep reinforcement learning that influence both the agent's objective and environmental interactions. We explore whether replacing these specialized components with adaptive alternatives (drawn from existing literature) impacts performance. While adaptive components sometimes underperformed compared to their domain-tailored counterparts, in other cases, they proved equally or even more effective.  

To assess the broader advantage of minimizing domain-specific elements, we evaluated both systems on a separate set of continuous control tasks without further tuning. As predicted, the system relying on adaptive components demonstrated superior generalization across these new problems.

This study addresses the challenge of processing both narrowband and wideband speech through a unified acoustic model (AM), referred to as a mixed-bandwidth AM. The proposed method incorporates an auxiliary input feature to supply bandwidth information to the model, with bandwidth embeddings learned simultaneously during AM training. Experimental results demonstrate that bandwidth embeddings enhance the model's ability to manage variations between narrowband and wideband speech, enabling effective mixed-bandwidth AM training. Additionally, we introduce parallel convolutional layers to better address the disparity between narrowband and wideband speech by employing separate convolution layers for each speech signal type. The optimized system achieves a 13% relative improvement in narrowband speech performance without compromising wideband speech accuracy.

We study an online learning-to-rank scenario where, in each round, an oblivious adversary presents a query along with a list of $m$ documents. The learner scores and ranks these documents, after which the adversary reveals a relevance vector. The learner then updates its ranking model using the feedback received. Importantly, the feedback is limited to the relevance levels of only the top $k$ ranked documents, where $k \ll m$. Despite this restricted feedback, the learner's performance is evaluated based on the full (unobserved) relevance vectors using a suitable ranking loss function. We propose efficient algorithms for established pointwise, pairwise, and listwise ranking losses. Additionally, we show that, with top-1 feedback, sublinear regret is impossible for any loss function calibrated with respect to NDCG. Empirical results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our algorithms effectively learn ranking functions from highly limited feedback.

The rapid growth in size of cutting-edge machine learning models stems from the proven benefits of over-parametrization. However, for deploying efficient, lightweight, and privacy-preserving on-device models on hardware with limited resources, researchers have prioritized compression techniques like pruning, quantization, and distillation. To promote standardization in neural network pruning for PyTorch, this work introduces the recently added **torch.nn.utils.prune** module—an open-source toolkit designed to simplify model compression. By offering shared pruning capabilities, it reduces implementation challenges for shrinking model size and capacity at any training stage. We explain the module's design, demonstrate its usage with practical examples, and discuss how to extend its functionality for new pruning approaches.

Analytical performance models play a crucial role in maintaining optimal service quality and deployment costs across varying conditions and workloads. Although numerous such models exist for earlier cloud computing paradigms, serverless computing still lacks reliable models capable of offering performance assurances to developers. Additionally, most serverless platforms demand manual configuration inputs from developers—settings that directly impact both performance and cost—without providing real-time feedback on these decisions.  

In prior research, we developed performance models for on-demand, scale-per-request serverless platforms like AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions. These models delivered immediate insights into service quality and deployment costs. Now, our focus shifts to creating analytical performance models for modern serverless platforms that use request concurrency and per-second request rates for autoscaling, such as Knative and Google Cloud Run. The proposed model will empower both developers and providers to forecast performance and costs under different configurations, enabling more informed decision-making.

We developed a liver cancer prediction model using machine learning algorithms, trained on epidemiological data from over 55,000 individuals spanning 2014 to the present. The model achieved its highest performance with an AUC of 0.71. Through parameter analysis, we identified key risk factors that significantly influence prediction accuracy.

Federated learning is a decentralized approach where models are trained across multiple devices while ensuring data remains on local devices. However, this framework encounters several system-level challenges, such as: (i) communication constraints due to numerous devices transmitting updates to a central server, and (ii) scalability issues arising from networks with millions of participating devices. These challenges, along with data heterogeneity and privacy concerns, make the development of an efficient and provably effective federated learning algorithm critically important—yet difficult to achieve.  

In this work, we introduce **FedPAQ**, a communication-efficient federated learning method that employs **Periodic Averaging** and **Quantization**. FedPAQ incorporates three core techniques:  
1. **Periodic averaging**—Models are updated locally on devices and synchronized with the server at regular intervals.  
2. **Partial device participation**—Only a subset of devices contributes to each training round, improving efficiency.  
3. **Quantized message-passing**—Edge devices compress their updates before transmission to reduce communication overhead.  

These strategies effectively mitigate communication and scalability challenges in federated learning. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that FedPAQ achieves near-optimal performance for both strongly convex and non-convex loss functions. Additionally, we empirically validate its ability to balance communication and computational efficiency.

Deep neural networks trained on extensive datasets can acquire transferable features that facilitate learning across multiple tasks. As features gradually shift from general to task-specific along the network depth, a key challenge in multi-task learning is effectively leveraging the inherent task relationships within parameter tensors to enhance feature transferability in task-specific layers.  

This paper introduces Multilinear Relationship Networks (MRN), a framework that uncovers task correlations through novel tensor normal priors on parameter tensors in task-specific layers of deep convolutional networks. By simultaneously learning transferable features and multilinear relationships among tasks and features, MRN mitigates the issues of negative transfer in feature layers and under-transfer in the classifier layer. Empirical results demonstrate that MRN achieves state-of-the-art performance across three multi-task learning benchmarks.

Our goal is to automate molecular design tailored to specific chemical properties. The key innovations of our work include:  

1. A streamlined approach for generating chemically valid SMILES strings, leveraging a novel context-free grammar combined with masking techniques to enforce validity.  
2. Framing molecular property optimization as a reinforcement learning task, specifically utilizing a best-of-batch policy gradient on a Transformer model.  

This method significantly reduces the computational steps required per atom compared to prior techniques, enabling the generation of larger molecules while outperforming existing state-of-the-art benchmarks. Beyond molecular design, our reinforcement learning approach—integrating a custom grammar with masking to handle non-local constraints—can be generalized to optimize graph structures under both local and non-local constraints.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have proven highly effective for natural language processing tasks. Conventional RNN approaches typically process each token in a sentence with equal weight, potentially overlooking valuable semantic structural information that could enhance language understanding. Since semantic structures like word dependency patterns aren't inherently parameterized, effectively capturing and utilizing this structural information presents a significant challenge.

To address this limitation, we introduce Multi-Channel RNN (MC-RNN), an enhanced RNN variant designed to dynamically identify and utilize local semantic structure information. The MC-RNN architecture features multiple channels, each representing distinct local dependency patterns at any given point in time. We incorporate an attention mechanism that intelligently combines these patterns at each processing step based on their semantic relevance. This framework allows for the parameterization of structural information through adaptive selection of optimal inter-channel connection patterns.

The MC-RNN demonstrates superior capability in capturing varied local structures and dependency relationships within sentences. We validate the model's performance through comprehensive testing across key NLP applications, including neural machine translation, abstractive text summarization, and language modeling. Our experimental results consistently show MC-RNN outperforming state-of-the-art systems across all evaluated tasks.

The rise of conversational assistants such as Amazon Alexa and Google Now has increased the prominence of dialogue systems, particularly in industrial applications. These systems usually include a spoken language understanding component, which consists of two key tasks: Intent Classification (IC) and Slot Labeling (SL). While these tasks are often jointly modeled to optimize performance, this approach can reduce transparency in the model.  

In this study, we first introduce a modular framework for the joint IC-SL task to improve architectural clarity. Next, we conduct an extensive evaluation of self-attention, convolutional, and recurrent models, providing a comprehensive comparison of modeling approaches for IC and SL across two datasets. Leveraging this framework, we propose a novel class of 'label-recurrent' models—despite their non-recurrent nature—by incorporating a 10-dimensional representation of label history.  

Our results demonstrate that these models are highly interpretable and achieve strong performance, reducing SL errors by over 30% compared to state-of-the-art methods on the Snips dataset. Additionally, they offer significant speed advantages, with inference times twice as fast as comparable recurrent models and training times reduced by one-third to half. These improvements make our approach particularly valuable for real-world deployments where efficiency and accuracy are critical.

Protein secondary structure serves as a critical link connecting primary sequences with three-dimensional (3D) protein conformations. Accurate prediction of eight-state protein secondary structure (PSS) plays a vital role in studying protein structure and function within bioinformatics. Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved eight-state (Q8) secondary structure prediction performance. However, theoretical limitations persist, particularly in enhancing the precision of eight-state PSS predictions.  

To address this challenge, we propose PS8-Net—a novel deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) designed to improve eight-class PSS prediction accuracy. The model processes an optimized feature matrix incorporating protein sequence and profile-based attributes. A key component of PS8-Net is the newly introduced PS8 module, which utilizes skip connections to capture long-range dependencies from deeper layers while preserving local contextual information from earlier layers, enabling effective global feature integration during prediction.  

Experimental results demonstrate that PS8-Net achieves Q8 accuracies of 76.89%, 71.94%, 76.86%, and 75.26% on the CullPdb6133, CB513, CASP10, and CASP11 benchmark datasets, respectively. This architecture effectively processes both local and global amino acid interactions to optimize class-specific prediction accuracy.

The implementation of machine learning models in critical real-world applications (such as healthcare) requires not just high accuracy but also fairness, reliability, and transparency. While Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) have long been valued in these high-stakes domains for their interpretability, they fall short in flexibility and efficiency compared to modern deep learning approaches. To bridge this gap, we introduce NODE-GAM and NODE-GA$^2$M—neural variants of GAMs that combine scalability and strong performance on large datasets while preserving interpretability, outperforming both traditional ensemble methods and complex deep learning architectures. Our experiments reveal that these models uncover meaningful data insights. Additionally, we demonstrate accuracy gains through self-supervised pre-training, an advantage inaccessible to conventional non-differentiable GAMs.

Convex optimization has seen extensive research on various optimality measures like function values, yet the problem of finding near-stationary points remains understudied. Even for deterministic settings, the optimal method (OGM-G, introduced by Kim and Fessler in 2021) was identified only recently. This work presents a systematic investigation of algorithmic approaches for locating near-stationary points in convex finite-sum problems. Key contributions include: (1) introducing a memory-efficient OGM-G variant using the performance estimation framework (Drori and Teboulle, 2014); (2) developing an accelerated SVRG method with fast convergence rates for both gradient norm minimization and function value reduction; (3) proposing an adaptive regularization technique for accelerated SVRG that eliminates dependence on unknown initial parameters while achieving near-optimal complexity. The proposed methods prioritize simplicity and practical applicability to support further research advancements.

In knowledge distillation, relying on a single, all-purpose teacher network often falls short in addressing diverse challenges. As a result, recent research has explored the use of multiple teachers for knowledge distillation. However, these approaches sometimes yield underwhelming improvements, as some less proficient teachers may impart incorrect knowledge to the student.  

To address this limitation while leveraging the strengths of multiple networks, we propose grouping them into distinct teacher and student sets. The student group comprises less mature networks that require guidance, while the teacher group consists of top-performing networks selected for their accuracy. Additionally, we introduce an online role-switching strategy, allowing high-performing student networks to advance to the teacher group at each iteration—and vice versa for underperforming teachers.  

To further refine the teacher group’s knowledge, we train it using the error samples from the student group before transferring the collective knowledge back to the students. Our method demonstrates superior performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, achieving high accuracy. We also validate its versatility across multiple backbone architectures, including ResNet, WRN, VGG, MobileNet, and ShuffleNet.

Recent studies have demonstrated that contemporary machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative solution to the classic joint source-channel coding (JSCC) challenge. Initial findings reveal superior performance compared to conventional digital methods employing separate source and channel coding, particularly for wireless image and video transmission using deep neural networks (DNNs).  

A key requirement for end-to-end training of such systems is a differentiable channel input representation, leading previous research to assume an unrestricted complex-valued transmission scheme. However, this assumption limits practical deployment in scenarios where hardware or protocol constraints restrict channel inputs to specific digital modulation constellations.  

To address this limitation, we introduce DeepJSCC-Q, an end-to-end optimized JSCC framework designed for wireless image transmission with a finite channel input alphabet. Our results demonstrate that DeepJSCC-Q achieves performance competitive with unconstrained channel input methods, particularly with higher modulation orders, and asymptotically approaches the performance of unconstrained transmission as modulation complexity increases. Crucially, DeepJSCC-Q maintains graceful degradation under varying channel conditions—an essential feature for reliable operation in mobile environments with dynamic channel quality.

Numerous learning applications involve high-dimensional regression tasks where important features belong to a limited set of (potentially overlapping) groups. While hard thresholding methods have shown remarkable efficiency for large datasets under standard sparsity constraints, they face NP-hard projection challenges when handling overlapping groups. Here, we demonstrate that submodular optimization techniques not only circumvent these NP-hard projections but also provide strong theoretical guarantees—even with highly correlated features (e.g., correlation ≥ 0.99)—a scenario existing methods struggle to address. These approaches reveal a compelling trade-off between computational efficiency and accuracy and can be extended to more complex problems like sparse overlapping group structures. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm our theoretical findings, showing that the proposed methods significantly outperform existing greedy and convex relaxation techniques in speed for group-structured sparsity learning tasks.

We introduce an efficient, scalable data-driven method for solving linear relaxations of 0-1 integer linear programs using a graph neural network. Building on the FastDOG algorithm (Abbas et al., 2022), which employs Lagrange decomposition, we develop a differentiable version that enables end-to-end training of algorithmic parameters via backpropagation through the dual update scheme. This preserves the method's theoretical guarantees, including solution feasibility and monotonic improvement of the lower bound.

To address FastDOG's susceptibility to suboptimal fixed points, we augment our graph neural network with the capability to predict non-parametric update steps that escape such points while maintaining dual feasibility. The model is trained using an unsupervised loss function on large-scale real-world datasets, demonstrating strong generalization from small to larger problem instances with only approximately 10,000 parameters.

Our learned solver outperforms both the original FastDOG algorithm in speed and solution quality, and competes favorably with commercial solvers - achieving near-optimal LP relaxation objectives while being up to 10× faster on large structured prediction problems and selected combinatorial instances.

Variance reduction is a powerful and efficient approach for speeding up stochastic optimization, whether convex or non-convex. Among current variance reduction techniques, SVRG and SAGA stand out due to their unbiased gradient estimators and widespread adoption in recent research. While numerous accelerated versions of SVRG—such as Katyusha and Acc-Prox-SVRG—have been developed, a direct acceleration method for SAGA has remained elusive. In this work, we introduce an accelerated variant of SAGA leveraging a novel Sampled Negative Momentum (SSNM), achieving state-of-the-art oracle complexity for strongly convex problems with a known strong convexity parameter. Our contribution addresses the gap in research by presenting the first directly accelerated version of SAGA.

This study introduces a platform built on Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) designed for collecting and analyzing large-scale data from social networks and IoT devices. The data is gathered through smart city applications and socially-aware aggregation services.  

The platform supports diverse urban applications—including Participatory Urbanism, Augmented Reality, and Sound-Mapping—across multiple cities. These applications generate millions of user-contributed events and social media reports, which are then integrated into the RADICAL platform.  

Additionally, we explore data analytics techniques such as sentiment analysis on combined IoT and social network data stored in an SQL database. The research also examines algorithmic optimizations and system configurations to reduce processing delays and improve response times for querying results.

We investigate interval estimation for the causal effect of a treatment T on an outcome Y in the presence of an unobserved confounder U. Applying Hölder’s inequality, we establish bounds on the confounding bias |E[Y|T=t] − E[Y|do(T=t)]|, which depend on the degree of unmeasured confounding—specifically, the strength of the relationships U→T and U→Y. These bounds are sharp when either U is independent of T or when U is independent of Y conditional on T (indicating no unobserved confounding).  

Focusing on a specific case of this bound, we consider the total variation distance between p(U) and p(U|T=t), along with the maximum deviation of E[Y|U=u,T=t] from the average E[Y|T=t] across all possible values of U. We explore calibration strategies to derive interval estimates for treatment effects and empirically evaluate the bound using synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.

Bayesian optimization faces scalability challenges in high-dimensional spaces since the acquisition step involves solving a non-convex optimization problem within the same search domain. To address this while preserving its advantages, we introduce LineBO, an algorithm that simplifies the process by breaking it down into a sequence of efficiently solvable one-dimensional sub-problems, selected iteratively. Our approach guarantees global convergence and achieves a rapid local convergence rate under strong convexity conditions. Additionally, if the objective function has an invariant subspace, our method inherently adapts to the effective dimensionality without requiring algorithmic modifications. By integrating LineBO with SafeOpt for solving sub-problems, we present the first theoretically guaranteed safe Bayesian optimization algorithm suitable for high-dimensional applications. Empirical evaluations on synthetic benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance. We also validate our method in a real-world application by optimizing the beam intensity of the Swiss Free Electron Laser across up to 40 parameters while maintaining safety constraints.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming numerous fields, including science, technology, and everyday life. One such area experiencing this shift is polymer informatics, where AI and machine learning (ML) techniques are streamlining polymer development, design, and discovery. By training surrogate models on existing polymer datasets, researchers can quickly predict material properties, enabling efficient screening of polymers tailored to specific needs. Statistical methods are also being employed to assess synthesizability and identify potential (retro)synthetic pathways for target polymers.  

A key challenge in polymer informatics stems from the vast chemical and physical diversity of polymers across different scales, prompting the exploration of data-driven solutions. Another obstacle is the limited availability of well-organized, machine-readable data that fully captures complex polymer structures, synthesis conditions, and processing details. Researchers are also tackling inverse design problems, using advanced AI algorithms to recommend polymers that meet desired performance criteria.  

As the polymer informatics field evolves and its components integrate more seamlessly, the potential for faster discoveries, improved efficiency, and increased productivity grows. This review examines emerging aspects of the polymer informatics ecosystem and its future trajectory.

HyperPrompt introduces an innovative approach to fine-tuning pre-trained language models with minimal parameter overhead by leveraging HyperNetworks to generate dynamic prompts. This architecture enables task-specific conditioning of self-attention mechanisms in Transformers through learnable hyper-prompts, produced end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. Serving as global task memories, these hyper-prompts allow queries to attend to task-relevant features while facilitating efficient cross-task information exchange. Remarkably, HyperPrompt matches the performance of robust multi-task learning baselines using just *0.14%* of additional task-conditioning parameters, optimizing both computational and parameter efficiency. Extensive evaluations on GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks demonstrate that HyperPrompt outperforms strong T5 multi-task models and parameter-efficient variants like Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++ across diverse model scales.

Our goal is to interpret a black-box classifier by generating explanations in the form: *"data X is classified as class Y because X **has** features A and B, and **lacks** feature C,"* where A, B, and C represent high-level interpretable concepts. The key challenge lies in identifying these concepts in an unsupervised manner for effective classifier explanation.  

To address this, we present a structured generative model designed to represent and uncover such explanatory concepts. We then introduce a learning framework that jointly optimizes the data distribution while maximizing the causal influence of selected concepts on the classifier’s decisions. Additionally, our approach seamlessly incorporates user-defined prior knowledge to enhance concept interpretability. Through experiments on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that our method successfully discovers meaningful binary concepts for model explanation.

Ridge regression, also known as $\ell_2$ regularization, appears frequently in statistics and machine learning. This indispensable technique is a must-know tool for every skilled data scientist. In this short exploration of ridge, I’ve gathered insights into its elegance and power—lessons my colleagues and I have uncovered through decades of applied statistical work.

A key challenge in automated audio captioning (AAC) lies in the variability of word choices for describing a given audio event or scene. This indeterminacy leads to an exponential increase in possible captions, complicating model training. To address this, we introduce TRACKE, a Transformer-based audio-captioning model incorporating keyword estimation. Our approach tackles word-selection ambiguity by jointly performing the primary AAC task alongside the auxiliary sub-task of acoustic event detection and scene classification (keyword estimation). TRACKE first identifies relevant keywords—a word set representing the input audio's events or scenes—then generates descriptive captions while leveraging these estimated keywords to minimize lexical uncertainty. Evaluations on a public AAC dataset demonstrate that TRACKE delivers state-of-the-art performance while effectively producing both accurate captions and their associated keywords.

We present DeepPSL, an enhanced version of Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL), designed to create an end-to-end trainable framework that combines reasoning and perception seamlessly. PSL expresses first-order logic through a convex graphical model—Hinge-Loss Markov Random Fields (HL-MRFs). Among probabilistic logic systems, PSL is notable for its scalability, having been successfully applied to models with over a billion ground rules.  

Our method’s core innovation lies in representing first-order logic predicates with deep neural networks, enabling approximate backpropagation through the HL-MRF to train the entire logical system end-to-end. We argue that this strategy offers a promising path for merging deep learning with reasoning, with potential applications in knowledge base learning, multi-task learning, and improving model interpretability.  

To validate DeepPSL, we test it on a zero-shot image classification task. Achieving state-of-the-art performance underscores the effectiveness and adaptability of our approach.

Most current federated learning approaches follow a two-step process each round: clients minimize a loss function to find optimal local models, followed by server-side aggregation of these models. However, this point estimation approach ignores the uncertainty inherent in client-side model estimations. Accounting for model uncertainty is particularly valuable in data-scarce scenarios, where it can enhance prediction accuracy and robustness. Additionally, uncertainty quantification aids in critical tasks like active learning and out-of-distribution detection. 

We propose a Bayesian federated learning framework where clients compute posterior predictive distributions from their local data, then explore multiple strategies for aggregating these client-specific distributions at the server. Recognizing the computational and communication challenges of handling full predictive distributions, our method distills each client's distribution into a single neural network. This distillation allows us to apply standard federated learning advancements to the Bayesian setting. Our approach differs from recent uncertainty-aware methods by avoiding restrictive assumptions while providing comprehensive uncertainty estimates.

Traditional classification methods, such as empirical risk minimization or maximum likelihood training, often experience significant performance declines when tested against adversarially crafted examples designed to exploit the classifier's decision rules. While extensive research has focused on the vulnerability of artificial neural networks (ANNs) to adversarial attacks—alongside developing robust training strategies—this paper is the first to examine the susceptibility of spiking neural networks (SNNs), or third-generation neural networks, to such threats. The investigation explores rate-based and temporal coding schemes, as well as rate-based and first-to-spike decoding approaches. Additionally, a novel robust training technique is introduced and shown to improve SNN resilience against white-box adversarial attacks.

This study introduces SDU-Net, an innovative U-Net variation employing stacked dilated convolutions for medical image segmentation. While maintaining U-Net's basic structure, SDU-Net modifies both encoder and decoder operations (where each operation handles feature maps of identical resolution). The proposed model replaces U-Net's dual standard convolutions per operation with a single standard convolution followed by multiple dilated convolutions, with all dilated outputs concatenated for subsequent processing. Comparative evaluations demonstrated SDU-Net's superior performance over vanilla U-Net, AttU-Net, and R2U-Net across four segmentation tasks, while achieving remarkable parameter efficiency – utilizing merely 40% of vanilla U-Net's parameters, 17% of AttU-Net's, and 15% of R2U-Net's.

Distributed gradient descent (DGD) is an efficient implementation of gradient descent (GD) for large datasets, where computation tasks are partitioned into smaller subtasks and distributed across multiple computing servers (CSs) for parallel execution. In conventional parallel processing, each iteration's waiting time is constrained by the slowest (straggling) servers. Recent advances in coded DGD techniques have addressed this issue by introducing redundancy in task assignments, enabling tolerance to stragglers.  

Most existing DGD schemes—whether using coded computation or coded communication—require non-straggling CSs to transmit a single message per iteration upon completing all assigned tasks. However, straggling servers, despite not finishing all tasks, often complete a portion of them. To maximize the utilization of these partial computations, we propose allowing multiple transmissions from each CS per iteration. This ensures that the aggregating server (AS) receives the highest possible number of completed computations, even from stragglers. Numerical results demonstrate that this approach substantially reduces the average iteration completion time with only a marginal increase in communication load per server.

Visual recognition tasks like object detection and keypoint estimation have gained significant traction in recent years. While most cutting-edge approaches rely on computationally intensive deep networks with large memory requirements, these resource demands create substantial challenges for deployment on low-power embedded systems. Consequently, reducing computational overhead and model size becomes critically important. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) suggests trained deep neural networks contain smaller, equally effective subnetworks. This study presents the first empirical investigation of LTH for model pruning in object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation tasks. Our findings show ImageNet-pretrained lottery tickets demonstrate poor transferability to downstream tasks. We establish practical methods for identifying high-performance lottery tickets achieving up to 80% sparsity across various sub-tasks while maintaining accuracy. Additionally, we examine how trained tickets perform across different task characteristics including object scale, occurrence frequency, and detection difficulty.

We establish rigorous bounds quantifying the $L^2$ discrepancy, in function space, between the trajectory of a finite-width network trained on finite data and its idealized counterpart under the infinite-width, infinite-data kernel dynamics. A key implication of these bounds is that the network inherently prioritizes learning the top eigenfunctions of the Neural Tangent Kernel—not just on the training set but across the entire input space. This inductive bias is solely determined by the model architecture and input distribution, independent of the target function, which need not lie within the kernel's reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Our results hold for deep architectures, including fully connected, convolutional, and residual layers. Additionally, the network width does not require polynomial scaling with sample size to achieve high-probability bounds up to a stopping time.  

The analysis leverages the low-effective-rank property of the Fisher Information Matrix at initialization, revealing that the model operates in a low effective dimension—significantly smaller than the parameter count. Our findings highlight that the theoretical implications of local capacity control, governed by the Fisher Information Matrix's low effective rank, remain insufficiently explored.

The global outbreak of pneumonia caused by a novel coronavirus has placed unprecedented strain on healthcare systems and public health measures worldwide. COVID-19 primarily targets the lungs, causing severe respiratory distress and life-threatening complications, but can also affect vital organs such as the heart, kidneys, and brain, potentially leading to long-term health consequences.  

Currently, COVID-19 detection relies on reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) testing. However, many countries facing outbreaks struggle with limited medical resources, unable to meet the overwhelming demand for genetic sequencing tests. As a result, countless patients may miss timely diagnosis and isolation, worsening the spread of the virus.  

To address this challenge, we explored deep learning techniques for analyzing and diagnosing COVID-19 through chest radiographs. We developed **Cascade-SEMEnet**, a cascaded model combining **SEME-ResNet50** and **SEME-DenseNet169**. Both networks utilize large input sizes, squeeze-and-excitation (SE) structures, and enhance data through **MoEx** and **histogram equalization**.  

Our approach involves a two-step classification:  
1. **SEME-ResNet50** first screens chest X-rays to distinguish between **normal**, **bacterial pneumonia**, and **viral pneumonia** cases.  
2. **SEME-DenseNet169** then performs fine-grained classification on viral pneumonia cases to determine whether COVID-19 is the cause.

The goal of model discovery is to autonomously identify the differential equations that govern a given dataset. While Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have demonstrated significant potential in this area, developing a fully differentiable model capable of explicitly learning the underlying equation has been challenging. Here, we introduce an approach that combines neural network-based surrogates with Sparse Bayesian Learning (SBL), resulting in a robust model discovery framework validated across multiple datasets. Additionally, we establish a link to multitask learning and leverage this insight to develop a Physics-Informed Normalizing Flow (PINF). As a proof of concept, we demonstrate how PINF can directly model densities from single-particle data. Our work not only broadens the application of PINNs to diverse neural architectures but also bridges the gap between neural network surrogates and Bayesian parameter inference.

**Objective:** This study explores the application of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to automate fetal biometric measurements—such as head circumference, biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference, and femur length—and predict gestational age and fetal weight using fetal ultrasound videos.  

**Approach:** We introduce FUVAI, a novel multi-task CNN-based spatio-temporal algorithm designed for fetal ultrasound feature extraction and standard plane detection. The method was tested on 50 freehand fetal ultrasound video scans and compared against measurements taken by five experienced sonographers at two separate time points (minimum two-week interval). Intra- and inter-observer variability were assessed.  

**Main Results:** Automated fetal biometric measurements generated by FUVAI demonstrated strong agreement with those made by expert sonographers. The observed discrepancies fell within the range of inter- and intra-observer variability. Statistical analysis confirmed no significant differences between FUVAI's outputs and the measurements of any individual sonographer.  

**Significance:** FUVAI shows promise in supporting clinical sonographers by recommending optimal measurement frames and providing automated fetal biometric assessments. Additionally, FUVAI performs these tasks in a fraction of the time compared to manual methods.

Federated Learning enables model training on decentralized data across multiple devices while preserving data privacy. A critical challenge for its broader adoption is handling data heterogeneity—specifically non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. This paper introduces an innovative Divide-and-Conquer training approach that enhances the applicability of the widely used FedAvg aggregation algorithm by addressing its limitations in non-IID settings.  

We present a novel technique leveraging Cosine-distance-based Weight Divergence to identify the optimal splitting point in a Deep Learning network. This method partitions the model into class-agnostic initial layers and class-specific deeper layers, facilitating effective Divide-and-Conquer training. Our results demonstrate that this approach achieves model accuracy comparable to—and in some cases surpassing—state-of-the-art aggregation algorithms like FedProx and FedMA. Additionally, we highlight scenarios where this methodology delivers computational and bandwidth efficiency gains.

Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) are widely used in machine learning, with frameworks like LightGBM and Scikit-Learn offering efficient implementations. However, many existing approaches generate trees offline and rely on greedy optimization. In this work, we investigate methods for transforming traditional GBDT models into neural network architectures with minimal performance degradation. By doing so, we enable online updates to decision splits and extend the framework to treat split point optimization as a neural architecture search problem. We also present theoretical learning bounds for the proposed neural network formulation.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) stand among the most prominent techniques in machine learning, yet their black-box nature limits interpretability in predictive tasks. To address this, neural additive models (NAMs) have emerged as a solution that preserves high predictive accuracy while offering greater transparency. This paper introduces a novel NAM-based approach designed specifically for multivariate nowcasting (NC) problems, a key application area in machine learning. Since NC relies on multivariate time-series data, interpretability must extend to each input value across distinct variables and timestamps. Leveraging generalized additive models, our proposed NAM-NC framework effectively quantifies the contribution of every input value to predictions across multiple variables and time steps. Through experiments—including a toy example and two real-world datasets—we demonstrate that NAM-NC delivers prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art neural networks while providing clear explanations of input importance. Additionally, we explore parameter-sharing strategies within NAM-NC to reduce model complexity and show that its hard-tied feature network maintains strong performance while extracting meaningful interpretations.

We introduce a novel approach for identifying anomalies in time series data—a critical task across diverse fields, including autonomous vehicles, finance, marketing, medical diagnostics, and epidemiology. Our method leverages self-supervised deep learning, a technique that has been pivotal in advancing anomaly detection in image data, where robust image transformations are readily available. Unlike images, however, time series lack such predefined transformations. To bridge this gap, we propose Local Neural Transformations (LNT), a data-driven technique that learns localized transformations directly from time series signals. LNT generates anomaly scores at each time step, enabling precise anomaly detection within sequences. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our training objective is better suited for transformation learning compared to prior deep anomaly detection (AD) methods. Empirical results show that LNT effectively identifies anomalies in speech segments from the LibriSpeech dataset and outperforms existing techniques in detecting disruptions in cyber-physical systems. Additionally, visualizations of the learned transformations provide valuable insights into the patterns LNT captures.

Intelligent transportation systems (ITS) rely on real-time traffic data collection to monitor and manage road conditions effectively. Key information, such as vehicle types (e.g., cars, trucks, buses), is gathered from major roads and highways to optimize operations. Conventional methods, including GPS-based tracking or camera networks, often compromise driver privacy or incur high installation expenses. To address these challenges, this paper presents SenseMag, a cost-efficient solution that identifies vehicle types using non-invasive magnetic sensors placed along straight road segments.  

SenseMag processes raw magnetic signals by eliminating noise and segmenting data based on precise timestamps of a vehicle’s arrival and departure at each sensor node. A hierarchical recognition model is then employed—first estimating speed, then determining vehicle length using the derived speed, sampling intervals, and sensor spacing. By combining vehicle length with temporal and spectral signal features, SenseMag accurately classifies vehicle types. Semi-automated learning techniques optimize filter design, feature extraction, and hyper-parameter selection.  

Real-world testing on highways in Shenzhen, China, demonstrates that SenseMag surpasses existing approaches in accuracy and efficiency.

Training deep learning models on large datasets demands significant time and computational resources, making it highly desirable to develop small synthetic datasets capable of sufficiently training these models. Recent studies have explored dataset condensation techniques for images using intricate bi-level optimization. For example, dataset condensation (DC) aligns network gradients between large real datasets and small synthetic ones, while optimizing network weights across multiple steps in each outer iteration.  

However, current approaches face inherent limitations: (1) they struggle with discrete graph-structured data, and (2) the condensation process becomes computationally expensive due to nested optimization loops. To address these challenges, we investigate an efficient dataset condensation method specifically designed for graph datasets. By modeling the discrete graph structure as a probabilistic model, we overcome structural constraints. Additionally, we introduce a one-step gradient matching scheme that eliminates the need for iterative weight updates, significantly reducing computational overhead.  

Theoretical analysis confirms that this approach produces synthetic graphs that reduce classification loss on real graphs. Extensive experiments across multiple graph datasets validate the method's effectiveness and efficiency. Notably, our approach successfully minimizes the dataset size while maintaining performance.

Although fine-grained recognition has gained growing attention in our field, the term "fine-grained" has yet to receive a clear, formal definition. Drawing on clustering theory, this work establishes a framework for quantifying dataset granularity. We contend that granularity should not be determined solely by data samples and their labels, but also by the selected distance function. Introducing an axiomatic framework, we outline essential properties for any granularity measure and present examples of measures that meet these criteria.

Through experiments on hierarchically labeled datasets of varying granularity, we evaluate each proposed measure. Applying our measurement to commonly used datasets reveals an unexpected trend: some datasets generally classified as fine-grained contain sizable subsets that are significantly more coarse-grained than datasets typically deemed coarse-grained. 

Furthermore, we examine the relationship between dataset granularity and various factors, demonstrating that fine-grained datasets pose greater challenges across multiple dimensions. Specifically, they prove harder to learn from, less amenable to transfer learning, more difficult for few-shot learning, and more susceptible to adversarial attacks.

This work investigates the approximation capabilities of ReLU neural networks with weight norm constraints. We establish both upper and lower bounds on the approximation error for smooth function classes using these constrained networks. The lower bound is obtained through an analysis of neural network Rademacher complexity, a result that holds broader significance beyond this study.  

These approximation results are then applied to analyze convergence in two contexts: regression with norm-constrained neural networks and distribution estimation via GANs. Notably, we derive convergence rates for over-parameterized networks. Additionally, we demonstrate that GANs can achieve optimal learning rates for probability distributions when the discriminator is implemented as an appropriately norm-constrained neural network.

Feature Learning seeks to automatically extract meaningful patterns and information from datasets. As the foundation of modern deep learning techniques, its practical impact has been well-demonstrated across numerous applications. However, a clear theoretical framework explaining various feature learning approaches remains absent. This study establishes a theoretical basis for feature learning while identifying conditions under which unsupervised feature extraction is possible. Additionally, we introduce evaluation methods for assessing feature quality using rate-distortion theory and its extended applications.

Deep learning models (DLMs) represent cutting-edge approaches for speech recognition, yet training high-quality DLMs can be resource-intensive, particularly for production-scale models and datasets. While multiple parallel training algorithms exist to enhance efficiency, selecting the optimal method remains challenging due to limited systematic and impartial comparisons. This study addresses this gap by evaluating four widely used parallel training techniques in speech recognition: asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD), blockwise model-update filtering (BMUF), bulk synchronous parallel (BSP), and elastic averaging stochastic gradient descent (EASGD). Our experiments on the 1000-hour LibriSpeech dataset employ both feed-forward deep neural networks (DNNs) and convolutional long short-term memory DNNs (CLDNNs). The findings suggest BMUF as the preferred method for acoustic model training, demonstrating stability, strong GPU scalability, reproducible outcomes, and performance that often surpasses single-GPU SGD. ASGD may serve as an alternative in certain scenarios.

Design optimization methods are commonly applied early in the design process to investigate potential solutions. In such scenarios, illumination algorithms like MAP-Elites offer advantages over traditional optimization approaches by generating diverse, high-quality solutions in a single run rather than delivering only a single near-optimal result. However, these algorithms currently demand extensive function evaluations, restricting their practical use.  

This paper presents Surrogate-Assisted Illumination (SAIL), a novel illumination algorithm that combines surrogate modeling to map the design space according to user-specified features while significantly reducing fitness evaluations. In a 2D airfoil optimization problem, SAIL generates hundreds of diverse, high-performing designs with dramatically fewer evaluations compared to MAP-Elites or CMA-ES. Additionally, we show that SAIL can effectively map high-performing solutions in complex 3D aerodynamic tasks using precise flow simulations. By enabling data-efficient design exploration, SAIL helps designers uncover possibilities beyond mere optimality, encouraging broader exploration beyond conventional objective-driven optimization.

Network data is playing a growing role in quantitative, evidence-based policy research. These datasets capture intricate relationships and dependencies, offering substantial potential for informing public policy—yet their complexity also presents challenges for extracting actionable insights. This necessitates the development of innovative analytical techniques.  

In this report, we outline a research agenda focused on key methodological challenges, the resolution of which could drive progress across diverse policy domains. We examine recent advances in deep learning for network data, demonstrating their applicability to these challenges. Special attention is given to deep generative models, which can produce synthetic yet realistic networks for microsimulation and agent-based modeling—tools critical for addressing pressing policy questions.  

Building on these developments, we introduce a novel generative framework designed for large-scale social contact networks often utilized in epidemiological studies. To provide perspective, we contrast neural network-based approaches with traditional methods like Exponential Random Graph Models. Finally, we highlight remaining open challenges where further research is essential.

As deep learning captures increasing interest in the research community for predicting and controlling real physical systems, the need to learn meaningful representations has become more critical than ever. Ensuring that these deep learning representations align with fundamental physics is essential. While incorporating prior knowledge into learning can help achieve this when working with discrete data, not all discretization methods preserve the underlying physical structures.  

In this paper, we present **Symplectic Momentum Neural Networks (SyMo)**, a class of models derived from a discrete mechanics formulation for non-separable mechanical systems. By integrating this framework, SyMo inherently preserves key geometric structures such as momentum and symplecticity while enabling learning from limited datasets. Notably, SyMo can learn system dynamics using only pose data as training input.  

We further enhance SyMo by incorporating variational integrators into the learning process, developing an implicit root-finding layer that leads to **End-to-End Symplectic Momentum Neural Networks (E2E-SyMo)**. Experimental results on the pendulum and cartpole systems demonstrate that this approach not only improves data efficiency but also preserves the symplectic structure, resulting in superior long-term behavior compared to conventional methods.

Our study presents novel insights into the advantages of depth in feed-forward neural networks, demonstrating that deeper architectures can outperform significantly wider shallow networks in approximating certain fundamental functions. Specifically, we establish improved approximation capabilities for deeper networks in modeling indicators of geometric shapes (such as balls and ellipses), radial functions based on the L1 norm, and general smooth nonlinear functions. These theoretical findings are supported by experimental evidence showing that depth-enhanced networks learn the indicator function of a unit ball more effectively than their wider shallow counterparts.
