Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) plays a critical role in modern video surveillance systems. However, extracting distinctive features for Re-ID remains difficult because of significant image space variations, such as shifting human poses, lighting conditions, and viewpoints. This paper introduces HAVANA, a scalable and lightweight HierArchical and VAriation-Normalized Autoencoder designed to learn intra-class variation-resistant features. Unlike existing generative methods that require extensive supervised signals to reduce variations, HAVANA mitigates these variations through a Variation-Normalized Autoencoder trained without extra supervision. We also propose a novel Jensen-Shannon triplet loss for contrastive distribution learning in Re-ID. Additionally, we introduce the Hierarchical Variation Distiller, a hierarchical VAE that decomposes latent representations to explicitly model variations. HAVANA represents the first VAE-based framework for person Re-ID to our knowledge.

Deep machine learning has proven effective for the automated delineation of tumor regions in intraoperative neuronavigation, utilizing active IR-mapping with cold testing. This method leverages a matrix IR-imager to capture the spatiotemporal distribution of surface temperature patterns, which reflect local cerebral blood flow dynamics. Key benefits include its non-invasive nature, absence of health risks for patients and medical personnel, low costs for implementation and operation, and rapid, straightforward application. However, conventional IR-diagnostic techniques have a significant limitation: reliance on a diagnostician to identify tumor boundaries introduces substantial uncertainty, potentially leading to uncontrolled diagnostic errors. This study shows that integrating deep learning algorithms effectively addresses this limitation.

Transfer learning offers an effective way to build predictive models by combining simulation and experimental data within a unified framework. The process begins with training a neural network on extensive simulation data, followed by fine-tuning it using limited experimental datasets to enhance real-world accuracy. This approach has already proven successful in developing models for Omega and NIF inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments, outperforming simulation-only predictions.  

In this study, we implement a transfer learning-guided hypothetical ICF campaign aimed at maximizing experimental neutron yield through Bayesian optimization. The model achieves yields within 5% of the theoretical maximum in a moderate design space after fewer than 20 experiments. Additionally, we show that this technique outperforms conventional model calibration methods in ICF design efficiency. By leveraging transfer learning, this approach could enable more reliable optimization of experimental performance, even when accounting for uncertainties.

Deep learning (DL) has emerged as the leading approach for numerous medical image segmentation tasks. However, it relies heavily on large volumes of manually annotated training data, which can be impractical to acquire in certain scenarios. Furthermore, DL models often struggle to generalize effectively to unseen data. In contrast, multi-atlas segmentation (MAS) delivers strong performance with limited training data while demonstrating superior generalizability. A hybrid approach that combines the precision of DL with the robustness of MAS is highly desirable, particularly in segmentation tasks where obtaining expert annotations is challenging.  

Previous research has primarily focused on enhancing individual components of MAS using DL techniques, rather than optimizing overall segmentation accuracy through an end-to-end framework. Only one prior study has investigated this concept, and it was limited to binary segmentation of 2D images—leaving its effectiveness for multi-class 3D segmentation uncertain.  

To address this gap, we introduce **Deep Label Fusion (DLF)**, a 3D end-to-end hybrid pipeline that leverages the complementary strengths of MAS and DL. Our experimental results show that DLF outperforms traditional label fusion techniques and U-Net, a standard DL-based approach, particularly in segmenting the medial temporal lobe.

The Jacobian matrix (or gradient in single-output networks) plays a fundamental role in key aspects of neural networks, including the function landscape, stationary points, (local) Lipschitz continuity, and adversarial robustness. This paper introduces RecurJac, a recursive method for calculating both upper and lower bounds on each entry of a neural network's input Jacobian matrix, applicable to a broad class of activation functions. As an important application, our approach efficiently computes (local) Lipschitz constants, which are essential for verifying network robustness and ensuring GAN training stability. Experimental results demonstrate that our method yields tighter (local) Lipschitz bounds compared to prior techniques, leading to more accurate robustness verification. With polynomial-time complexity, RecurJac remains computationally tractable even for moderately large networks. Furthermore, we leverage these Jacobian bounds to analyze the network's landscape, such as identifying the presence of stationary points within local regions. Source code is available at \url{http://github.com/huanzhang12/RecurJac-Jacobian-bounds}.

Automating the digitization of paper maps presents a major academic and industrial challenge. Currently, semantic segmentation—a key step in map digitization—depends heavily on time-consuming manual visual interpretation. This research focuses on urban planning maps as a case study, exploring the potential of U-shaped fully convolutional networks for end-to-end map semantic segmentation. Tests conducted in Tokyo’s Shibuya district yielded a Jaccard similarity coefficient of 93.63% and an overall accuracy of 99.36%. When implemented using GPGPU and cuDNN, processing the entire Shibuya area took under three minutes. These findings suggest the proposed method offers an accurate and efficient solution for semantic segmentation in urban planning maps.

This study approaches the creation of personalized fonts as an image style transfer challenge. The primary objective is to develop a neural network architecture capable of effectively extracting and recombining character content and stylistic elements. Such a framework enables the synthesis of complete font sets using only minimal character samples.  

The research integrates multiple deep learning architectures—including Convolutional Neural Networks, Multi-layer Perceptrons, and Residual Networks—to identify the optimal model for capturing distinctive font features. Evaluation using Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) metrics demonstrates that the generated characters closely approximate real-world typefaces.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a widely used technique for sampling from high-dimensional distributions in statistics and machine learning. Known for its efficiency, HMC's second-order "leapfrog" implementation has long been hypothesized to require only $d^{1/4}$ gradient evaluations. In this work, we demonstrate that this conjecture holds when sampling from strongly log-concave target distributions that meet a weak third-order regularity condition tied to the input data.  

Our regularity assumption is less stringent than the Lipschitz Hessian condition, enabling us to establish faster convergence rates for a broader class of distributions than traditional Lipschitz Hessian analysis permits. Notably, this includes posterior distributions in Bayesian logistic regression where the data exhibits an "incoherence" property. Our findings improve upon the best-known bounds for strongly log-concave distributions, which typically scale as $d^{1/2}$ gradient evaluations with dimension.  

Additionally, empirical results on synthetic data indicate that when our regularity condition is met, leapfrog HMC outperforms alternative methods—both in accuracy and in the number of gradient evaluations needed.

Recent advances in medical image Super-Resolution have leveraged deep learning approaches like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to produce perceptually convincing high-resolution reconstructions from single low-resolution inputs. However, these methods face limitations in generalizing across varying scale factors, requiring dedicated neural networks for each integer scaling ratio—a computationally intensive solution with high memory and energy demands. A breakthrough solution using meta-learning with a Weight Prediction Network has been proposed to enable Super-Resolution at arbitrary scales with a single network. Building on this, we introduce a new architecture that integrates this scalable approach with SRGAN, a leading GAN-based framework, to deliver high-quality, flexible Super-Resolution for medical imaging.  

Testing our model on the BraTS dataset for brain tumor segmentation, we achieve up to 20% higher Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) scores compared to conventional interpolation techniques while maintaining strong generalization on MRI scans. Crucially, our method maintains consistent performance across different scaling factors and matches the results of cutting-edge approaches like EDSR—despite being 50 times more compact. Merging efficiency, accuracy, and adaptability, this framework has the potential to serve as a new benchmark for flexible, high-fidelity medical image enhancement.

The orthogonal Haar scattering transform is constructed as a deep neural network using a layered combination of additions, subtractions, and absolute value operations applied to coefficient pairs. This framework offers a mathematically tractable approach to unsupervised deep learning. The transform performs nonlinear contractions optimized for classification through an efficient unsupervised pair matching algorithm with polynomial-time complexity.  

For graph-structured data, the structured Haar scattering produces permutation-invariant representations by analyzing connected groups of points within the graph. In cases where the graph’s connectivity is unknown, unsupervised Haar pair learning can effectively estimate connected dyadic point groups in a statistically consistent manner. Empirical results demonstrate the method’s classification performance across image datasets—whether defined on regular grids or graphs—with both known and unknown connectivity structures.

Normalization techniques are fundamental components of deep learning systems. They enhance training speed and stability while reducing reliance on carefully adjusted learning rate schedules. Although batch normalization (BN) remains one of the most widely adopted methods, its performance suffers when applied to multi-modal data distributions. To address this limitation, we introduce a more adaptable solution: by expanding normalization beyond a single mean and variance, our approach dynamically identifies data patterns and normalizes related samples together. Experimental results show that our method surpasses both BN and other common normalization approaches across various benchmarks, including single- and multi-task datasets.

Variable screening serves as an efficient dimensionality reduction approach that facilitates feature selection in high-dimensional datasets. Functioning as an initial filtering step, it identifies a manageable subset of potential variables for subsequent refinement through more sophisticated feature selection techniques to derive the final predictive model. The effectiveness of variable screening hinges on two key factors: computational speed and the capacity to significantly reduce variable count while retaining meaningful predictors.  

In scenarios where the feature dimension (p) far exceeds sample size (n), variable screening assumes critical importance for two reasons: 1) It necessitates faster feature selection algorithms, and 2) Traditional conditions ensuring selection consistency may no longer apply. This paper examines a specific category of linear screening methods and develops a theoretical framework for their consistency. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Restricted Diagonally Dominant (RDD) condition serves as both necessary and sufficient for achieving strong screening consistency.  

As practical illustrations, we establish that two screening methods—Sure Independence Screening (SIS) and High-Dimensional Ordinary Least Squares Projection (HOLP)—exhibit strong screening consistency (with certain additional constraints) with high probability under random designs when \( n > O((\rho s + \sigma/\tau)^2 \log p) \). Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the RDD condition and the irrepresentable condition, while also discussing inherent limitations of SIS.

Optimizing doubly stochastic objective functions is necessary for approximate inference in complex probabilistic models, including deep Gaussian processes. These objectives involve randomness from two sources: data subsampling through mini-batches and Monte Carlo approximations of expectations. High gradient variance makes stochastic optimization challenging, leading to slow convergence. While control variates can lower variance, existing methods fail to account for the interaction between mini-batch and sampling stochasticity, limiting their effectiveness. We introduce a novel solution where a recognition network efficiently estimates the optimal control variate per mini-batch without extra model gradient computations. The performance and characteristics of this approach are demonstrated through experiments on logistic regression and deep Gaussian processes.

**Objectives:** Introduce a new deep learning approach for skull stripping in MRI that operates directly on k-space data.  

**Materials and Methods:** A deep learning model was trained using 36,900 MRI slices from two institutional datasets, processing complex raw k-space data. The ground truth for skull stripping was derived from HD-BET (Brain Extraction Tool) in the image domain.  

**Results:** Performance closely matched the ground truth, achieving DICE scores of 92–98% and Hausdorff distances below 5.5 mm. Accuracy was highest above the eye region (DICE up to 99%) but decreased near and below the eyes, occasionally producing blurred outputs. The method tended to smooth edges at skull boundaries, with binary masks generated through thresholding.  

**Conclusion:** This proof-of-concept demonstrates the viability of k-space-based skull stripping while retaining phase information. Future work should explore expanded applications of k-space analysis for innovative imaging workflows.

Traditional recommendation systems have long grappled with two persistent challenges—data sparsity and cold-start issues—which have driven the rise and advancement of Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR). The central premise of CDR is to utilize data from auxiliary domains to mitigate these problems in a target domain. Over the past decade, significant research efforts have been dedicated to cross-domain recommendation. More recently, advancements in deep learning and neural networks have spurred the development of numerous novel methods. Despite this progress, systematic reviews of CDR remain scarce, particularly those examining state-of-the-art techniques, the recommendation scenarios they apply to, and the specific tasks they address.  

In this survey, we first present a two-tiered taxonomy for cross-domain recommendation, categorizing distinct recommendation scenarios and tasks. Next, we methodically outline and analyze existing CDR approaches across these scenarios. Additionally, we compile a comprehensive list of commonly used datasets in the field. Finally, we conclude by highlighting several promising research directions for future exploration in CDR.

While rule-based attribution methods effectively provide local explanations for Deep Neural Networks, explaining modern and diverse architectures presents new challenges in generating reliable interpretations. Traditional rule sets may not adequately address novel network structures. To address this, network canonization has emerged as an elegant solution. This approach capitalizes on the implementation-specific nature of rule-based attributions, transforming a model into a functionally equivalent alternative design where established attribution rules can be seamlessly applied. Although the concept of canonization and its benefits have so far been assessed qualitatively, this work quantitatively demonstrates its advantages for rule-based attributions on VGG-16 and ResNet18 models with BatchNorm layers, advancing current best practices for ensuring trustworthy neural network explanations.

Although adversarial training and its variants are among the most effective defense mechanisms against adversarial attacks, their computationally intensive training process presents significant scalability challenges for large datasets such as ImageNet. Recent efforts to accelerate adversarial training have focused on replacing multi-step attacks (e.g., PGD) with computationally efficient single-step methods (e.g., FGSM). However, these approaches are prone to catastrophic overfitting—a sudden collapse in robustness during training where PGD attack accuracy plummets to near zero.  

This work investigates catastrophic overfitting through the lens of training instances, revealing its instance-dependent nature. We demonstrate that examples with larger gradient norms are more susceptible to triggering this breakdown in robustness. Building on this insight, we introduce Adversarial Training with Adaptive Step size (ATAS), a simple yet effective method that dynamically adjusts step sizes for individual instances, scaling inversely with their gradient norms. Theoretical analysis confirms that ATAS achieves faster convergence compared to traditional non-adaptive approaches. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet demonstrate that ATAS reliably prevents catastrophic overfitting while improving robust accuracy across varying adversarial attack budgets.

Importance-weighting is a widely used and extensively studied method for addressing sample selection bias and covariate shift. It offers advantages such as unbiasedness, consistency, and computational efficiency. However, weighting can also negatively impact estimator performance. This study demonstrates empirically that the sampling distribution of an importance-weighted estimator may become skewed. Under sample selection bias conditions, particularly with limited sample sizes, the importance-weighted risk estimator tends to overestimate risk for datasets within the main body of the distribution while producing significant underestimates for datasets in the tail regions. These systematic biases in risk estimation result in suboptimal choices of regularization parameters when applied in importance-weighted validation scenarios.

Building trustworthy prediction sets remains a challenge for neural network applications: While theoretical limitations prevent distribution-free conditional coverage, traditional split-conformal methods lose their coverage guarantees when domain shifts break exchangeability assumptions. Faced with these limitations, we introduce and evaluate a data-driven approach that achieves practical conditional coverage by computing individualized quantile thresholds for each test point and label. Our method leverages reliability signals from both KNN-based approximations across the training data and constrained sampling of the calibration set. Through experiments in protein secondary structure prediction, grammatical error detection, sentiment analysis, and fact verification—spanning supervised sequence labeling, zero-shot feature detection, constrained document classification, and retrieval-classification tasks—we reveal significant (and otherwise undetectable) under-coverage in standard split-conformal methods that only ensure marginal coverage. These results hold across class-imbalanced distributions and domain shift scenarios, demonstrating the necessity of incorporating distance metrics and constraint awareness.

Cross-validation (CV) is a method for estimating the generalization error of prediction models. In pipeline modeling—where multiple sequential steps are involved—best practices suggest executing the entire pipeline during each CV iteration to simulate its application on an independent test set. While this approach is theoretically valid, it can become computationally intensive if the pipeline includes costly operations like missing value imputation.  

It is widely accepted that unsupervised variable selection (independent of the outcome) can precede CV without introducing bias, but opinions diverge regarding unsupervised imputation of missing values. We investigated whether performing unsupervised imputation before CV introduces bias in generalization error estimates, leads to suboptimal tuning parameter selection, and ultimately harms downstream model performance. Our findings reveal that while early imputation may introduce some optimistic bias, the reduced variance compared to imputing within each CV fold results in a lower overall root mean squared error for estimating true external R-squared. Additionally, models tuned via CV with pre-imputation versus within-fold imputation show negligible differences in external performance.

The study presented an approximate formulation where the inner objective is addressed iteratively, along with convergence guarantees to the exact problem under specific conditions. Images captured in rainy conditions often suffer from reduced visibility, which can negatively impact the performance of computer vision systems. Rainy scenes can generally be divided into two categories: moderate rain and heavy rain. Moderate rain primarily consists of visible rain streaks, while heavy rain involves both rain streaks and a veiling effect similar to haze. Although existing methods perform well in handling these scenarios separately, there remains a lack of a unified framework capable of effectively addressing both heavy and moderate rain conditions.  

This paper presents a hierarchical multi-direction representation network utilizing the contourlet transform (CT) to simultaneously address moderate and heavy rain scenarios. The CT decomposes images into multi-direction subbands (MS) and semantic subbands (SS). First, the multi-orientation property of the CT is leveraged to extract rain streak information into the MS. Next, a hierarchical architecture is introduced to reconstruct background details, including lost semantic content and the veiling effect in the SS. Finally, we propose a multi-level subband discriminator with a feedback error map to optimize all subbands effectively.  

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework designed to handle both heavy and moderate rain scenarios efficiently.

Event detection plays a vital role in enabling real-time decisions within graph analytics applications. While deep learning for graphs has advanced significantly, identifying events in dynamic graphs remains particularly challenging for current architectures. Real-world events typically manifest as abrupt anomalies in a graph’s typical behavior, yet existing dynamic node embedding methods fail to capture these graph-level event-related dynamics.  

We introduce DyGED, an innovative yet simple deep learning model designed for event detection in dynamic graphs. DyGED identifies relationships between macro-level graph dynamics—represented as sequences of graph-level embeddings—and labeled events. Additionally, our approach incorporates structural and temporal self-attention mechanisms to effectively weigh node and time importance based on application needs.  

Through extensive evaluation across multiple datasets, DyGED achieves up to 8.5% higher accuracy in event detection compared to competing solutions while maintaining superior scalability. We also present case studies highlighting the model's key characteristics.

For lossy image compression, we introduce a neural-based system that learns a nonlinear decoder to reconstruct images from quantized representations. The framework pairs two recurrent networks that collaboratively reconstruct target image patches by leveraging complementary spatial context, connected through gradient signals.  

This dual-agent architecture extends previous work on iterative refinement for RNN-based decoding, which demonstrated superior image reconstruction compared to conventional techniques. Compatible with any encoder—neural or non-neural—our method iteratively minimizes patch reconstruction error over a fixed number of steps.  

Experiments with various RNN memory cells, both with and without future context, show our model consistently produces images with lower distortion and better perceptual quality than competing methods. On the Kodak Lossless True Color Image Suite, our system achieves gains of up to **1.64 dB** over JPEG, **1.46 dB** over JPEG 2000, **1.34 dB** over the Google neural baseline, **0.36 dB** over E2E (a modern neural competitor), and **0.37 dB** over a single iterative neural decoder.

Advances in deep learning for computer vision have driven significant progress in super-resolution image reconstruction. Yet studies indicate that inadequate feature extraction by neural networks can degrade the quality of reconstructed images, while excessive smoothing often produces artificial-looking results. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel self-calibrated convolutional generative adversarial network. The generator employs a dual-stage architecture for feature extraction and image reconstruction. Using a four-part self-calibrated convolution mechanism, our approach achieves both expanded receptive fields and captures long-range spatial and inter-channel relationships. Comprehensive evaluations on Set5, Set14, and BSD100 datasets using SSIM metrics demonstrate the network's superior performance.

Adversarial attacks have now extended to speaker recognition (SR) systems, yet current evaluations of these attacks vary widely in terms of SR models, recognition tasks, and datasets. Additionally, many defenses adapted from computer vision remain untested against adaptive attacks. This leaves a significant gap in understanding the real-world effectiveness and limitations of adversarial attacks and defenses in SR. More robust defensive strategies are also needed to enhance the security of these systems.  

To address this challenge, we introduce SEC4SR—the first comprehensive platform for systematically evaluating adversarial attacks and defenses in SR. SEC4SR integrates 4 white-box and 2 black-box attacks, along with 24 defenses (including novel feature-level transformations we developed). It also supports adaptive attack techniques. Leveraging SEC4SR, we conducted the most extensive empirical study to date on SR adversarial attacks and defenses, assessing 23 defenses, 15 attacks, and 4 attack settings.  

Our research yields several key insights that could guide future work:  
1) While all transformations slightly reduce accuracy on benign samples, their effectiveness varies across different attacks.  
2) Most transformations lose effectiveness when facing adaptive attacks, though some actually perform better.  
3) Combining certain transformations with adversarial training can produce stronger defenses.  

These findings highlight the nuanced performance of existing methods and point to promising directions for improving SR system security.

Natural gradient descent incorporates partial second-order information by preconditioning gradient updates with the Fisher information matrix of the underlying statistical model. While some prominent studies have promoted the empirical Fisher as an approximation—linking it to second-order approximations and optimization techniques like Adam—we challenge this perspective. Our analysis demonstrates that, unlike the true Fisher, the empirical Fisher does not reliably provide second-order information. We also show that the conditions required for the empirical Fisher to approximate either the Fisher or the Hessian are seldom achieved in practical scenarios. Moreover, even in simple optimization tasks, the inherent shortcomings of the empirical Fisher can lead to problematic outcomes.

Redundancy in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is well-documented, allowing the removal of less critical filters from convolutional layers to streamline the network with minimal performance degradation. Leveraging the linear and combinative nature of convolution, we aim to bring selected filters increasingly closer until they become identical, facilitating network compression. 

To achieve this, we introduce Centripetal SGD (C-SGD), an innovative optimization technique designed to merge multiple filters into a single point within the parameter hyperspace. Upon training completion, removing these redundant filters trims the network without any performance penalty, eliminating the need for finetuning. This approach partially addresses the challenge of constrained filter pruning in structurally complex CNNs, where certain layers must be pruned in tandem with others.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet validate the efficacy of C-SGD-based filter pruning. Additionally, we provide empirical support for the hypothesis that neural network redundancy aids training convergence by demonstrating that a redundant CNN trained with C-SGD surpasses a conventionally trained network of equivalent width.

Machine learning workflows frequently depend on optimization methods to handle discrete decisions (such as sorting, selecting nearest neighbors, or finding shortest paths). While these discrete operations are computationally straightforward, they disrupt gradient flow in backpropagation. To broaden the range of learning problems solvable end-to-end, we introduce a method for converting optimizers into differentiable, non-constant operations.  

Our solution employs stochastically perturbed optimizers, compatible with standard solvers. These modified operations allow efficient gradient computation, with smoothness controlled by adjusting noise intensity. Furthermore, we link this framework to structured prediction loss functions, providing theoretical guarantees for learning applications. Experimental results across multiple tasks validate the effectiveness of our approach.

We introduce **Layer-Sequential Unit-Variance (LSUV) initialization**, a straightforward yet effective approach for weight initialization in deep neural networks. The method involves two key steps:  

1. **Pre-initialization**: Assign orthonormal matrices to the weights of each convolutional or inner-product layer.  
2. **Variance normalization**: Sequentially adjust each layer’s output variance to one, progressing from the first to the final layer.  

Experiments with various activation functions (maxout, ReLU-family, tanh) demonstrate that LSUV initialization enables efficient training of very deep networks, offering two key advantages:  

- **Comparable or superior test accuracy** relative to standard initialization techniques.  
- **Training speed on par with specialized methods** like FitNets (Romero et al., 2015) and Highway Networks (Srivastava et al., 2015), designed explicitly for deep architectures.  

Evaluated across GoogLeNet, CaffeNet, FitNets, and Residual Networks, LSUV achieves **state-of-the-art (or near state-of-the-art) performance** on standard benchmarks including MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet.

Interest in computational auditory scene analysis has grown significantly in recent years. While it lags behind the more established field of speech recognition, general sound event detection is increasingly capturing researchers' focus. A key challenge in developing robust models lies in accessing sufficient high-quality training and testing data—until now, comprehensive sound event databases have been scarce.  

We introduce a database featuring 714 high-quality, isolated sound events across 14 distinct categories, along with 303 additional wav files containing miscellaneous sounds outside these categories. Each sound event is precisely labeled with perceptual onset and offset timings, ensuring that silent intervals are excluded. What sets NIGENS apart is its large collection of isolated sound events, the precision of its annotations, and its inclusion of a dedicated general sound class.

Big Data refers to high-volume, rapidly expanding datasets with complex structures and multiple independent sources. Traditional technologies struggled to store and process such vast amounts of information, leading to the emergence of the Big Data concept. Managing unstructured data poses significant challenges for users, necessitating mechanisms to organize it systematically for easier access.  

Classification techniques applied to large transactional databases simplify data retrieval from massive datasets by presenting information in a structured manner. These techniques primarily fall into two categories: supervised and unsupervised. This paper specifically examines various supervised classification methods, evaluating their advantages and limitations.

Neural networks encode data as projections onto learned weights within a high-dimensional manifold, where these weights form a knowledge base of causal class relationships. This form of inference, known as feed-forward reasoning, relies on identifying features that reveal these dependencies and is rooted in traditional cause-to-effect inductive reasoning. While widely adopted for its mathematical simplicity and computational efficiency, feed-forward models often struggle with generalization beyond trained scenarios. 

To address this limitation, we introduce an effect-to-cause inference approach based on abductive reasoning. In this framework, features capture deviations from established weight relationships when presented with an observed effect. We define this deviation as *contrast* and the resulting reasoning process as *contrastive reasoning*. This paper formalizes the structure of contrastive reasoning and presents a method to extract a neural network’s implicit notion of contrast. We validate the utility of this approach in two critical stages of neural network reasoning—decision inference and visual explanation—focusing on object recognition. By applying contrastive reasoning to distorted images, we demonstrate performance enhancements, achieving average accuracy improvements of 3.47%, 2.56%, and 5.48% under the proposed framework.

Complex image segmentation challenges—such as MRI-based left atrium delineation—can benefit from integrating shape priors to yield solutions aligned with known anatomical structures. However, a single multivariate Gaussian proves insufficient for capturing substantial nonlinear shape variations or multimodal prior distributions. While nonparametric density estimation offers greater flexibility, it demands extensive training data and presents formidable optimization hurdles, particularly in high-dimensional settings.  

To address these limitations, we introduce a maximum-a-posteriori approach that leverages a generative image model combining both local intensity and global shape priors. Deep autoencoders are employed to model intricate intensity distributions, bypassing the need for manual feature engineering. For the shape prior, we adopt a Gaussian mixture model, learning its parameters directly in a high-dimensional shape space instead of relying on dimensionality reduction.  

During segmentation, we treat the mixture component identity as a latent variable and marginalize it within a generalized expectation-maximization framework. Our solution employs a conditional maximization strategy that alternates between:  
- A closed-form update for component-specific shape parameters, enabling global optimization.  
- Intensity-driven energy minimization to enforce a globally consistent nonlinear shape prior.  

This hybrid approach ensures robust segmentation while maintaining computational efficiency and adaptability to complex anatomical variability.

The **Social Internet of Things (SIoT)**, which merges the principles of **Internet of Things (IoT)** and **Social Networks**, creates a network of intelligent nodes capable of forming social connections. To safeguard against unreliable service providers, service requestors must assess the trustworthiness of these nodes. This paper presents a **novel trust management mechanism** for the **SIoT**, designed to identify the most dependable service providers for each requestor, thereby minimizing exposure to malicious actors.  

We represent the **SIoT** as a **flexible bipartite graph**, consisting of two node sets: **service providers** and **service requestors**. A **social network** is then constructed among service requestors using **Hellinger distance**. Using **node centrality and similarity measures**, we develop a **social trust model** to infer trust behaviors within the network.  

Additionally, we employ a **matrix factorization technique** to derive latent features of SIoT nodes, identify trustworthy entities, and address **data sparsity** and **cold start issues**. Our analysis evaluates the impact of various parameters on the trust prediction mechanism’s accuracy. The findings demonstrate that **feedback from highly Hellinger-similar neighboring nodes** significantly enhances prediction reliability.

Real-world edge AI applications frequently see their accuracy compromised by external environmental factors like noise, sensor placement/calibration, and temporal variations. This paper presents a lightweight, on-device neural network learning method designed to tackle these challenges without complex computations. Departing from conventional backpropagation-based training, our solution is specifically optimized for resource-constrained edge devices. We detail the algorithm and its implementation on a wireless sensor node built with Raspberry Pi Pico and a low-power radio module. Experimental results using rotating machine vibration patterns show our on-device learning approach markedly enhances anomaly detection accuracy in noisy conditions, while simultaneously reducing computational overhead and communication demands for energy efficiency.

Developing the ability to act based on environmental observations represents a fundamental capability for artificial agents to achieve reliable task performance. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a proven framework for acquiring such decision-making strategies, existing approaches face limitations including dependence on reward engineering, poor generalization across environments, and low sample efficiency. This work investigates active inference and the free energy principle—a neuroscientific framework describing how biological systems maintain world models and treat action selection as an inference process. We demonstrate this approach by applying it to the classic mountain car benchmark, illustrating how active inference naturally integrates both reinforcement learning and demonstration-based learning paradigms.

In this conventional setup, a data owner (API provider) typically develops models using private datasets, then partners with cloud vendors to host and manage API services. This arrangement inherently relies on trust between the API provider and the cloud service provider.

However, this trust-based model presents significant vulnerabilities. Dishonest or unreliable cloud vendors might replicate APIs to create competing services, manipulate usage statistics to reduce payments, or unfairly distribute revenue among API providers. To address these concerns, we propose a blockchain-powered decentralized marketplace that eliminates the need for centralized trust. Our solution enables all participants in the API ecosystem to independently verify transactions and interactions without relying on a single authority.

Our analysis demonstrates that model compression can enhance a pre-trained model’s population risk by balancing the reduction in generalization error against the rise in empirical risk. We first establish that compression lowers an information-theoretic bound on generalization error, framing it as a regularization method to mitigate overfitting. Next, we quantify the empirical risk increase using rate-distortion theory. These findings suggest that population risk improves when the drop in generalization error outweighs the empirical risk increase. Using linear regression, we illustrate that such a reduction in population risk is feasible through compression. Additionally, our theoretical insights indicate that the Hessian-weighted $K$-means clustering compression method benefits from regularizing the distances between cluster centers. Experimental results on neural networks validate our theoretical claims.

In the field of visual decoding, reconstructing presented images based on corresponding human brain activity recorded through functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) remains challenging, particularly for natural scenes. This task involves conditional image generation guided by fMRI data, which has recently led to the adoption of generative adversarial networks (GANs) for natural image synthesis. Despite significant progress with GAN-based approaches, reconstruction quality—both in terms of fidelity and realism—remains limited due to sparse fMRI datasets and the inherent instability of GAN training.  

To address these challenges, we introduce GAN-BVRM, a Bayesian visual reconstruction method that leverages a classifier to decode image categories from fMRI signals, a pretrained conditional generator for category-specific image synthesis, and encoding models paired with an evaluator to assess generated outputs. By utilizing BigGAN’s pretrained generator, GAN-BVRM produces diverse natural images and selects those most aligned with recorded brain activity as the final reconstructions. Here, semantic content is guided by decoded categories, while finer details are refined through encoding models. Crucially, the Bayesian framework resolves potential conflicts between naturalness and fidelity in the reconstruction process.

This study introduces an innovative end-to-end deep learning framework designed to jointly estimate demand baselines and incentive-driven agent demand response models using net demand measurements and incentive signals. The framework consists of two key components:  

1) A differentiable optimization layer that models the decision-making process of demand response participants, accepting incentive inputs to predict user responses.  

2) A standard neural network for baseline demand forecasting, which processes relevant features to estimate users' unperturbed demand.  

These intermediate predictions are combined to generate the net demand forecast. Additionally, we present a gradient-descent-based training method that jointly optimizes the agent model and baseline forecast by backpropagating net demand prediction errors.  

The effectiveness of this approach is validated through computational experiments using synthetic demand response traces and a large-scale real-world dataset. Results demonstrate that the framework successfully recovers the demand response model without requiring prior knowledge of baseline demand.

Precise hardware performance models are essential for optimizing code generation. Compilers rely on them for heuristic choices, superoptimizers use them as optimization targets, and autotuners depend on them to identify the best configuration for a given program. However, creating these models is challenging due to the complexity of modern processors, compounded by the rapid expansion of deep learning accelerators.  

We present a technique for training performance models using a dataset of tensor computation graph programs tailored for Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) instances. Our results show that the learned model surpasses a highly refined analytical performance model in two key tasks—selecting tile sizes and optimizing operator fusion. Additionally, it enables autotuners to discover faster programs when TPU access is restricted or costly.

We present an algorithm designed for first-order stochastic optimization of a broad family of functions defined on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), including both convex and non-convex cases under the class of *variationally coherent* functions. The algorithm’s iterates are shown to converge almost surely to the global minimizer \(\boldsymbol{x}^*\) for this function class. Moreover, with identical hyperparameters and after \(T\) iterations, the algorithm guarantees an expected suboptimality gap of \(\widetilde{O}(\|\boldsymbol{x}^* - \boldsymbol{x}_0\| T^{-1/2+\epsilon})\) for any \(\epsilon>0\) on convex functions. Notably, this is the first method to simultaneously achieve these two properties, while also nearly matching the performance of parameter-free algorithms in the convex setting.  

Our approach is based on a Follow The Regularized Leader framework, incorporating two key innovations: the use of *rescaled gradients* and time-varying linearithmic regularizers.

This study introduces and evaluates an automated hippocampal surface generation method using a 3D U-net combined with active shape modeling (ASM). The framework comprises three key stages: First, bilateral hippocampus segmentation is automatically performed on each MRI scan using a 3D U-net. Next, ASM analyzes preregistered template surfaces to derive mean shape and principal components capturing shape variations. Finally, hybrid particle swarm optimization identifies the optimal shape parameters that best fit the segmented regions, reconstructing the hippocampal surface from these parameters and the mean shape. The results demonstrate that this approach produces highly accurate hippocampal surfaces with proper anatomical topology and smoothness for both hemispheres.

The practice of image repurposing is a widespread tactic for disseminating false information across social media platforms and online forums. This technique involves sharing unaltered images while deliberately manipulating their metadata to fuel misleading narratives and further propaganda. Although manual verification remains feasible—given the abundance of credible information online—the escalating frequency and simplicity of such semantic manipulation underscore the need for reliable automated methods to evaluate multimedia data for authenticity.  

This paper introduces an innovative approach to detecting image repurposing by modeling the adversarial relationship between two key players: a malicious actor who fabricates metadata to misrepresent images and a watchdog tasked with ensuring semantic alignment between images and their accompanying metadata. Both parties leverage a reference database of verified content to advance their objectives. Our proposed method demonstrates cutting-edge performance in verifying location-identity, subject-identity, and artist-painting relationships, proving its effectiveness across multiple use cases.

There is growing interest in interactive learning algorithms that integrate human-machine collaboration. Among the most intuitive forms of feedback are comparison-based queries, where humans evaluate pairs of options. However, a key challenge in designing such algorithms is handling noisy responses. A typical solution involves repeating queries multiple times, but this approach is often impractical due to high costs and the unrealistic assumption that noise is independent across repetitions.  

In this work, we propose a novel weak oracle model in which users only respond to pairwise comparison queries when they are confident in their answers. This framework effectively captures human behavior in scenarios where responses are error-prone. We apply this weak oracle model to the content search problem—a variation of nearest neighbor search—where the goal is to efficiently identify a target object in a database using a dissimilarity metric and comparison-based queries.  

To address this problem, we introduce two algorithms, WORCS-I and WORCS-II (Weak-Oracle Comparison-based Search), which are designed to locate the target object with minimal comparisons while leveraging the weak oracle's reliability constraints. Theoretical analysis confirms that these algorithms achieve near-optimal query efficiency.

This research focuses on predicting glaucomatous visual field loss using patient datasets, with the aim of accurately forecasting disease progression for individuals. Due to the limited number of measurements available per patient, developing reliable individual predictors is challenging. A recently introduced clustering-based approach improves prediction accuracy by grouping patients with similar spatiotemporal patterns. Patients are assigned to clusters, and predictive models are built using aggregated data within each group.  

Although prediction quality heavily relies on clustering accuracy, selecting the optimal clustering method remains difficult. To address this, we propose an aggregation technique that combines cluster-based predictors to achieve higher accuracy than relying on a single clustered model. Additionally, our method demonstrates superior performance by hierarchically integrating predictors generated from multiple clustering approaches.  

Using real-world datasets, we show that our approach significantly outperforms traditional cluster-based and patient-specific regression methods. This improvement is attributed to the hierarchical aggregation strategy, which allows high-performing predictors within smaller clusters to contribute effectively to the overall prediction accuracy.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks optimized through gradient descent and backpropagation have achieved significant success across diverse applications. Yet, relying solely on point estimates of network weights often leads to overfitting and fails to capture the uncertainty inherent in these estimates. While exact Bayesian neural network approaches offer a potential solution, their computational complexity makes them impractical for real-world scenarios.  

To address this, we present an approximate method for estimating weight uncertainty using the Ensemble Kalman Filter, a technique that efficiently scales even to networks with a high number of parameters. Additionally, we refine the noise distribution’s covariance during the ensemble update step by leveraging maximum likelihood estimation. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm by testing it on outlier detection in five real-world event datasets sourced from Twitter.

Interpretable machine learning has become increasingly prominent in recent years. Effective explanations for black-box decision systems require both conciseness and thoroughness to deliver substantial information clearly. Yet, current interpretable machine learning approaches often overlook the balance between brevity and comprehensiveness, resulting in overly verbose explanations.  

To address this, we introduce **Variational Information Bottleneck for Interpretation (VIBI)**, a model-agnostic interpretability framework that produces succinct yet exhaustive explanations. VIBI leverages the information bottleneck principle as a guiding criterion to identify optimal explanations. For any given input, VIBI extracts key features that are both highly condensed (ensuring brevity) and maximally informative about the black-box model’s decision (ensuring comprehensiveness).  

We assess VIBI’s performance across three datasets, benchmarking it against leading interpretable machine learning techniques using both human-evaluated interpretability and quantitative fidelity measures.

We present a novel technique for text generation—specifically for song lyrics—by analyzing the speech-like acoustic properties of an audio input. By adapting a vocal separation algorithm and an acoustic speech recognition model, we process instrumental music or ambient sounds as input. The system transcribes perceived "errors" from the vocal separator, producing a textual interpretation of words seemingly "heard" in the audio. We outline the core methodology, provide preliminary findings, and explore the possibilities for human-AI creative collaboration using this approach.

Noise reduction is a core challenge in scientific imaging. While deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) deliver cutting-edge performance for denoising natural images, their application in scientific imaging remains largely unexplored. Traditional denoising CNNs rely on training with artificially noised versions of clean natural images—a method inapplicable to scientific imaging, where pristine reference images are typically unavailable. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a simulation-based denoising (SBD) approach that trains CNNs exclusively on synthetic image data. We evaluate this framework using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) data, a widely used imaging technique in material science, biology, and medicine. SBD significantly outperforms existing methods on both simulated benchmark datasets and real-world experimental data. Beyond producing denoised images, SBD also generates likelihood maps that visually assess structural consistency between the denoised output and the original observations. Our findings highlight key limitations in current denoising architectures, particularly their restricted field-of-view. By expanding this receptive field, CNNs can better capture non-local repeating patterns—an essential capability under high-noise conditions. We further investigate the generalization potential of the SBD method.

We address the challenge of selecting high-dimensional Ising (graphical) models. A straightforward structure estimation algorithm is presented, utilizing thresholding of empirical conditional variation distances. We define a new tractability criterion for graph families where this approach is effective, relying on the existence of sparse local separators between node pairs in the graph. For these graph structures, our algorithm requires a sample complexity of $n=\Omega(J_{\min}^{-2}\log p)$, with $p$ representing the variable count and $J_{\min}$ denoting the minimum absolute edge potential. Additionally, we derive nonasymptotic necessary and sufficient conditions for accurate structure estimation.

Melanoma is widely recognized as the most aggressive type of skin cancer. Diagnosing these lesions is particularly challenging for physicians due to the visual resemblance between malignant and benign growths. Currently, malignancy assessment relies heavily on invasive histological analysis of suspicious tissue. Creating an accurate classification system for early and efficient detection could help mitigate the damaging effects of skin cancer while improving patient outcomes.  

This study introduces a multi-class classification approach using the CoAtNet architecture—a hybrid model that merges the depthwise convolution operations of traditional convolutional neural networks with the advantages of Transformer models and self-attention mechanisms. The fusion of these techniques enhances generalization and model capacity. The proposed multi-class classifier demonstrates strong performance, achieving an overall precision of 0.901, recall of 0.895, and average precision (AP) of 0.923, outperforming other leading models in the field.

Simulation holds immense promise for advancing the creation of reliable algorithms used in mobile agents operating within safety-critical environments. Yet current simulation platforms face significant limitations—chiefly their low visual realism and restricted sensor diversity—which hinder this transformative potential. We introduce VISTA, an open-source, data-driven simulator designed for autonomous vehicles, supporting multiple sensor modalities. By leveraging high-quality real-world datasets, VISTA accurately simulates RGB cameras, 3D LiDAR, and event-based cameras, allowing the generation of novel synthetic viewpoints. This expands the pool of training data by incorporating rare edge cases often challenging to collect in real-world scenarios. Our experiments with VISTA demonstrate the effective training and evaluation of perception-to-control policies across all sensor types. We further validate this approach by deploying the policies on a full-scale autonomous vehicle. Remarkably, policies trained in VISTA achieve seamless sim-to-real transfer and outperform those trained solely on real-world data, exhibiting superior robustness.

Poor sitting posture has been recognized as a contributing factor to musculoskeletal disorders and lower back pain, particularly among the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and office workers. In today’s digitally driven society, people often remain seated for prolonged periods—whether during work or leisure activities—leading to spinal discomfort and related issues. Consequently, developing methods to monitor sitting habits and suggest corrective measures, such as targeted exercises, is essential. While posture recognition has been explored extensively for standing positions, research on seated postures remains limited. Previous studies have employed wearable sensors, pressure or force sensors, and video or image-based analysis for posture detection.  

This study focuses on developing machine learning models to classify a person’s sitting posture using data obtained from a chair equipped with two 32x32 pressure sensors—one on the seat and another on the backrest. Five algorithms were employed to build the models: Random Forest (RF), Gaussian Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Deep Neural Network (DNN). Performance evaluation was conducted using the K-Fold cross-validation technique. The paper details experiments performed on two distinct datasets, controlled and realistic, and analyzes the resulting findings.

One-shot Neural Architecture Search (NAS) seeks to reduce the computational cost of identifying top-performing models. However, recent findings highlight the competitive performance of simple random search within the same search spaces used by advanced NAS approaches. To tackle this challenge, we investigate the impact of significantly relaxing the NAS search space and introduce Bonsai-Net, an efficient one-shot NAS technique designed to navigate this expanded space. Bonsai-Net leverages an enhanced differential pruner, consistently uncovering high-performance architectures that surpass random search while maintaining fewer parameters than existing methods. Moreover, Bonsai-Net integrates model search and training into a single process, drastically cutting the time required to produce fully trained models from scratch.

Numerous critical data analysis tasks involve highly imbalanced datasets, particularly in the distribution of the target variable. A common scenario arises in medical imaging, where positive cases are rare yet crucial for accurate performance evaluation. To address this challenge, we reframe the problem as an anomaly detection task using generative models. Our approach involves training an unsupervised generative model on "negative" (majority) samples, then leveraging this model to estimate the likelihood of new data points. An effective model enables the identification of "positive" cases as low-probability anomalies.  

In this paper, we explore the application of cutting-edge deep generative models—GANs and VAEs—for data likelihood estimation. Our experiments demonstrate that while both GANs and VAEs successfully distinguish between "positive" and "negative" samples in the MNIST dataset, they struggle to capture the intricate patterns of the NLST dataset at the necessary level for effective anomaly detection. These findings suggest that despite existing literature showcasing successful applications of generative models in similar contexts, significant challenges remain in handling more complex real-world data.

We investigate networks of learning agents that collaborate to solve a shared nonstochastic bandit problem. These agents communicate through an underlying network, exchanging messages about chosen actions while discarding those that exceed a delay threshold of $d$ hops. We propose \textsc{Exp3-Coop}, a cooperative extension of the {\sc Exp3} algorithm, and establish that for $K$ actions and $N$ agents, the average per-agent regret after $T$ rounds is bounded by $\sqrt{\bigl(d+1 + \tfrac{K}{N}\alpha_{\le d}\bigr)(T\ln K)}$. Here, $\alpha_{\le d}$ denotes the independence number of the $d$-th power of the connected communication graph $G$.  

For any connected graph, setting $d=\sqrt{K}$ yields a regret bound of $K^{1/4}\sqrt{T}$, outperforming the noncooperative minimax regret $\sqrt{KT}$. By selecting $d$ more strategically, the regret bound can approach the full information minimax rate $\sqrt{T\ln K}$ for dense graphs. In cases where $G$ has sparse components, a modified version of \textsc{Exp3-Coop}—where agents adjust parameters based on their centrality—further reduces regret.  

Additionally, our analysis provides the first characterization of minimax regret for bandit learning with delayed feedback.

Prediction markets are widely employed in real-world scenarios to forecast outcomes like presidential elections. This study introduces a mathematical framework for artificial prediction markets designed for supervised learning of conditional probability estimators. The artificial prediction market offers an innovative approach for combining predictive insights from features or trained classifiers, with the fusion outcome represented as contract prices on potential results. The market can be dynamically trained by adjusting participant budgets through online updates based on training data.  

Drawing inspiration from real-world prediction markets, the governing equations of the artificial system are derived from intuitive and logical assumptions. The paper also presents efficient numerical methods for solving these equations. The resulting market model is proven to function as a maximum likelihood estimator. It extends beyond linear aggregation techniques found in boosting and random forests, encompassing logistic regression and certain kernel methods. Additionally, the market's structure accommodates specialized classifiers that operate only on specific instances.  

Empirical evaluations demonstrate that artificial prediction markets frequently surpass random forests and implicit online learning in performance, both on synthetic datasets and real-world UCI benchmarks. In machine learning, gathering and labeling data can be highly time-intensive, particularly for large-scale challenges. A widely used solution involves transferring knowledge from a related labeled domain to the target one. Two prevalent methods for this purpose are adversarial learning and self-training. This article begins by examining two key issues in adversarial learning: training instability and the problem of mistaken confusion. Building on insights from domain confusion and self-ensembling techniques, we introduce a unified model called Domain Confusion with Self Ensembling (DCSE), which jointly learns feature and class-invariant representations. Experimental results demonstrate that DCSE outperforms existing methods across multiple unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks.

Deep generative modeling with normalizing flows has become increasingly popular due to its tractable exact log-likelihood computation and efficient training and sampling. However, a key limitation of flow models is their high-dimensional latent space, which matches the dimensionality of the input space. To address this challenge, Dinh et al. (2016) introduced a multi-scale architecture that progressively factors out a subset of dimensions at predefined intervals. Existing flow models employing multi-scale architectures rely on static masking for dimensionality reduction.  

In this work, we present a novel multi-scale architecture that dynamically selects dimensions for factorization based on their importance to the overall log-likelihood. Our approach introduces a data-dependent heuristic that measures each dimension’s contribution to the likelihood, guiding the factorization process. This heuristic is inherently derived during training, making our likelihood-aware multi-scale framework easily adaptable to various flow models.  

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by integrating it into several state-of-the-art flow architectures, achieving improvements in log-likelihood scores and sample quality across standard image benchmarks. Additionally, we perform ablation studies comparing our dynamic factorization strategy with traditional static masking, showcasing its superior performance.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) and Internet of Things (IoT) devices are now widely integrated into diverse applications, including healthcare wearables, critical infrastructure like nuclear power plants, autonomous vehicles, smart cities, and smart homes. However, these systems often lack robust security across their software, hardware, and network layers, creating a broad attack surface for malicious actors.  

This article introduces a novel method for identifying previously unknown vulnerabilities, effectively managing them, and enhancing incident response when exploits occur. The approach involves analyzing documented CPS/IoT attacks, encoding them as regular expressions, and using machine learning (ML) to derive new attack vectors and security weaknesses.  

Our findings demonstrate the successful generation of 10 previously unidentified attack vectors and 122 new vulnerability exploits capable of targeting CPS and IoT systems. The ML model achieves a 97.4% accuracy rate and reduces the search space for potential attacks by 87.2%. We validate the technique by applying it to a real-world scenario—compromising the in-vehicle network of a connected car—and propose defensive measures to mitigate such threats.

ICD coding serves as the global standard for documenting and classifying health conditions and diagnoses within healthcare revenue cycle management. The manual assignment of ICD codes is susceptible to errors given the extensive code vocabulary and frequent similarities between codes. Since machine learning techniques rely on accurate training data, inconsistencies among human coders introduce label noise, complicating both training and evaluation for ICD classifiers. This study examines the nature of noise in manually assigned ICD-10 codes and introduces a method to train robust classifiers despite such label inaccuracies. Our findings reveal that this noise follows a systematic pattern. Traditional approaches for handling label noise often assume randomness and independence from features or labels—an assumption that does not hold for ICD data. To address this, we propose a novel training methodology. By analyzing ICD-10 codes frequently misapplied by human coders—based on their hierarchical positions, code types, and baseline classifier behavior—we develop a tailored training strategy to mitigate systematic noise effects.

This study addresses the challenge of $\ell_{p}$ norm linear regression, a technique with broad applications including sparse recovery, data clustering, and semi-supervised learning. Despite being a convex problem, it lacks a closed-form solution. Existing iterative algorithms, while advanced, often face convergence difficulties—either diverging for $p>3$ or exhibiting sensitivity to initial conditions. Additionally, these methods are not universally applicable across all values of $p$. 

To overcome these limitations, we introduce PROMPT (Parallel IteRative AlgOrithM for $\ell_{P}$ norm regression via MajorizaTion Minimization), a novel iterative approach grounded in Majorization Minimization principles. We establish that PROMPT guarantees monotonic convergence to the optimal solution for any $p$. A key advantage of PROMPT is its ability to update each regression variable element in parallel, enabling efficient handling of large-scale datasets—a critical capability in today’s data-rich environment. 

Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm’s applicability to graph-based semi-supervised learning. Through numerical experiments, we confirm that PROMPT consistently converges to the optimal solution regardless of random initialization and outperforms existing methods.

Studying cell morphology in microscopy images offers valuable insights into compound mechanisms or gene functions. To tackle this challenge, methods must extract meaningful biological data while filtering out technical variations—such as differences in experimental protocols or imaging equipment. We introduce Treatment ExemplArs with Mixture-of-experts (TEAMs), an embedding learning method that trains specialized experts to recognize technical variations in the training data and combines their predictions during testing. By minimizing noise from each expert, TEAMs generates robust embeddings with reduced technical bias. Our model leverages Treatment Exemplars to represent the full dataset distribution in each minibatch while remaining memory-efficient for GPU training. We validate TEAMs on three datasets for drug discovery tasks, improving accuracy in identifying true cell treatment mechanisms by 5.5–11% over existing state-of-the-art methods.

The $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem extends both $k$-clustering and $j$-subspace clustering approaches. Given data points $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the objective is to identify $k$ $j$-dimensional affine subspaces (flats) that optimally represent $P$ according to a specified distance metric. This work presents the first polynomial-size $L_\infty$ coreset algorithm for this problem in $d$-dimensional space. Additionally, we introduce the first strong coreset framework for general $M$-estimator regression, demonstrating its effectiveness for various robust regression models including Cauchy, Welsch, Huber, Geman-McClure, Tukey, $L_1-L_2$, and Fair regression, as well as broader classes of concave and power-bounded loss functions. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets validate the practical utility of our method.

The remarkable ability of adversarial attacks to deceive deep neural networks presents a major challenge for deploying deep learning in safety-sensitive and security-critical applications. Despite numerous defensive strategies emerging since the discovery of neural networks’ vulnerability to such attacks, a complete understanding and solution remain elusive. This research proposes that adversarial attacks achieve their high success rate by implicitly exploiting the gradient flow within deep neural networks—an inherent advantage that complicates defense efforts. Building on this hypothesis, we suggest that if neural networks could consciously utilize their own gradient flow during training, their adversarial robustness could be substantially enhanced. Based on this principle, we propose self-gradient networks, an innovative architecture that actively incorporates gradient flow to improve resistance against adversarial manipulation. By integrating gradient information directly into the learning process, these networks achieve superior perturbation stability compared to conventional training methods. A theoretical framework is developed to analyze and interpret the behavior of this new approach.

This study explores the challenge of clustering extremely brief texts through subspace clustering techniques. Such tasks frequently emerge in real-world scenarios including product classification, fraud identification, and opinion mining. The primary difficulty stems from the nature of short text representations, which are simultaneously high-dimensional (owing to extensive vocabularies) and highly sparse (given minimal word counts without repetition in each text). We introduce a straightforward subspace clustering approach based on linear algebra principles specifically designed for such datasets. Validation tests on Amazon US product name categorization demonstrate the method's competitive performance compared to current leading clustering algorithms.

Machine learning models frequently compromise the privacy of individuals whose data is used for training. Recent attacks, such as model inversion and attribute inference, have demonstrated how trained models can disclose sensitive information about participants in the training dataset. These attacks can expose private attributes of individuals by analyzing the model's behavior. Research indicates that multiple factors—including feature influence—can heighten the risk of model inversion.  

However, not all features carry equal sensitivity. Certain attributes used in training are often deemed highly confidential, making them prime targets for inversion attempts. To address this vulnerability, we propose a method for mitigating model inversion attacks in tree-based models by restricting the influence of sensitive features. This approach remains largely unexplored, with only preliminary efforts to use it as a defense against attribute inference attacks.  

Our findings reveal that models can often be trained with varying degrees of feature influence while maintaining accuracy. This flexibility allows us to reduce the impact of sensitive attributes without compromising predictive performance.

Children continuously expand their knowledge by seeking answers to their most pressing questions. As robots increasingly integrate into our daily lives, they too must develop the ability to progressively acquire new knowledge through human interaction. This study examines a cutting-edge method for continual learning and introduces a novel self-supervised technique that identifies uncertain objects by leveraging cluster representations of previously mastered categories. Our approach is evaluated on a standard robotic continual learning dataset, demonstrating superior performance over random sampling and softmax-based uncertainty methods—both in classification accuracy and the breadth of learned concepts.

We introduce **ARLPCG: Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Procedural Content Generation**, a novel approach for procedurally generating and testing unseen environments while using an auxiliary input as a control variable. Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents in diverse environments is a well-known challenge, often addressed by procedurally generating varied scenarios to enhance agent generalization. Unlike traditional methods, ARLPCG adopts an adversarial framework consisting of two RL agents: a PCG-based **Generator** and a **Solver**. The Generator receives rewards based on the Solver’s performance, ensuring generated environments remain challenging yet feasible. To enhance diversity and controllability, we incorporate auxiliary inputs into the Generator. This approach has dual advantages: the Solver improves generalization through the Generator’s adaptive challenges, while the trained Generator itself becomes a tool for creating novel, verifiably solvable environments.  

To validate our model, we design two 3D environments representing popular game genres—a third-person platformer and a racing game. Our results demonstrate that ARLPCG achieves a significantly higher solve ratio, and the auxiliary inputs effectively shape level design.
