The widespread application of factor models to account for unobserved confounders, \(\mathbf{Z}\), in observational studies with multiple treatments, \(\mathbf{A}\), spans disciplines such as genetics, networks, medicine, and political science. Wang and Blei (2019, WB) formalized these approaches by introducing the "deconfounder," a causal inference technique that employs factor models of \(\mathbf{A}\) to derive "substitute confounders," \(\hat{\mathbf{Z}}\). The method then estimates treatment effects by regressing the outcome, \(\mathbf{Y}\), on a subset of \(\mathbf{A}\) while controlling for \(\hat{\mathbf{Z}}\). WB assert that the deconfounder yields unbiased estimates when no single-cause confounders exist and \(\hat{\mathbf{Z}}\) is "pinpointed." We clarify that pinpointing necessitates each confounder to influence an infinite number of treatments. Under these conditions, we demonstrate that a simple semiparametric regression of \(\mathbf{Y}\) on \(\mathbf{A}\) is asymptotically unbiased. Consequently, deconfounder variants that incorporate this regression also achieve asymptotic unbiasedness, but those relying on \(\hat{\mathbf{Z}}\) and partial treatment subsets demand additional untestable assumptions. Replicating all available deconfounder analyses, we find the method does not systematically outperform basic regression. In practice, the deconfounder generates unrealistic estimates in WB’s movie earnings study, suggesting Stan Lee’s cameos contributed \$15.5 billion—nearly all Marvel movie revenue. Ultimately, neither method replaces rigorous research design.

We examine a fair machine learning (ML) scenario in which an 'upstream' model developer must create a fair ML model for multiple similar yet distinct 'downstream' users. This framework presents unique challenges not addressed by many existing fairness approaches, reinforcing criticisms that current methods fail to accommodate the varied demands of real-world fair ML applications. To tackle this upstream/downstream challenge, we adopt a distributional perspective on fair classification.  

Specifically, we propose a novel fairness metric called *distributional parity*, which quantifies disparities in outcome distributions across protected groups. We also introduce a post-processing technique to minimize this disparity using optimal transport methods. Our approach consistently produces fairer outcomes for all downstream users across multiple fairness criteria and operates at inference time on unlabeled data. We validate these claims experimentally by comparing our method to several alternatives across four benchmark tasks.  

Our findings demonstrate that improved fairness in classification can be achieved by developing interventions tailored to specific use cases.

The issue of fairness in machine learning has garnered significant interest. While existing research primarily explores fairness in either supervised or unsupervised learning, semi-supervised scenarios remain largely overlooked. In practice, however, many real-world machine learning applications rely on datasets containing both labeled and unlabeled data. A central challenge in fair learning is striking the right balance between fairness and accuracy. Prior work suggests that expanding the training dataset can improve this trade-off. We hypothesize that incorporating unlabeled data may yield similar benefits.  

To address this, we propose a fair semi-supervised learning framework formulated as an optimization problem. This framework incorporates three key components: classifier loss for accuracy optimization, label propagation loss for unlabeled data prediction, and fairness constraints applied to both labeled and unlabeled data to enhance fairness. We implement this approach using logistic regression and support vector machines, evaluating fairness under the disparate impact and disparate mistreatment metrics.  

Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of discrimination sources in semi-supervised learning through bias, variance, and noise decomposition. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method successfully achieves fair semi-supervised learning while achieving a more favorable accuracy-fairness trade-off than fair supervised learning approaches.

Accurate earnings prediction is crucial for investment strategies, dividend forecasts, and stock valuation. This task typically requires processing multidimensional datasets with complex nonlinear relationships, spatiotemporal patterns, and varying degrees of data sparsity. Existing nonlinear tensor completion methods often produce noisy embeddings and suffer from overfitting. Addressing the embedding learning challenge in tensor completion, we present MLCTR—a novel multilayer neural network architecture for tensor factorization and completion. The proposed model offers several key features: a hierarchical structure of low-rank matrix factorization blocks to prevent overfitting, layered transfer functions that introduce nonlinearity, and skip connections to mitigate vanishing gradients while enabling deeper network architectures. Optimized with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), our approach ensures rapid training convergence. Specifically designed for handling missing values in Earnings Per Share (EPS) data, MLCTR demonstrates superior performance in embedding learning and end-to-end tensor modeling. Experimental results show our method of embedding nonlinearity within factor matrices significantly outperforms approaches that apply nonlinearity only during tensor reconstruction from factorized components.

Bike sharing has become a vital component of urban mobility networks. Effective demand forecasting plays a crucial role in optimizing system rebalancing and maintaining operational efficiency. Current demand prediction models typically treat bike sharing as an isolated system, relying only on its own historical usage patterns while ignoring interactions with other transportation modes. This oversight is significant since bike sharing often serves as a complement to public transit and other mobility options. Although some studies have attempted to incorporate multimodal data, existing approaches lack the capability to process spatiotemporal information across different transport modes that use varying spatial units.  

To bridge this gap, this research introduces **B-MRGNN**, a novel graph-based deep learning framework for bike sharing demand prediction that integrates historical data from multiple transportation modes. The model represents spatial relationships through both intra- and inter-modal graphs, enabling it to account for dependencies between bike sharing stations, subway hubs, and ride-hailing zones. A **multi-relational graph neural network (MRGNN)** is employed to capture cross-modal correlations among these spatially heterogeneous units.  

The proposed method is rigorously evaluated using real-world bike sharing, subway, and ride-hailing data from New York City. Experimental results confirm that B-MRGNN outperforms existing demand prediction techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness in leveraging multimodal data for enhanced forecasting accuracy.

The Gaussian-smoothed optimal transport (GOT) framework, introduced by Goldfeld et al. (2020) and expanded in subsequent work, has rapidly gained recognition in statistics, machine learning, information theory, and related disciplines. A central insight from this research is that adopting the GOT approach—rather than its unsmoothed counterpart—alleviates the curse of dimensionality when using empirical measures to approximate the true data-generating distribution.  

This paper demonstrates a similar phenomenon in estimating nonparametric mixing distributions within discrete exponential family models. Under the GOT cost, the estimation accuracy of the nonparametric MLE accelerates to a polynomial rate, a significant departure from the sub-polynomial rates achieved with unsmoothed metrics, which are fundamentally constrained in information-theoretic terms.  

A pivotal contribution of our analysis is a new Jackson-type approximation bound for Gaussian-convoluted Lipschitz functions. This result connects established techniques for analyzing nonparametric MLEs with the emerging GOT framework, offering a fresh perspective on convergence rates in estimation problems.

Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful and flexible tool for disease diagnosis, attracting significant interest from both researchers and practitioners. As ML techniques advance and studies in this field multiply, there is a growing need for a comprehensive review of Machine Learning-Based Disease Diagnosis (MLBDD). This study conducts a bibliometric analysis of MLBDD research published between 2012 and 2021.  

Using targeted keywords, 1,710 relevant papers with associated metadata were retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science (WoS) databases and consolidated into an Excel dataset for deeper examination. The analysis first explores publication trends, highlighting annual output, key contributing countries/regions, institutions, and authors. Next, co-citation networks among these entities are visualized using RStudio, followed by an assessment of citation patterns and the most impactful works.  

By offering both an overview and an in-depth examination of MLBDD, this article serves as a valuable resource for researchers new to the field as well as those seeking to expand their work in this rapidly evolving domain.

We present a novel inference approach for stochastic epidemic models that employs recursive multinomial approximations to marginalize over latent variables, avoiding intractable likelihood computations. This technique applies to discrete-time, finite-population compartmental models with partially observed, underreported, or missing count data. Unlike advanced alternatives like Approximate Bayesian Computation methods, our approach eliminates the need for model simulation and tuning parameters. The approximate marginal likelihood of parameters is efficiently computed using a straightforward filtering recursion.  

We validate the approximation's accuracy by analyzing both real and simulated data from the 1995 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Additionally, we demonstrate how this method integrates with Sequential Monte Carlo to estimate the time-varying reproduction number of COVID-19 in Wuhan, China, as recently studied by Kucharski et al. (2020).

Machine Learning has experienced rapid advancement in recent years, accelerating its integration into critical domains like educational evaluations, credit scoring, healthcare diagnostics, hiring processes, and legal systems. Ensuring the reliability of ML and NLP models is essential, demanding assurances that their outputs are both fair and resilient. To address this need, we present GYC—a novel framework for generating high-quality counterfactual text samples vital for evaluating such systems. Our key innovations include: a) GYC’s methodology for producing plausible, diverse, and goal-driven counterfactuals while maintaining effectiveness, and b) Controlled counterfactual generation guided by specific conditions, including named entities, semantic roles, or sentiment labels. Extensive experiments across multiple domains demonstrate GYC’s ability to create counterfactual texts embodying these four critical attributes. Additionally, GYC’s outputs serve as robust test cases for assessing model performance and bias mitigation techniques in text-based applications.

Producing realistic long-range skeleton-based human motion sequences remains a challenging task, as minor errors in a single frame can propagate and distort the entire action sequence. Previous approaches often apply video generation techniques that treat skeletal joints as simple image pixels, failing to capture the complex spatial and temporal relationships between frames. While graph convolutional networks (GCNs) show promise in modeling these structural dependencies, directly applying them to continuous spatiotemporal action sequences is computationally demanding due to the scale of the resulting action graphs.  

To address this challenge, we introduce an enhanced GCN framework that incorporates self-attention to dynamically sparsify the temporal action graph. Our approach automatically identifies and focuses on the most relevant historical frames, constructing a sparse yet informative graph structure that preserves essential motion patterns. This adaptive method efficiently captures both intra-frame spatial relationships and inter-frame temporal dynamics in action sequences. Comprehensive evaluations across two standard human action datasets confirm that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This study explores deep multimodal learning techniques for integrating speech and visual data in Audio-Visual Automatic Speech Recognition (AV-ASR). We first investigate a method involving independently trained unimodal deep networks, where their final hidden layers are combined to create a joint feature space, enabling the construction of an additional deep network. While the audio-only network achieves a phone error rate (PER) of 41% in clean conditions on the IBM large vocabulary audio-visual studio dataset, this fusion approach reduces the PER to 35.83%, highlighting the significant contribution of visual information to phone classification, even in high signal-to-noise audio environments.  

Additionally, we introduce a novel deep network architecture incorporating a bilinear softmax layer to model class-specific relationships between modalities. By combining the posterior probabilities from these bilinear networks with those from the previously described fusion model, we achieve a substantial reduction in PER, reaching a final rate of 34.03%.

We introduce powerful pre-training approaches for neural machine translation (NMT) that leverage parallel corpora with a pivot language (source-pivot and pivot-target pairs), substantially enhancing source-target translation performance. Our framework includes three key techniques to strengthen the connection between source, pivot, and target languages during pre-training: 1) sequential training of a unified model across different language pairs, 2) an auxiliary adapter module to bridge pre-trained encoder and decoder components, and 3) cross-lingual encoder pre-training through pivot language autoencoding. These methods demonstrate superior performance over multilingual baselines, achieving gains of up to +2.6 BLEU on WMT 2019 French-German and German-Czech tasks. Our results remain robust even in zero-shot and zero-resource settings.

Event generators are essential tools in high-energy nuclear and particle physics, enabling detailed investigations of particle interactions. This work examines the latest advancements in machine learning (ML) applications for developing physics event generators. We analyze the generative models employed in ML-based event generation, highlighting their unique challenges, and explore strategies for integrating physics principles into model architectures to address these limitations. Additionally, we identify key unresolved issues concerning super-resolution, accuracy, and generalization capabilities in ML-driven event generation.

An asynchronous Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) using imagined speech enables users to control external devices or communicate by decoding EEG signals associated with imagined words. For effective implementation, it is crucial to identify the precise onset of imagined speech within continuous EEG data. This study evaluates five feature extraction techniques—wavelet decomposition, empirical mode decomposition, frequency energy analysis, fractal dimension, and chaos theory features—as potential solutions for detecting imagined speech segments. These methods serve as foundational research for developing an imagined speech-based asynchronous BCI.  

The approaches were tested across three datasets using four distinct classifiers, achieving peak F1 scores of 0.73, 0.79, and 0.68, respectively. These promising results suggest that automated segmentation of imagined speech for subsequent classification is feasible and warrants further exploration.

Platonic solids like cubes and icosahedrons, when pixelized, have become common tools for visualizing spherical data ranging from climate patterns to Cosmic Microwave Background maps. These geometric shapes possess inherent global symmetries, while each pixelized face also maintains local symmetries through Euclidean isometries. While hierarchical methods can combine these symmetries, they fail to fully capture their interaction. Using group theory principles, we demonstrate how to model this relationship, identify equivariant linear transformations, and develop symmetry-respecting equivariant padding. Neural networks incorporating these operations extend gauge-equivariant CNNs for pixelized spheres, delivering top performance in climate data segmentation and omnidirectional image processing. Code: https://git.io/JGiZA.

Effective commonsense reasoning systems must possess strong generalization capabilities across diverse scenarios. Yet current state-of-the-art methods often rely on costly labeled data and become overly specialized to particular benchmarks, failing to develop broader semantic reasoning skills. Zero-shot QA systems offer a promising alternative by converting structured knowledge graphs into synthetic question-answer pairs for training, addressing these limitations.  

With the growing variety of available commonsense knowledge graphs, this work expands zero-shot transfer learning to multi-source environments, enabling synergistic use of different knowledge graphs. To achieve this, we introduce a modular knowledge aggregation approach within our novel zero-shot reasoning framework, specifically designed to minimize knowledge loss caused by interference between disparate sources.  

Experimental validation across five commonsense reasoning benchmarks confirms our framework's effectiveness, showing significant performance gains when leveraging multiple knowledge graphs.

This study introduces Lattice Cross Fusion, a novel fusion strategy for multistream convolutional networks. The method intersects signals from convolution layers by performing mathematical operation-based fusions immediately preceding pooling layers. Experimental results using a degraded version of the CIFAR-10 dataset and an adapted AlexNet-LCNN architecture demonstrate that this approach achieves a 46% performance improvement over the baseline single stream network while exhibiting faster convergence, greater stability, and enhanced robustness.

Comprehending and forecasting chemical reactions is essential for investigating complex chemical systems. Reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide valuable atomic-level insights, aiding in the interpretation of reaction mechanisms. In this work, two benchmark datasets were developed, and corresponding neural network (NN) potentials were trained using these datasets. These NN potentials accurately predict potential energy and atomic forces with density functional theory (DFT) precision while significantly outperforming traditional DFT calculations in speed. Leveraging these models, reactive MD simulations were conducted to analyze hydrogen and methane combustion mechanisms. Due to the efficiency of the NN approach, nanosecond-scale MD trajectories for systems containing hundreds of atoms were generated, revealing detailed combustion pathways. With further refinement, the methods presented here could be applied to explore reaction mechanisms in diverse complex systems—including combustion, synthesis, and heterogeneous catalysis—without requiring predefined reaction coordinates or elementary steps.

The opaque nature of deep learning systems makes interpretability methods essential for building human trust and facilitating AI-human collaboration. This study examines both model-agnostic and CNN-specific explanation techniques for text classification, evaluating them through three human-centric assessments focused on distinct explanation objectives: (1) exposing model logic, (2) validating prediction reliability, and (3) assisting users in analyzing ambiguous outputs. Our findings demonstrate varying effectiveness among the evaluated methods and reveal their suitability for each of these different explanatory purposes.

The past decade witnessed exponential growth in data volumes and computational complexity across many fields, driving demand for highly parallel distributed computing systems. Operating these systems effectively presents significant challenges, particularly when uncertainties arise regarding job and task performance under diverse resource configurations – a critical factor for scheduling and allocation decisions.  

This paper examines predictive performance modeling (PPM) techniques that estimate key metrics such as execution time, memory requirements, and wait times for future jobs based on historical data. Our analysis emphasizes non-intrusive methods, which analyze workloads without modification since these systems typically treat workloads as black-box operations. We categorize and evaluate factors influencing performance variability, the types of metrics predicted, training data requirements, practical applications, and the predictive methodologies employed. Finally, we highlight unresolved challenges and emerging research priorities in the field.

Since autonomous systems typically impact multiple users simultaneously, ensuring fairness in their design is essential. Unlike traditional deep reinforcement learning (RL), we study the challenge of training a policy that ensures equitable treatment for all users. In this paper, we formalize this novel RL problem by optimizing an objective function that incorporates a precisely defined fairness measure.  

We provide a theoretical analysis, examining both discounted and average reward scenarios. Notably, our investigation yields a new result in standard RL: a bound on the approximation error between the optimal average reward and the reward of a policy optimized for discounted returns. This finding, which holds independent interest, underscores the advantage of leveraging discounted reward policies—often easier to learn—to derive fair solutions for average rewards.  

Additionally, we demonstrate how existing deep RL algorithms can be adapted to address our fairness-focused optimization problem. Our approach is rigorously evaluated through extensive experiments across three distinct domains.

The growing prevalence of network datasets—spanning social, biological, and information systems—has heightened the significance of relational data representations, alongside a surge in statistical relational learning (SRL) algorithm applications. This article explores key representation challenges in graph-based relational data, where the selection of node, link, and feature representations significantly influences SRL algorithm effectiveness. We review techniques and opportunities for optimizing relational representation transformations to enhance algorithmic performance.  

To organize these approaches, we present a straightforward taxonomy for relational data transformations, treating link and node transformations as complementary tasks. Both transformations encompass:  
1. **Existence prediction** – determining whether nodes or links are present.  
2. **Label/type prediction** – inferring categorical properties.  
3. **Weight/importance estimation** – measuring influence or strength.  
4. **Feature construction** – systematically defining relevant attributes.  

Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate the taxonomy’s utility and use it to analyze different methodologies for each task. We also outline general principles for transforming links, nodes, and features while identifying unresolved challenges in the field.

Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) models offer sophisticated approaches for uncovering hidden patterns in data, though their inference procedures often suffer from computational inefficiency. We leverage the decomposability of completely random measures—including popular models like the Dirichlet process and beta-Bernoulli process—into independent sub-measures. By partitioning the latent measure into two parts—a finite component with active features and an infinite component covering uninstantiated features—we tailor the inference strategy for each: uncollapsed samplers efficiently explore the finite part, while collapsed samplers handle the sparse, infinite tail effectively. This hybrid approach is broadly applicable to many models and supports distributed computation, enabling scalable inference while maintaining theoretical convergence guarantees.

We investigate the cross-entropy method (CEM) for optimizing continuous, parameterized objective functions in non-convex settings and propose a differentiable version that allows computing gradients of CEM outputs with respect to the objective function's parameters. This advancement integrates CEM into end-to-end learning pipelines—previously unachievable in machine learning applications. We demonstrate our approach through experiments in synthetic energy-based structured prediction and non-convex continuous control problems. For control tasks, we present a method to project optimal action sequences into lower-dimensional spaces. Our differentiable CEM (DCEM) framework enables fine-tuning of CEM-based controllers using policy optimization techniques.

This study introduces an efficient variational inference framework designed to develop a class of structured Gaussian process regression network (SGPRN) models. The core approach involves integrating auxiliary inducing variables into latent functions and treating both the distributions of these variables and hyperparameters as variational parameters. We then introduce structured variable distributions and marginalize latent variables, enabling the decomposition of a tractable variational lower bound and facilitating stochastic optimization.  

Our inference framework efficiently models datasets where outputs have distinct input sets, with computational complexity independent of input and output sizes, making it particularly suitable for handling missing data. Through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in imputing missing values. Additionally, we present a visualization technique for analyzing time-varying correlations in electrocorticography data, offering valuable insights into neural population dynamics.

Processing literary works like novels or short stories presents challenges when extracting structured information for knowledge graphs due to the vast number of potential relationships between characters and the difficulty of obtaining supervised data about them. This problem is tackled here through an unsupervised approach using transformers. First, relational sentences from the text are embedded using SBERT and then clustered to group semantically similar relationships. The sentences within each cluster are summarized using BART, and a descriptive label is derived from the summary. Initial experiments suggest that this clustering approach can effectively identify similar relationships, serving as a useful preprocessing step for semi-supervised methods.

Manifold learning serves as a technique for reducing dimensionality by identifying a projection subspace that maximizes interclass variance while minimizing intraclass variance. However, subspace learning methods often face limitations due to the high dimensionality of datasets. This paper introduces a hierarchical approach to enhance the scalability of subspace learning techniques, aiming to boost classification performance in large datasets by 3% to 10%. Various method combinations are explored for optimization.  

The proposed approach is evaluated on five publicly available large datasets using eigenvalue-based subspace learning techniques, including linear discriminant analysis, principal component analysis, generalized discriminant analysis, and reconstruction independent component analysis. To investigate the method’s broader impact, the derived results are input into multiple classifiers—linear discriminant analysis, quadratic linear analysis, k-nearest neighbor, and random forest. Comparative analysis of classification accuracies demonstrates the effectiveness of the hierarchical approach, achieving an average improvement of 5% in classification performance.

Recent advancements in deep learning have greatly enhanced brain tumor segmentation performance. While fully supervised approaches deliver strong results, they require extensive manually annotated masks, which are labor-intensive and demand specialized expertise. Weakly supervised learning using scribbles offers a practical balance between model accuracy and annotation effort. However, even drawing scribbles for each hierarchical tumor substructure can still be time-consuming.  

In this work, we propose using just two types of weak labels—scribbles covering the whole tumor and healthy tissue, along with global labels indicating the presence of each substructure—to train a deep learning model for multi-region segmentation. Our method involves a two-phase network training strategy: first, we train a whole tumor (WT) segmentation network using only scribble annotations, generating approximate WT masks for training data. Next, we cluster the WT regions guided by global labels, producing rough substructure segmentations that serve as weak labels for training a second network. To refine segmentation boundaries, we incorporate dense CRF loss.  

Evaluated on the BraTS2017 dataset, our approach achieves competitive whole tumor segmentation accuracy while delivering comparable results for substructure segmentation.

This study investigates adversarial attacks targeting Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). We demonstrate techniques for altering data points to achieve either a specific latent representation (supervised attack) or a significantly distorted encoding (unsupervised attack). The analysis evaluates how architectural variations—such as $\beta$-VAE and NVAE—affect VAE robustness and proposes quantitative measures to assess their resilience.

A newly introduced SLOPE estimator (arXiv:1407.3824) has been demonstrated to adaptively attain the minimax $\ell_2$ estimation rate in high-dimensional sparse linear regression settings (arXiv:1503.08393). This minimax optimality applies when the sparsity level $k$, sample size $n$, and dimension $p$ follow the conditions $k/p \rightarrow 0$ and $k\log p/n \rightarrow 0$. In this work, we analyze the estimation performance of SLOPE in the complementary regime where both $k$ and $n$ grow proportionally with $p$, offering fresh perspectives on SLOPE estimator behavior. We begin by establishing a concentration bound for the finite-sample mean squared error (MSE) of SLOPE, which converges around a complex and implicitly defined quantity. Through careful analysis of this quantity, we show that among all SLOPE estimators, LASSO achieves optimal performance for estimating $k$-sparse parameter vectors without tied non-zero components in low-noise conditions. Conversely, in high-noise settings, SLOPE estimators underperform compared to bridge regression methods, including the Ridge estimator.

This study presents two key advancements. First, it develops mixed compositional kernels and mixed neural network Gaussian processes (NNGPs). These kernels emerge from composing probability generating functions (PGFs), while mixed NNGPs represent Gaussian processes with such kernels, derived from infinitely-wide multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) employing distinct activation functions per layer.  

Second, the work introduces θ activation functions for neural networks and θ compositional kernels, expanding branching process theory through θ PGFs. Although recursive in nature, θ compositional kernels possess closed-form expressions. The analysis demonstrates that under specific conditions, these kernels maintain non-degenerate asymptotic behavior. Consequently, Gaussian processes utilizing θ compositional kernels avoid computationally intensive recursive evaluations while offering tunable infinite-depth properties.  

An important open question remains: whether Gaussian processes with θ compositional kernels correspond to infinite-width MLPs equipped with θ activation functions.

Early detection of sacroiliitis allows for timely intervention, which can greatly enhance the patient's long-term quality of life. Frequently, CT scans of the lower back or abdomen are performed to investigate back pain. However, the subtle distinctions between healthy and early-stage inflamed sacroiliac joints can lead to overlooked cases. To address this, we have created an automated algorithm designed to identify and grade sacroiliitis incidentally in CT scans taken for lower back pain evaluation.  

Our approach leverages supervised machine and deep learning methods. The process begins with a pelvic CT scan as input and provides a diagnostic evaluation for each sacroiliac joint. The algorithm follows four key stages:  
1) **Initial ROI Calculation**: A heuristic-based method combined with a U-Net classifier identifies the pelvic joint region.  
2) **ROI Refinement**: A four-tree random forest fine-tunes the region to accurately locate both sacroiliac joints.  
3) **Slice-Level Grading**: A custom CNN classifier evaluates and grades sacroiliitis in each CT slice for individual joints.  
4) **Final Diagnosis**: A random forest classifier aggregates slice-level results to determine the overall sacroiliitis diagnosis and severity.

Automated medical image segmentation is a complex challenge that relies heavily on extensive manually labeled datasets. Yet, current learning-based methods often struggle with the scarcity of annotated medical data, hindering the development of precise and reliable segmentation models. While semi-supervised approaches exist, they typically fall short in robustness compared to supervised methods and fail to adequately model geometric structures and semantic relationships, ultimately restricting segmentation performance.  

To address these limitations, we introduce *SimCVD*—a straightforward yet effective contrastive distillation framework that significantly improves voxel-wise representation learning. Our approach begins with an unsupervised training strategy where two different views of an input volume are processed, predicting their signed distance maps of object boundaries using a contrastive objective. Remarkably, this method achieves competitive performance with minimal supervision, matching results from fully supervised techniques while requiring far fewer labeled samples. We attribute this success to dropout serving as a simple yet effective form of data augmentation, preventing representation collapse.  

Additionally, we enhance the framework by incorporating structural distillation through pairwise similarity learning. We validate *SimCVD* on two widely used benchmarks: the *Left Atrial Segmentation Challenge (LA)* and the...

We present the Convolutional Conditional Neural Process (ConvCNP), a novel addition to the Neural Process family designed to capture translation equivariance in data. This property serves as a crucial inductive bias for diverse learning tasks such as time series analysis, spatial data processing, and image understanding. Unlike conventional approaches that map data sets to finite-dimensional vector spaces, our model embeds them into an infinite-dimensional function space.  

To mathematically formalize this concept, we develop a theoretical extension of neural set representations to incorporate functional representations. We prove that any translation-equivariant embedding can be expressed using a convolutional deep set architecture.  

Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks show that ConvCNPs outperform existing Neural Process models, achieving state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, by incorporating translation equivariance, the model demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization to complex, out-of-domain tasks.

Max-cut, clustering, and various other partitioning problems that are crucial to machine learning and scientific research fall under the NP-hard category, driving the development of numerous approximation algorithms and heuristics. While the optimal algorithm often depends on the specific application domain, worst-case analysis is commonly employed to compare performance—a potentially misleading approach if worst-case scenarios are rare. This creates a need for optimization methods capable of identifying the best algorithm configuration for typical input distributions in a given application.  

To tackle this challenge for clustering, max-cut, and related partitioning problems—including integer quadratic programming—we develop computationally and sample-efficient learning algorithms. These algorithms leverage samples from an application-specific distribution over problem instances to learn partitioning methods with high expected performance. Our approach covers widely used algorithm families: SDP rounding techniques for integer quadratic programming and agglomerative clustering algorithms enhanced with dynamic programming.  

For our sample complexity analysis, we derive tight bounds on the pseudodimension of these algorithm classes. Notably, we show that even for algorithm families parameterized by a single parameter, the pseudodimension can be superconstant—an unexpected finding with fundamental implications. Through this work, we advance the theoretical foundations of algorithm selection for partitioning problems while offering practical insights into efficient learning-based optimization.

Although deep learning models and techniques have demonstrated remarkable empirical performance, the underlying reasons for their success remain poorly understood in many respects. To address this gap, we analyze the decision boundary of a standard deep learning architecture with minimal assumptions about both the training data and the model.  

Our theoretical and empirical results reveal that the final weight layer of a neural network converges to a linear SVM when trained on the output of the last hidden layer—this holds true for both binary and multi-class classification using the standard cross-entropy loss. Beyond this finding, we empirically demonstrate that end-to-end training of the entire neural network, rather than fine-tuning only the final weight layer, can lead to an improved bias constant in the last layer, which plays a crucial role in generalization.  

These insights not only deepen our theoretical understanding of deep learning but also have practical implications for addressing common challenges such as catastrophic forgetting and adversarial attacks. The experimental code is publicly available at: https://github.com/lykaust15/NN_decision_boundary.

End-to-end learning frameworks are increasingly prominent in robot control, processing states or images to directly output torque or action parameters. However, these methods often face criticism for demanding extensive data to master a single task. Concerns about scalability across multiple tasks are valid, given that training typically requires hundreds or thousands of examples. But must end-to-end approaches rely on separate models for each task? Intuitively, shared learning should benefit performance since different tasks rely on a common understanding of the environment.  

This paper advances data-driven end-to-end learning by shifting from task-specific models to joint training across multiple robot tasks. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that multi-task learning outperforms individual models trained on equivalent data. For instance, a deep network trained on 2.5K grasp and 2.5K push examples achieves better grasping performance than one trained solely on 5K grasp examples.

A set of transition probability functions defines a Shannon channel, while a set of truth functions defines a semantic channel. Label learning aligns semantic channels with Shannon channels, whereas label selection aligns Shannon channels with semantic channels. The Channel Matching (CM) algorithm is designed for multi-label classification, operating under the maximum semantic information criterion. This criterion is consistent with both the maximum likelihood and regularized least squares criteria. For sufficiently large datasets, Shannon channels can be directly transformed into semantic channels using the third form of Bayes' theorem. For smaller datasets, parameterized truth functions can be trained using sampling distributions.  

A label may represent a Boolean combination of atomic labels. To simplify learning, truth functions can be derived only for atomic labels. Instances are classified into three categories—positive, negative, or unclear—avoiding the binary relevance limitation common in many studies. For each instance, the classifier selects the compound label that provides the highest semantic information or the most meaningful connotation.  

As a predictive model, the semantic channel remains invariant to changes in the prior probability distribution (source) of instances, ensuring reliability even when the source varies.

Reinforcement learning agents that incorporate interactive human input rely on feedback or guidance to navigate complex environments. Typically, this feedback takes the form of simple binary signals—either positive or negative. Though useful, such limited input can be challenging for the agent to interpret and generalize. This study investigates how natural language advice can enhance the feedback signal for reinforcement learning agents by adapting policy shaping, an established interactive reinforcement learning method.  

Traditional policy shaping uses human-provided feedback to guide the agent’s learning process. Here, we replace this human feedback policy with one generated from natural language advice. Our objective is to determine whether reasoning expressed in natural language can effectively assist a deep reinforcement learning agent in selecting optimal actions within its environment.  

To explore this, we design a model composed of three key components: an experience-driven network, an advice generator, and an advice-driven network. The experience-driven reinforcement learning agent makes decisions based on environmental rewards, while the advice-driven neural network relies on feedback generated by the advice generator for unfamiliar scenarios.

We introduce an algorithm designed to minimize a sum of functions, blending the computational speed of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with the second-order curvature insights of quasi-Newton methods. Our approach bridges these two methodologies by maintaining separate Hessian approximations for each component function in the sum. To ensure efficiency, even in high-dimensional problems, we store and transform these quadratic approximations within a shared, dynamically evolving low-dimensional subspace.  

Key features of the algorithm include:  
- Each update step requires only a single function or minibatch evaluation (similar to SGD).  
- Steps are scaled using an approximate inverse Hessian with minimal hyperparameter tuning (characteristic of quasi-Newton methods).  

Unlike prior stochastic second-order techniques, which treat individual function Hessians as noisy estimates of the full Hessian, our method directly estimates each one. We validate the algorithm’s effectiveness through experiments on seven diverse optimization problems and provide open-source implementations in Python and MATLAB.

This study focuses on a learning algorithm for probabilistic spiking neural network (SNN) models. Building on the work of Jimenez Rezende and Gerstner (2014), who introduced a stochastic variational inference method for training SNNs with hidden neurons, we address a key limitation of their approach. Their algorithm relies on the score function gradient estimator, which suffers from high variance that can hinder learning performance.  

We propose an alternative gradient estimator based on the path-wise gradient approach. The primary technical challenge lies in differentiating realizations of arbitrary point processes—a crucial requirement for deriving path-wise gradients. To overcome this, we introduce a novel differentiable point process, which serves as the paper’s key technical contribution, and use it to formulate the path-wise gradient estimator for SNNs. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed estimator through numerical simulations.

Traditional clustering methods often rely on feature space analysis. Yet real-world datasets frequently contain spatial information, and their ground truth exhibits spatially grouped classes that conventional clustering may not accurately capture. Inspired by hyperspectral imaging applications, this study presents clustering techniques built on orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization, incorporating total variation (TV) regularization to promote spatial continuity in cluster assignments. We develop multiple optimization strategies, applying TV regularization either as a postprocessing step or integrating it directly into the clustering process. Through numerical tests on hyperspectral data from matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization imaging, we demonstrate that these approaches yield markedly improved clustering performance compared to standard methods.

We introduce DMV, a novel memory-based tracker leveraging part-level dense memory and voting-based retrieval. With the integration of deep learning in tracking research, Siamese trackers have gained significant attention for their balance between speed and precision. Nevertheless, most existing approaches rely on single-template matching, constraining their potential by restricting access to only the initial target features. Our work addresses this limitation by incorporating an external memory module that stores tracking history. Part-level retrieval from this memory expands the available information beyond static templates, enabling improved handling of appearance variations and occlusions. The memory is dynamically updated during tracking, strengthening the target representation without requiring online learning. Additionally, we introduce a voting mechanism for memory retrieval to eliminate unreliable stored data. Extensive evaluations on OTB-100, TrackingNet, GOT-10k, LaSOT, and UAV123 demonstrate that our method achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art trackers.

As online payment platforms grow increasingly prevalent, detecting fraudulent transactions has become essential for safeguarding accounts and maintaining platform integrity. This work introduces an innovative fraud detection approach that integrates both static user profiles and dynamic behavioral patterns within a unified framework. To effectively capture behavioral trends in continuous time, we employ *time attention-based recurrent layers* to encode temporal details—such as action durations, intervals between activities, and sequential behavior patterns—into a shared latent space. Our method further unifies these learned embeddings with static profile data. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods across multiple evaluation metrics, particularly in *recall at top percent*, a critical measure for balancing user experience with fraud prevention.

This study examines the fundamental distinctions between evolutionary strategies and reinforcement learning approaches by comparing two leading algorithms: OpenAI-ES (an evolutionary strategy) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (a reinforcement learning method) — the most closely related techniques from their respective families.  

We evaluate these methods across five key dimensions:  
1. Overall effectiveness  
2. Performance in sparse reward environments  
3. Tendency to find minimal solutions  
4. Sensitivity to reward shaping  
5. Robustness to environmental variations  

Through performance analysis and behavioral observations in benchmark scenarios, we uncover previously unrecognized qualitative differences between the approaches, pinpoint their respective limitations, and suggest potential improvements. Our findings reveal that reward function characteristics significantly influence outcomes, with qualitatively different effects not only between OpenAI-ES and PPO but also among other reinforcement learning algorithms. This highlights the critical need to tailor reward function design to specific algorithmic requirements.

Adversarial Training (AT) and Virtual Adversarial Training (VAT) are regularization methods that enhance Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) by training them with adversarially perturbed inputs. These perturbations are small yet strategically crafted to be the most disruptive. In this work, we introduce xAT and xVAT—novel adversarial training algorithms that employ **multiplicative** perturbations rather than the traditional **additive** ones used in AT and VAT. Multiplicative perturbations offer greater perceptibility and interpretability compared to additive noise. Additionally, they can be generated either transductively or inductively, whereas standard AT and VAT are limited to transductive approaches. Through extensive experiments, we analyze the properties of multiplicative perturbations and show that xAT and xVAT achieve comparable or superior classification performance on established benchmarks while being approximately 30% faster than additive methods. The trained DNNs also exhibit unique weight distribution patterns.

From the joint probabilities of two random variables, key quantities such as mutual information can be derived. In Bayesian analysis, unknown probabilities are treated by computing a posterior distribution, combining a second-order prior with the observed data likelihood. For handling incomplete data, a standard approach assumes ignorability and estimates probabilities using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. While these two methods are well-developed, they are often treated independently.  

This work unifies both approaches under Dirichlet priors, providing efficient approximations for the mean, mode, and (co)variance of the probabilities, as well as for mutual information. We also establish the unimodality of the posterior distribution, ensuring EM’s convergence to the global maximum within this framework.  

These findings are applied to feature selection for incremental learning and naive Bayes classification. A fast mutual-information-based filter is developed and shown to outperform conventional empirical mutual information filters across multiple real-world incomplete datasets.

We present a versatile family of fairness regularizers designed for linear and logistic regression models. These regularizers offer convexity for efficient optimization while covering a broad spectrum of fairness concepts, from group-level to strict individual fairness. By adjusting the regularization weight, we can explore the trade-off between accuracy and fairness, quantifying this balance through a metric termed the Price of Fairness (PoF). Our key contribution is a comprehensive empirical analysis of the PoF across six datasets where fairness plays a central role.

Recent advancements in point-cloud based 3D object detection have shown significant progress, yet most research focuses solely on enhancing accuracy through deep learning architectures. In this work, we introduce an autoencoder-style framework that leverages channel-wise compression and decompression via interchange transfer for knowledge distillation.  

To effectively learn the teacher network’s map-view features, we separately process the teacher and student network features through a shared autoencoder. A compressed representation loss acts as a regularization by aligning channel-wise compression knowledge between the two networks. The decompressed features are then transferred bidirectionally to minimize the gap in interchange reconstructions.  

Additionally, we propose an attentive head loss to align critical detection information captured by the multi-head self-attention mechanism. Extensive experiments confirm that our method successfully trains lightweight models optimized for 3D point cloud detection, with superior performance demonstrated on leading public datasets, Waymo and nuScenes.

This brief paper introduces an image classification dataset containing 10 types of executable code, including roughly 50,000 virus samples. The dataset comprises nine distinct computer virus families alongside one benign class. The Portable Executable (PE) files are represented as images using the first 1024 bytes, formatted similarly to the MNIST handwriting dataset to enable easy adaptation of existing machine learning methods.  

The nine malware families were identified through unsupervised learning—specifically, KMeans clustering, which excluded benign samples to define class labels. Using MobileNetV2 for evaluation, we achieved 80% overall accuracy in classifying malware families, including benign samples. Additionally, once malware is detected (via signature or heuristic analysis), converting the first 1024 bytes into a thumbnail image allows for virus type classification with 87% accuracy.  

This work builds on prior research demonstrating that convolutional neural networks—originally designed for visual tasks—can effectively classify malware when applied to executable byte patterns rendered as images. The dataset is publicly accessible on Kaggle and GitHub.

Width-based planning has demonstrated strong performance on Atari 2600 games with pixel input while requiring significantly fewer environment interactions than traditional reinforcement learning methods. Prior width-based approaches have relied on manually designed feature sets or used a variational autoencoder (VAE-IW) trained on game screens to compute feature vectors, pruning screens without novel features during search.  

We introduce Olive (Online-VAE-IW), which dynamically updates VAE features through active learning during planning to optimize the usefulness of observed screens. In evaluations across 55 Atari games, Olive surpasses Rollout-IW 42-to-11 and VAE-IW 32-to-20. Additionally, it outperforms policy-learning methods ($\pi$-IW, DQN) trained with 100x more data by margins of 30-to-22 and 31-to-17, as well as the state-of-the-art data-efficient reinforcement learning approach (EfficientZero) running with a 1.8x larger planning budget by 18-to-7 in the Atari 100k benchmark—all without any policy learning.  

The source code is available at [github.com/ibm/atari-active-learning](https://github.com/ibm/atari-active-learning).

Most industry recommender systems depend on collaborative filtering (CF) to deliver personalized suggestions to users. Yet CF inherently conflicts with privacy, as it requires users to disclose their preferences to identify similar users and generate precise recommendations. While existing privacy-preserving methods have partially hidden user data from centralized systems, they compromise privacy, scalability, or accuracy and remain susceptible to breaches by malicious parties.  

To address these limitations, we introduce a selective privacy-preserving (SP2) approach that lets users specify which of their data remains private or public. Users can label their personal ratings as public (shared) or private (retained only on their device). The SP2 framework operates in two phases: (i) initially constructing a recommendation model using aggregated public ratings and (ii) refining this public model locally on each user’s device with their private preferences.

We perform a comprehensive investigation into the connection between out-of-sample predictive accuracy and Bayesian evidence (marginal likelihood) in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), along with evaluating the effectiveness of BNN ensembles, all tested on the Boston housing dataset. Leveraging advanced nested sampling techniques, we numerically explore the complete (non-Gaussian and multimodal) posterior distribution of the networks, deriving precise estimates of the Bayesian evidence for models containing up to 156 trainable parameters.  

The network architectures examined range from zero to four hidden layers, incorporating either $\tanh$ or ReLU activation functions, and testing both hierarchical and non-hierarchical priors. Ensembles of BNNs are constructed by computing the posterior distribution across networks, where individual BNN posterior samples are reweighted by their corresponding Bayesian evidence values.  

Our findings reveal a strong correlation between out-of-sample performance and Bayesian evidence, as well as a striking symmetry when comparing evidence versus model complexity with out-of-sample performance versus model complexity. Networks utilizing ReLU activations demonstrate consistently higher evidence values compared to those with $\tanh$ functions, which is also mirrored in their superior out-of-sample predictive performance. Additionally, ensembling across different architectures further enhances performance beyond the capabilities of individual BNNs.

Effective modeling of multi-order feature interactions within user event sequences is crucial for enhancing prediction performance in real-world applications. Current approaches face two primary limitations: they either capture feature interactions without considering sequential dependencies, or model sequence patterns while neglecting internal feature relationships within individual events. To address these shortcomings, we propose a hierarchical framework that simultaneously learns: (1) enhanced event representations through comprehensive feature interaction modeling, and (2) sequential patterns across historical user events. Extensive experiments on both industrial and public benchmark datasets show our method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions.

This paper investigates various methods for time series modeling. It outlines forecasting techniques using linear models, the ARIMA algorithm, and the XGBoost machine learning method. The results from combining different models are presented. Additionally, probabilistic modeling approaches involving copulas and Bayesian inference are examined.

The primary goal of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) is to safeguard the confidentiality and security of data utilized in developing machine learning models. PPML employs several techniques, including Secure Multi-Party Computation, Differential Privacy, and Homomorphic Encryption (HE), which are integrated with various machine learning and deep learning models to ensure data privacy and user anonymity. In this study, we introduce a fully homomorphic encrypted wavelet neural network designed to preserve privacy without sacrificing model efficiency. We evaluated the proposed approach on seven datasets from the finance and healthcare sectors, demonstrating that its performance closely matches that of non-encrypted models.

Current graph neural networks (GNNs) primarily learn node embeddings through message passing and aggregation frameworks. These conventional GNNs lack the ability to capture the relative positional relationships between nodes within a graph. To address this limitation, some approaches designate certain nodes as anchors, enabling GNNs to deduce relative positions by measuring distances to these reference points. However, existing Position-aware Graph Neural Networks (P-GNNs) rely on arbitrarily selected anchors, resulting in suboptimal trade-offs between positional awareness and feature learning.  

We demonstrate that effective anchor selection requires both uniform distribution and structural asymmetry. Meanwhile, we prove that identifying anchors capable of aggregating embeddings for all nodes within a graph is an NP-hard problem, making deterministic optimal solutions computationally impractical. To overcome these challenges while maintaining positional awareness, we introduce Position-Sensing Graph Neural Networks (PSGNNs), which learn anchor selection in a differentiable, backpropagation-compatible manner.  

Experimental results show that PSGNNs significantly outperform state-of-the-art GNNs across multiple synthetic and real-world graph datasets, with stable scalability. Notably, PSGNNs achieve average improvements of over 14% in AUC for pairwise node classification and 18% in link prediction compared to existing position-aware methods. Our source code is publicly available.

We address the task of verifying individual fairness (IF) in feed-forward neural networks (NNs). Specifically, we focus on the $\epsilon$-$\delta$-IF framework, which requires that for any two $\epsilon$-similar inputs under a learned similarity metric, the NN's output difference must not exceed a specified decision tolerance $\delta \geq 0$.  

Using various metrics, such as the Mahalanobis distance, we develop a method to overapproximate the associated optimization problem by employing piecewise-linear functions to establish global lower and upper bounds on the NN's nonlinearities across the input space. This computation is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem, enabling us to derive IF guarantees on four widely used fairness benchmarking datasets.  

Additionally, we demonstrate how this framework can promote fairness during training by adjusting the NN's loss function. Empirical results show that our approach produces models significantly fairer than existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant advancements in numerous computer vision applications. Yet, their effectiveness in handling high-dimensional input and output spaces—such as high-resolution image and video segmentation or 3D medical imaging—remains constrained by several challenges. A key limitation arises during training, where storing network activations for backpropagation demands substantial memory. For large-scale 3D problems, these memory requirements often surpass the capabilities of existing hardware.

Inspired by signal propagation in physical networks governed by the hyperbolic Telegraph equation, this work proposes a fully conservative hyperbolic network tailored for high-dimensional inputs and outputs. We present a coarsening mechanism that enables fully reversible CNNs by leveraging a learnable Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and its inverse. This approach efficiently manages both spatial resolution and channel count during state coarsening and interpolation.

Our experiments demonstrate that fully reversible networks deliver performance on par with state-of-the-art methods in tasks like 4D time-lapse hyperspectral image segmentation and complete 3D video segmentation, while maintaining a significantly reduced memory footprint. Notably, memory usage remains constant regardless of network depth. Additionally, we expand the applicability of...

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are known to be susceptible to adversarial attacks, and their robustness can be enhanced by incorporating adversarial noise into training data—as seen in standard adversarial training (SAT). However, improperly calibrated noise can degrade model performance, leading to the well-documented trade-off between accuracy and robustness. While this issue has been extensively investigated for whole-image classification tasks, it remains understudied in the context of medical image analysis, including segmentation, landmark detection, and object detection.  

This study identifies a critical limitation of SAT in medical applications: it applies a fixed, uniform noise level across all training samples, compromising its practical utility. Excessive noise can severely diminish model performance, while insufficient noise may fail to improve robustness. To address this challenge, we propose an Adaptive-Margin Adversarial Training (AMAT) method, which generates sample-specific adversarial noise for robust DNN training. Unlike existing adversarial training methods tailored for classification, AMAT employs a loss-defined-margin strategy, enabling its application to diverse medical image analysis tasks.

In medical applications, limited availability of large training datasets and benchmarks often restricts the effectiveness of deep neural networks. While computer simulations can efficiently produce extensive, fully annotated datasets with minimal manual intervention—offering a cost-effective alternative to tedious human labeling—models trained on synthetic data typically underperform in real-world settings. 

To address this domain disparity between simulated and actual laparoscopic imagery, we leverage cutting-edge techniques in unpaired image-to-image translation. Building upon an existing translation framework, we enhance its capability to produce a rich variety of realistic synthetic images derived from basic laparoscopy simulations. Crucially, we integrate mechanisms to maintain content consistency during translation, ensuring that annotations from the simulated images remain accurate for their photorealistic counterparts. 

This approach enables the creation of a comprehensive, fully labeled synthetic dataset of laparoscopic images with lifelike visual fidelity. We demonstrate its practical utility by training models for liver segmentation in laparoscopic imagery, achieving average Dice scores as high as 0.89 in certain cases—without relying on any manually labeled laparoscopic data.
