Machine learning-based network traffic classification has been extensively researched. Current methods primarily focus on analyzing complete traffic flows, yet face significant practical constraints. Since routers must process packets with minimal latency, classification decisions cannot be deferred until flow completion. Additionally, sophisticated machine learning models often exceed the computational capacity of router hardware.  

This study proposes flow-packet hybrid traffic classification (FPHTC), an approach where routers classify packets individually using a routing policy derived from a flow-based classifier running externally. We examine FPHTC’s generalization capabilities and demonstrate its superiority over traditional packet-based classification. Through real-world traffic experiments, we show that FPHTC maintains strong classification accuracy despite traffic variability while operating efficiently within limited computational resources.

This study introduces a new method for reconstructing multivariate functions from training data by simultaneously determining an optimal network architecture and initialization through polynomial approximations. The training process of deep neural networks via gradient descent involves navigating the parameter space along the loss landscape to minimize the objective function. Effective parameter initialization plays a crucial role in iterative descent-based training. Our method constructs a network whose initial state represents a polynomial approximation of the training data.  

The key benefit of this approach lies in starting the training process from an informed initial state, enabling efficient refinement through standard optimization techniques. Because the network already captures the underlying data structure, subsequent training is more likely to converge to a favorable local minimum. We outline the theoretical framework for building such networks and present numerical experiments demonstrating that our initialization strategy leads to improved training performance, yielding accurate approximations for a wide range of target functions.

Biological perception relies on attention mechanisms to selectively process specific subsets of sensory data, avoiding the overwhelming computational demands of analyzing all inputs simultaneously. In contrast, computer vision has predominantly focused on soft attention—where features are reweighted and combined rather than discarded—while largely overlooking hard attention, which actively filters out less relevant information.  

This study presents a novel hard attention method that demonstrates competitive performance on recent visual question answering benchmarks, matching or even outperforming comparable soft attention models despite deliberately ignoring certain features. Although hard attention is traditionally considered non-differentiable, we discovered that feature magnitudes serve as a reliable indicator of semantic importance, enabling effective attentional selection.  

Since hard attention focuses only on essential input features, it offers greater efficiency than soft attention, particularly in architectures employing non-local pairwise operations—where computational and memory requirements scale quadratically with feature set size.

We investigate the optimization of finite sums of geodesically smooth functions on Riemannian manifolds. While variance reduction techniques for finite-sum optimization have gained significant interest in recent years, prior research has been confined to vector space settings. We propose Riemannian SVRG (RSVRG), a novel variance-reduced optimization method for Riemannian manifolds. Our analysis covers both geodesically convex and nonconvex (smooth) functions, showing that RSVRG retains the advantages of standard SVRG while incorporating curvature-dependent convergence factors tied to the manifold. To our knowledge, RSVRG is the first stochastic Riemannian optimization method with provable fast convergence. Additionally, we present the first non-asymptotic complexity analysis for nonconvex Riemannian optimization—an advancement even for batch optimization. These findings have broad implications, including a streamlined Riemannian interpretation of variance-reduced PCA, yielding a concise and clear convergence analysis.

This research investigates the cluster head detection challenge in a two-tier unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm network (USNET) comprising multiple UAV clusters, where the intrinsic follow strategy (IFS) between lower-level follower UAVs (FUAVs) and higher-level cluster head UAVs (HUAVs) remains unspecified. We introduce a graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (GASSL) designed to identify HUAVs within individual UAV clusters while simultaneously learning the underlying IFS. Subsequently, we extend this approach by developing a multi-cluster graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (MC-GASSL) capable of handling networks with multiple UAV clusters. The MC-GASSL employs a gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based metric learning scheme for network clustering and utilizes GASSL for HUAV detection within each identified cluster. Experimental results demonstrate that GASSL achieves over 98% average accuracy in detecting HUAVs across single UAV clusters following diverse IFS patterns. Comparative simulations reveal that MC-GASSL surpasses conventional clustering algorithms by at least 10% in clustering purity while efficiently identifying all HUAVs in USNETs with varying IFS configurations and cluster counts, maintaining minimal detection redundancy.

Machine learning models are frequently used to analyze human brain imaging data, aiming to link functional or structural patterns with behavior, health, or other individual traits. These models often depend on simplified representations generated through intricate processing workflows. However, computational pipelines contain inherent numerical instabilities that reduce the accuracy of these representations and introduce systematic errors.  

To address this, we employed Monte Carlo Arithmetic—a method that introduces controlled numerical variations—to modify a structural connectome estimation pipeline. This produced a set of plausible network variations for each sample. The resulting variability was incorporated into an augmented dataset for training an age classification model. Our findings reveal that incorporating these computationally perturbed network variations enhanced classifier performance across all tested methods, preprocessing approaches, and dimensionality reduction techniques. Notably, even minimal perturbations improved model outcomes, demonstrating that small but meaningful variations in the data can enhance predictive accuracy.

Variable selection plays a crucial role in high-dimensional data analysis, with numerous algorithms developed for this purpose. An ideal variable selection method should combine flexibility, scalability, and theoretical reliability—qualities rarely achieved simultaneously by existing approaches. This paper introduces a novel three-step variable selection algorithm that incorporates kernel-based estimation of both the regression function and its gradients, followed by hard thresholding. The method's strength lies in its model-free approach, accommodating general predictor effects while maintaining computational efficiency and strong asymptotic sparsity guarantees.  

The algorithm is adaptable to any reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with diverse kernel functions and can be easily modified for interaction selection. With a computational cost that scales linearly with data dimensionality—and potential for further acceleration through parallel processing—the method offers practical efficiency. Theoretical analysis establishes sparsistency for general RKHS under mild conditions, encompassing both linear and Gaussian kernels as special cases. Extensive simulations and real-world applications demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness across various scenarios.

While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at learning discriminative features, they often struggle to generalize to new, unseen domains. Domain generalization seeks to solve this challenge by training models on multiple source domains to enhance adaptability to unfamiliar environments. This paper introduces an innovative approach that probabilistically blends instance-level feature statistics across source domain training samples. Named MixStyle, our method stems from the insight that visual domains are closely tied to image style (such as photographs versus sketches) – information primarily encoded in a CNN's early layers where we perform style mixing. By synthesizing new domains through style combinations, MixStyle implicitly expands source domain diversity, thereby boosting model generalizability. Designed for seamless integration with mini-batch training, MixStyle offers straightforward implementation. We validate its effectiveness across diverse applications including category classification, instance retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

Computed tomography (CT) often employs automatic exposure control (AEC) to minimize patient radiation exposure. Organ-specific AEC requires an initial CT reconstruction to estimate organ shapes for dose optimization, with real-time reconstruction limited to only a few projections. This study evaluates the performance of automated transform by manifold approximation (AUTOMAP) in such scenarios.  

As a proof of concept, we first tested AUTOMAP’s performance on the MNIST dataset. The dataset, containing all 10 digits, was randomly divided into training and test sets. The model was trained to reconstruct images from either 2 or 4 projections directly. Test results showed accurate reconstructions with false rates of 1.6% and 6.8%, respectively.  

In a follow-up experiment, the MNIST dataset was split differently—the training set included only 9 digits, while the test set contained the excluded digit (e.g., "2"). When reconstructing the digit "2" from 2 projections, the model frequently misclassified it as "3" or "5," resulting in a false rate of 94.4%.  

For medical imaging applications, AUTOMAP was also trained on patient data...

Deep learning holds immense promise for medical imaging applications. However, medical image datasets often suffer from severe class imbalance due to varying disease incidence rates, resulting in poor model performance for rare conditions. While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) offer a potential solution through synthetic image augmentation of underrepresented classes, conventional GANs themselves require substantial training data. To address this challenge, we introduce General-to-detailed GAN (GDGAN), a novel architecture comprising two sequentially connected GANs—one trained on general labels and another on detailed labels. Our approach successfully generated diverse medical images, and models trained on GDGAN-augmented datasets achieved superior performance as measured by the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) compared to existing methods.

Deep convolutional networks typically incorporate additive constant ("bias") terms in their convolution operations to enhance functional mapping capabilities. These bias terms also play a role in training by helping adjust mean responses across image batches—a key aspect of batch normalization. While leading blind denoising approaches like DnCNN rely on these components, we demonstrate that such networks exhibit significant overfitting to their training noise levels, performing poorly when tested on out-of-distribution noise intensities.  

Surprisingly, a simplified architecture completely devoid of bias terms—including those in batch normalization—maintains competitive performance within the trained noise range while demonstrating remarkable generalization to unseen noise levels. Without biases, the network exhibits a locally linear relationship with the input image, allowing its behavior to be examined through linear algebraic techniques. This analysis reveals insights into the network’s operation, showing parallels with adaptive nonlinear filtering and subspace projection methods, bridging the gap between data-driven and classical denoising approaches.

Recent studies in overparametrized learning theory have focused on developing generalization bounds for interpolating models. While these guarantees have been demonstrated for several standard algorithm classes, they remain unexplored for ensemble methods. We introduce an ensemble classification approach that both fits the training data perfectly and maintains consistency across diverse data distributions.  

To achieve this, we propose the manifold-Hilbert kernel for Riemannian manifold-structured data. Our analysis demonstrates that kernel smoothing regression with this kernel achieves weak consistency under the framework established by Devroye et al. (1998). In the case of spherical data, we further show that the manifold-Hilbert kernel can be expressed as a weighted random partition kernel, emerging naturally as an infinite ensemble of partition-based classifiers.

This paper investigates constrained robust (min-max) optimization in a black-box setting, where the optimizer lacks gradient access but can query objective function values. We introduce a novel optimization framework combining a zeroth-order (ZO) gradient estimator with an alternating projected stochastic gradient descent-ascent approach. The ZO estimator requires minimal function queries, while the descent/ascent method performs single-step updates. Our proposed ZO-Min-Max framework achieves sub-linear convergence under mild conditions and exhibits favorable scalability with problem dimension.  

We also examine a compelling link between black-box min-max optimization and adversarial attacks in machine learning, including evasion and poisoning scenarios. Experimental results on these applications confirm the method's effectiveness and demonstrate its scalability to high-dimensional problems where existing black-box solvers fail.

To address the challenges posed by rapidly expanding datasets, improving the efficiency of data analysis and machine learning tools has become a critical focus. While significant progress has been made in traditional array-based computing, these methods often remain constrained by the limitations of single-node systems. This necessitates innovative solutions capable of leveraging distributed architectures, such as multi-node systems with distributed memory.  

In response, we present HeAT—a scalable numerical computing framework designed for high-performance distributed processing with an intuitive NumPy-like interface. Built on PyTorch for local eager execution, HeAT efficiently distributes workloads across large-scale computing clusters using MPI. The framework offers both foundational array operations and advanced algorithmic functionality, enabling seamless scaling for NumPy users and reducing the complexity of distributed data analysis. Benchmark results demonstrate that HeAT outperforms comparable frameworks, delivering performance gains of up to 100x.

This study evaluates and compares commonly employed Bayesian model selection techniques in practical applications, emphasizing their distinctions and providing recommendations for optimal approaches. Specifically, we examine variable subset selection in regression and classification tasks through a series of numerical experiments using both simulated and real-world datasets.  

Our findings reveal that optimizing utility estimates such as cross-validation (CV) scores tends to favor overfitted models, particularly when data is limited, due to high variance in utility estimation. This approach can also introduce significant selection-induced bias and overly optimistic performance assessments for the chosen model.  

From a predictive standpoint, superior results are achieved by incorporating model uncertainty—such as through Bayesian model averaging across candidate models—using a full encompassing model. If the encompassing model is overly complex, robust simplification can be attained via the projection method, which transfers the full model's information onto simpler submodels. Compared to CV-based selection, this strategy demonstrates markedly reduced susceptibility to overfitting. Overall, the projection method proves more effective than selecting the maximum a posteriori model or the most probable candidate.

Research has demonstrated that data-derived features often outperform manually engineered features across various machine learning applications. In music information retrieval (MIR), spectrogram-based learned features frequently exhibit sensitivity to transformations such as transposition or time-shifting, which can be problematic when these variations are unrelated to the target task. To address this, we introduce the Complex Autoencoder (CAE) architecture, designed to learn features that remain stable under orthogonal transformations. The CAE projects signals onto learned complex basis functions, producing two distinct representations: a transformation-invariant "magnitude space" and a transformation-sensitive "phase space." While the phase space helps identify transformations between data pairs, leveraging the invariant properties of the magnitude space enables state-of-the-art performance in audio-to-score alignment and audio segment repetition detection. The CAE's PyTorch implementation, including our repetition detection method, is publicly available.

This study investigates techniques for estimating current occupancy in dynamic environments and forecasting future occupancy levels. The inherent complexity of real-world settings—such as urban streets or densely populated zones—presents ongoing challenges in effectively integrating temporal dynamics with traditional static occupancy models. Our approach quantifies spatial uncertainty of moving entities and integrates this probabilistic data into a continuous occupancy framework modeled within a high-dimensional feature space. Experimental validation using LIDAR datasets confirmed the algorithm's real-time operational capability.

This paper presents a method for learning a control policy in dynamical systems that is both provably safe and guarantees convergence to a desired goal. Safety is defined as avoiding unsafe state regions, while goal-reaching ensures the system's trajectory asymptotically approaches a target region—a generalization of stability. The approach jointly learns two certificate functions using neural networks: a barrier function for safety assurance and a Lyapunov-like function for goal attainment. The method’s effectiveness is demonstrated across multiple systems, including pendulums, cart-poles, and UAVs.

This study introduces a more challenging and realistic framework for intent detection in natural language understanding: Generalized Few-Shot Intent Detection (GFSID). GFSID addresses the task of classifying a combined label space that includes both well-represented intents with abundant labeled data and novel intents with limited examples per class. To tackle this problem, we present a novel approach called Conditional Text Generation with BERT (CG-BERT). Our model harnesses the power of large pre-trained language models to generate label-conditioned text. Through variational inference for utterance distribution modeling, CG-BERT produces diverse samples for novel intents even when trained on minimal examples. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CG-BERT establishes new performance benchmarks for GFSID, achieving superior results in both 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios across two real-world datasets.

Consumers are typically exposed to various online digital advertising channels—such as email marketing, display ads, and paid search engine marketing—throughout their purchasing or subscription journey (commonly referred to as conversion). Marketers collect data from these customer interactions to evaluate the effectiveness of each advertising channel. Understanding the influence of each channel is critical for optimizing budget allocation and pricing strategies.  

Although rule-based and data-driven attribution methods are widely used in marketing, many fail to account for key factors such as cross-channel interactions, temporal dynamics, and user-specific characteristics. To address these limitations, we introduce a deep learning-based attribution algorithm that evaluates the impact of each advertising channel. Our proposed model, the **Deep Neural Net With Attention Multi-Touch Attribution (DNAMTA)**, operates in a supervised learning framework, predicting whether a sequence of touchpoints will lead to conversion. This approach provides deeper insights into the dynamic interplay between media channels.  

Additionally, DNAMTA integrates user-context data—including demographics and behavioral patterns—as control variables to minimize bias in estimating media effects. Through computational experiments on a large real-world marketing dataset, we validate the effectiveness of our model.

Spatial clustering methods excel at multi-channel noise reduction for diverse microphone setups but often struggle to incorporate sophisticated speech and noise models. On the other hand, single-channel LSTM neural networks effectively distinguish speech from noise yet fail to fully leverage the rich spatial data in multi-channel recordings. This paper bridges these approaches by training LSTM speech models to refine the masks produced by the Model-based EM Source Separation and Localization (MESSL) spatial clustering technique. The combined system capitalizes on both the adaptability of multi-channel spatial clustering and the precision of parallel single-channel LSTM speech enhancement. Evaluations on the CHiME-3 dataset of noisy tablet recordings demonstrate that our method enhances speech quality (measured by PESQ) and lowers the word error rate of the baseline CHiME-3 speech recognizer compared to the standard BeamformIt beamformer.

Noise is a major factor contributing to poor-quality Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images. While Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based models have shown exceptional performance in image denoising, OCT image denoising remains a significant challenge. Many existing neural network approaches rely on large amounts of labeled training data, which can be time-consuming and costly to acquire. Additionally, these CNN-based methods often require extensive parameters and careful tuning, placing high demands on hardware resources.  

To address these limitations, we introduce a novel Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Network called **Dual-Merged Cycle-WGAN** for retinal OCT image denoising. This model delivers outstanding results while requiring fewer unlabeled training samples. Our architecture incorporates two Cycle-GAN networks with enhanced generators, discriminators, and Wasserstein loss to improve training stability and performance. By merging features between the two Cycle-GAN networks, our model captures finer details, leading to superior training outcomes.  

Ablation and comparative experiments validate the effectiveness and versatility of our approach. When benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods, our unsupervised technique achieves the best visual quality and higher objective evaluation metrics.

A neural network operating in real-world scenarios may encounter inputs that follow a different distribution than its training data. Extensive research has shown that it’s surprisingly simple to identify or create inputs that deceive neural networks into making highly confident—yet incorrect—predictions. While generative models are often considered resilient to such overconfidence due to their ability to model input feature density and detect out-of-distribution samples, this paper challenges that assumption. Our findings reveal that flow-based models, VAEs, and PixelCNNs fail to reliably distinguish between common object images (e.g., CIFAR-10’s dogs, trucks, and horses) and house number images (SVHN), assigning higher likelihoods to the latter when trained on the former. This anomaly extends to other dataset pairings: FashionMNIST vs. MNIST, CelebA vs. SVHN, and ImageNet vs. CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or SVHN. To explore this unexpected behavior, we focus on flow-based generative models, given their explicit training and evaluation through exact marginal likelihood. Remarkably, this phenomenon persists even when we constrain the flow models to...

Modern end-to-end (E2E) models frequently incorporate language models (LMs) through shallow fusion to enhance both their general performance and rare word recognition. However, existing research indicates that LMs can inadvertently memorize uncommon or unique sequences from their training data. In this study, we develop a framework to identify memorization of artificial textual sequences (termed canaries) in LM training data when limited to black-box query access of an LM-fused speech recognizer rather than direct LM access. Using a production-ready Conformer RNN-T E2E model combined with a Transformer LM, we demonstrate successful detection of memorization for single-occurrence canaries within an LM trained on 300 million samples. Addressing privacy concerns, we further show that per-example gradient-clipped LM training substantially reduces such memorization while maintaining model quality.

We study the universal approximation capability of two-layer neural networks with random weights that are approximately Gaussian, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence. This investigation is inspired by recent research on lazy training, where stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates produce only minor deviations from the initial i.i.d. Gaussian weight distribution.  

First, we examine the mean-field scenario, replacing the finite set of hidden-layer neurons with a continuous ensemble. Here, the problem transforms into globally minimizing a free-energy functional defined on the space of probability measures over the weights. This functional balances the \(L^2\) approximation error against the KL divergence relative to a centered Gaussian prior. We identify the unique global minimizer of this functional and subsequently construct a controlled nonlinear dynamics framework in the space of weight probability measures, solving a McKean–Vlasov optimal control problem.  

This control problem is closely linked to the Schrödinger bridge (or entropic optimal transport) problem, with its optimal value being proportional to the minimal free energy. Finally, we demonstrate that SGD under lazy training conditions—achieved by jointly adjusting the Gaussian prior’s variance and the entropic regularization—approximates this optimal dynamics.

A key objective in research on deep generative models is their ability to produce novel samples beyond those encountered in the training data. This study examines the extent to which variational autoencoders (VAEs)—commonly used architectures—fulfill this property. VAEs optimize a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood, indicating that, given sufficient decoder capacity, they should theoretically overfit the training data. With an infinitely expressive decoder, the ideal generative model becomes a uniform mixture over the training dataset. More broadly, an optimal decoder would generate outputs as weighted averages of training examples, where the weights depend on latent space proximity. This suggests that high-capacity VAE encoders and decoders should effectively perform nearest-neighbor reconstruction based on latent coordinates.

To evaluate this hypothesis, we assess generalization performance on the MNIST dataset, considering both within-class generalization (new samples of seen classes) and out-of-class generalization (unseen classes). In both scenarios, we observe that reconstructions closely approximate nearest-neighbor matches.

This paper presents **CANDIES (Combined Approach for Novelty Detection in Intelligent Embedded Systems)**, a novel method for detecting emerging anomalies in technical systems. 

Technical systems often involve multiple interacting processes monitored through sensors. These sensor observations can be modeled probabilistically, with each component in our parametric mixture density ideally corresponding to an underlying real-world process. During operation, however, unexpected events—such as system failures—can introduce new processes, generating previously unseen data that necessitates model adaptation.  

CANDIES leverages Gaussian mixture models, which also support classification tasks. Novel processes may arise in either low-density regions (where few samples were previously observed) or high-density regions (already well-populated with data). While most existing solutions focus on low-density novelty detection, identifying anomalies in high-density regions is more challenging. Our approach introduces an efficient online technique to detect emerging processes even in high-density areas.

Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum serves as a cornerstone algorithm for training large-scale predictive models. This paper introduces a novel analytical framework to study mini-batch SGD in linear models, examining the interplay between momentum and batch size. Our central insight involves characterizing the sequence of loss values through its generating function, which takes a concise form under a diagonal approximation of the model weights' second moments. Through this analytical lens, we derive insights into convergence criteria, the model's phase dynamics, and optimal training configurations. Key findings include: 1) Optimization trajectories typically transition from a "signal-dominated" to a "noise-dominated" regime at predictable time scales; 2) While large effective learning rates prove advantageous in the "signal-dominated" phase, they must be constrained for finite batch sizes to prevent instability; 3) Negative momentum can yield optimal convergence rates. We validate these theoretical predictions through extensive numerical experiments on MNIST and synthetic datasets, demonstrating strong quantitative agreement.

We present a model-free relax-and-round approach for k-means clustering, building upon Peng and Wei's semidefinite relaxation. This method treats the SDP solution as a denoised representation of the input data before converting it into a discrete clustering solution. Our framework offers a general proof technique for establishing performance bounds, with specific analysis conducted for subgaussian mixture models. Additionally, we examine the fundamental estimation limits of Gaussian cluster centers via k-means clustering to benchmark our approximation guarantee against the theoretically optimal k-means solution.

Segmentation methods that rely on supervised learning generally need extensive annotated training data to achieve strong generalization during testing. However, in medical applications, assembling such datasets is impractical, as obtaining large volumes of expert-annotated samples is both costly and time-intensive. As a result, various techniques have been developed to address learning with limited labeled examples. Yet, existing approaches have not shown substantial improvements over simple random data augmentation for image segmentation, which itself struggles to achieve high accuracy.  

In this work, we introduce a novel task-driven data augmentation approach designed for learning with scarce labeled data. Our method optimizes a synthetic data generator specifically for the segmentation task. The generator captures variations in intensity and shape through two transformation sets: additive intensity adjustments and deformation fields. Both transformations are refined using labeled and unlabeled data within a semi-supervised learning framework.  

Experiments conducted on three medical datasets—cardiac, prostate, and pancreas—demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses standard augmentation techniques and other semi-supervised methods in limited-annotation scenarios. The code is available at: [https://github.com/krishnabits001/task_driven_data_augmentation](https://github.com/krishnabits001/task_driven_data_augmentation).

In recent years, machine learning has grown increasingly prevalent in the study of lattice field theories. A key feature of these theories is their symmetries, which—when incorporated into neural network design—can significantly enhance performance and generalization. Among these, translational equivariance is particularly important for physical systems on lattices with periodic boundary conditions. This work explores the benefits of using translationally equivariant neural networks compared to non-equivariant architectures.  

Our analysis focuses on a two-dimensional lattice system described by a complex scalar field with quartic interaction, operating in the flux representation. Here, neural networks perform various regression and classification tasks. Through a systematic search, we identify promising equivariant and non-equivariant architectures. Our results show that, in most cases, the best equivariant models outperform their non-equivariant counterparts not only in interpolating physical parameters beyond the training set but also in scaling to different lattice sizes—demonstrating superior generalization.

This study presents a Transformer Neural Network approach for learning a Generative Model from just one path-based example image. Additionally, we illustrate how to create a dataset derived from the sample image and leverage the model to produce numerous variations that preserve the original image's style and underlying concept.

The recently introduced "generalized min-max" (GMM) kernel can be efficiently linearized, enabling direct applications in large-scale statistical learning and fast approximate nearest neighbor search. Extensive comparisons have been made between the linearized GMM kernel and the linearized radial basis function (RBF) kernel. Across numerous classification tasks, the tuning-free GMM kernel surprisingly performs competitively against even the best-tuned RBF kernel. However, it stands to reason that introducing tuning parameters could further enhance the GMM kernel's performance.  

This paper explores three straightforward approaches to creating tunable GMM kernels:  
(i) the exponentiated-GMM (eGMM) kernel,  
(ii) the powered-GMM (pGMM) kernel, and  
(iii) the exponentiated-powered-GMM (epGMM) kernel.  

Notably, the pGMM kernel retains the possibility of efficient linearization by adapting the original GMM kernel's hashing procedure.  

Through experimentation on approximately 60 publicly available classification datasets, we confirm that these tunable GMM kernels generally outperform the original GMM kernel. The performance gains are sometimes remarkably substantial—on 11 benchmark datasets previously used to evaluate deep learning algorithms and tree-based methods, our results demonstrate that the proposed tunable GMM kernels compete strongly against both deep neural networks and tree-based approaches. Earlier research developed tree methods such as "abc-robust-logitboost," which, along with these findings, further highlight the potential of enhanced GMM kernels.

In electronic health records (EHRs), research takes a backseat to patient care and billing as a tertiary priority. This results in data that is neither standardized nor optimized for machine learning applications. Inconsistencies arise from variations in clinician input, differing diagnostic approaches—such as choice of lab tests—and frequent missing data points. Additionally, research-grade annotations are scarce, reducing sample sizes and introducing variability in reference standards. While longitudinal patient data is crucial for disease understanding, most machine learning models rely on static, single-timepoint inputs for analysis. Another barrier is the lack of interpretability in black-box algorithms, which limits their clinical utility.  

This chapter explores these challenges and others related to applying machine learning to structured EHR data—such as demographics, family history, medications, vitals, lab results, and genetic testing. While it does not address feature extraction from imaging or unstructured clinical notes, the methods discussed can integrate such features if available.

Chemical kinetics and reaction engineering provides the theoretical foundation for analyzing reaction mechanisms, enhancing reaction efficiency, and designing chemical processes systematically. In this work, we employ feed-forward artificial neural networks as fundamental components to numerically solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) governed by differential algebraic equations (DAEs) that represent microkinetic models (MKMs). We introduce an algebraic framework for mathematically defining and categorizing reaction networks, elementary reaction types, and chemical species.  

Using this framework, we show that jointly optimizing neural networks and kinetic model parameters within a regularized multi-objective optimization scheme enables solving the inverse problem—estimating kinetic parameters from simulated experimental data. We explore various scenarios to determine the feasibility of extracting kinetic parameters from transient kinetic data and evaluate the method’s resilience against statistical noise. This approach to solving inverse kinetic ODE problems can facilitate the determination of reaction mechanisms using transient experimental observations.

Learning management systems (LMS) have become integral to education across all levels, serving as platforms for student administration, course delivery, progress tracking, and performance reporting. Within this context, automated exam generation has gained attention as a means to enhance learning outcome evaluation. However, research in this area remains nascent, with significant opportunities for improving the quality of generated exams.  

Current approaches overlook two critical challenges. First, existing methods cannot ensure that an exam produces a target score distribution for a class or across multiple classes. Second, while common in practice, there is no solution for generating paired exams that are assessment-equivalent (yielding comparable student results) while containing substantially different questions.  

To address these gaps, this paper introduces **ExamGAN** (Exam Script Generative Adversarial Network), a framework for producing high-quality exam scripts. We further extend this model to **T-ExamGAN** (Twin-ExamGAN), capable of generating exam pairs that meet both equivalence and diversity criteria.

Collaborative personalization—particularly through learned user embeddings—can substantially enhance prediction accuracy in neural network models. We introduce Federated User Representation Learning (FURL), a simple, scalable, and privacy-preserving approach that efficiently leverages existing neural personalization techniques within Federated Learning (FL). FURL partitions model parameters into federated and private categories. Unlike federated parameters, private parameters—including user embeddings—are trained locally and never shared or aggregated on the server.  

Theoretically, we demonstrate that this parameter division does not disrupt training for most personalization methods. By storing user embeddings locally, FURL not only safeguards privacy but also enhances memory locality for personalization compared to server-based training. Our experiments on two datasets show significant improvements, with model performance increasing by 8% and 51%, while maintaining near-centralized accuracy with only 0% and 4% reductions. Additionally, we find that user embeddings learned in FL closely resemble those from centralized training, confirming that FURL effectively enables collaborative learning through shared parameters without compromising privacy.

Rural electrification requires cost-effective solutions like single wire earth return (SWER) networks. Remote areas face rising energy demands, and existing infrastructure may soon be insufficient. Additionally, high impedance arcing faults (HIF) in SWER systems can trigger devastating bushfires, as seen during the 2009 Black Saturday disaster. To address these challenges, reliable remote electricity networks can be created by dividing existing systems into microgrids, repurposing SWER lines to link these microgrids. Building resilient networks with improved demand management depends on implementing a comprehensive condition monitoring system across the entire network.  

As the first key contribution of this research, a distributed online monitoring platform is introduced, integrating power quality monitoring, real-time HIF detection, and transient classification in SWER networks. AI-based techniques are developed to accurately classify faults and transients, achieving a 98.67% HIF detection accuracy while reducing latency to 115.2 ms. Secondly, a method for identifying remote consumer loads is proposed, detecting load types through transient analysis. An edge computing-based architecture enables high-frequency analysis for real-time load identification, with the approach validated through real-world testing.

The effectiveness of semi-supervised learning depends heavily on its ability to scale to vast amounts of unlabeled data, which is essential for capturing the underlying manifold structure and improving classification. However, computing pairwise similarities across large datasets is computationally impractical for most input types, leaving a gap in accessible, ready-to-use semi-supervised learning methods capable of handling tens of millions or more data points.  

In this paper, we leverage two low-rank label propagation techniques—Global Linear Neighborhood Propagation (GLNP) and Kernel Nyström Approximation—and introduce a parallelized implementation optimized using Nesterov’s accelerated projected gradient descent, forming our Big-data Label Propagation (BigLP) framework. These parallel algorithms were evaluated on five real-world datasets, spanning from 7,000 to 10 million samples, along with a synthetic dataset of 100 million samples.  

Our experiments show that the BigLP implementation efficiently scales to datasets with 100 million samples and hundreds of features, while also enhancing prediction accuracy even when only a minimal fraction of the data is labeled. These findings highlight BigLP’s strong scalability for large-scale data and its effectiveness in leveraging unlabeled samples for semi-supervised learning.

High-dimensional integration is essential across various scientific disciplines. To address this computational challenge, advanced numerical techniques have been devised. We present **i-flow**, a Python package designed for high-dimensional numerical integration using normalizing flows—machine-learned bijective transformations between probability distributions. Beyond integration, i-flow efficiently generates random samples from complex high-dimensional distributions. Benchmarks demonstrate its superior performance over alternative methods when evaluating correlated high-dimensional integrals. The open-source code is available on GitLab: [https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow](https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow).

In machine learning, likelihood-free inference involves analyzing data without relying on an explicit analytical model. This study explores the use of Neural Spline Flows—a neural density estimation technique—for likelihood-free inference in measuring neutrino oscillation parameters within Long Baseline experiments. A specialized approach for physics parameter estimation is introduced and tested specifically on the muon neutrino disappearance analysis within the T2K experiment.

We introduce a generalized framework that encompasses the Cauchy/Lorentzian, Geman-McClure, Welsch/Leclerc, generalized Charbonnier, Charbonnier/pseudo-Huber/L1-L2, and L2 loss functions. By parameterizing robustness as a continuous variable, our loss function extends the capabilities of robust loss minimization algorithms, enhancing performance in fundamental vision tasks like registration and clustering.  

When interpreted as the negative log of a univariate density, our formulation gives rise to a broad probability distribution that includes both normal and Cauchy distributions as specific instances. This probabilistic perspective allows neural networks to automatically adapt loss robustness during training, boosting performance in learning-based applications such as generative image synthesis and unsupervised monocular depth estimation—eliminating the need for manual parameter adjustment.

We present **Sparse Sinkhorn Attention**, an efficient and sparse approach for learning attention mechanisms. Our method leverages differentiable sorting of internal representations through a learned meta sorting network that produces latent sequence permutations. By operating on sorted sequences, we enable quasi-global attention using only local windows, significantly boosting memory efficiency. Key innovations include **Causal Sinkhorn Balancing** and **SortCut**—a dynamic sequence truncation technique that adapts Sinkhorn Attention for both encoding and decoding tasks. Extensive experiments across seq2seq sorting, language modeling, image generation, document classification, and natural language inference demonstrate that our memory-efficient approach matches standard attention performance while surpassing recent efficient Transformer variants like Sparse Transformers.

Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) with complex leaf probability distributions are known to be highly effective tractable-inference probabilistic models. While extensive research has focused on learning the internal parameters, training complex leaf distributions remains largely unexplored, with only limited solutions for specific cases.  

This paper presents an efficient Expectation-Maximization (EM)-based approach to learn a broad class of leaf distributions. The EM updates take the form of simple weighted maximum likelihood problems, enabling the use of any distribution trainable via maximum likelihood—even with approximate methods. The algorithm scales linearly with model size and maintains convergence even under partial optimization.  

We validate our method through density estimation experiments on twenty real-world datasets, using tree-structured graphical models as leaves. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art parameter learning techniques while employing SPNs with significantly fewer parameters.

Deep reinforcement learning has proven highly effective for training policies that process complex, high-dimensional sensory inputs to perform actions in challenging environments like Atari games. This paper investigates how temporal abstraction through output representation modeling can enhance the convergence and stability of deep reinforcement learning methods. Focusing specifically on macro-actions, we demonstrate their effectiveness across various Atari 2600 games, where they substantially accelerate learning. Our results indicate that these macro-actions not only speed up training but can also surpass the performance of DQN in certain cases. We provide detailed analysis of both convergence patterns and final outcomes, highlighting a key challenge faced by deep RL methods when dealing with sparse reward signals.

This study examines physics-based and data-driven reconstruction methods for combined positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems, highlighting their clinical benefits in oncology, neurology, and cardiology. The reconstruction strategies integrate structural or statistical priors with the physical modeling of PET system responses. Given the nested formulation of the forward problem, direct PET/MRI reconstruction remains nonlinear. We demonstrate how hybrid data-physics machine learning enables 3D PET/MRI reconstruction, outlining recent advances in deep learning over the past five years to overcome challenges in attenuation correction, scatter reduction, low-count statistics, and data fidelity. Additionally, we explore how these multimodal techniques enhance radiation therapy planning beyond PET/MRI applications. Finally, we identify future directions for advancing the field through emerging trends in physics-informed deep learning and next-generation detector technologies.

Inverse problems—including parameter estimation and optimal control—play a crucial role in scientific research. Experimental setups frequently gather data iteratively, relying on machine learning algorithms to rapidly solve these inverse problems. However, existing state-of-the-art training methods often struggle with physical processes due to unstable gradients, where both magnitude and direction vary widely.  

To address this, we introduce a hybrid training strategy that integrates higher-order optimization with machine learning. By replacing standard gradients with a novel "physical gradient," we incorporate domain-specific knowledge directly into the training process, embedding prior assumptions about the solution space. Our approach demonstrates substantial improvements across diverse physical systems, proving effective in optimizing and learning tasks.

In optimization, gradient-based methods are highly efficient when applied to strictly convex and well-conditioned objective functions, often achieving exponential convergence rates. However, traditional Lasso-type estimators typically fail to reach optimal convergence rates because of the poor behavior of the absolute function near zero.  

To address this, a homotopic approach employs a series of surrogate functions to approximate the $\ell_1$ penalty used in Lasso estimators. These surrogate functions gradually converge to the $\ell_1$ penalty while maintaining strict convexity, ensuring a provably faster numerical convergence rate.  

This paper demonstrates that by carefully designing these surrogate functions, we can achieve a superior convergence rate compared to existing methods for Lasso-type estimators. While state-of-the-art algorithms currently guarantee only $O(1/\epsilon)$ or $O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ rates, our proposed method attains an $O([\log(1/\epsilon)]^2)$ convergence rate. Empirical results further confirm the enhanced performance of our algorithm in practice.

A novel approach for training variational autoencoders (VAEs) is introduced, leveraging Stein variational gradient descent. This method eliminates the need for parametric assumptions about the encoder distribution, offering greater flexibility. By combining the proposed encoder with importance sampling, performance is significantly improved. The technique achieves strong results on various unsupervised and semi-supervised tasks, including large-scale semi-supervised learning on ImageNet, showcasing its effectiveness for high-dimensional datasets.

We present a low-complexity decentralized learning method for training a large neural network across distributed processing nodes (workers). The system operates on a synchronized communication network modeled as a doubly-stochastic mixing matrix, eliminating the need for a central master node. The training data remains distributed among workers and is not shared during training to preserve privacy and security. By combining the alternating-direction-method-of-multipliers (ADMM) with layerwise convex optimization, our approach reduces both computational complexity and inter-worker communication costs. The method achieves comparable learning performance to centralized training where all data is pooled together. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's time efficiency and convergence properties.

Maillard's 2013 PhD dissertation introduces a relatively obscure algorithm for the $K$-armed bandit problem. This lesser-known approach, referred to as Maillard sampling (MS), calculates arm selection probabilities in closed form—a key advantage over the more widely used Thompson sampling. This closed-form property makes MS-generated bandit data immediately suitable for counterfactual evaluation, unlike Thompson sampling. Recognizing this benefit, we revisit MS and provide an enhanced analysis demonstrating its asymptotic optimality along with a $\sqrt{KT\log{T}}$ minimax regret bound, matching the performance bounds of asymptotically optimal UCB algorithms. We further develop an improved variant, MS$^+$, which reduces the minimax bound to $\sqrt{KT\log{K}}$. Notably, MS$^+$ can be adjusted for more aggressive exploration (reduced exploration) while maintaining asymptotic optimality—a distinctive capability not found in existing bandit algorithms. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of MS$^+$.

The modeling unit and model architecture are crucial components of the Recurrent Neural Network Transducer (RNN-T) in end-to-end speech recognition. To enhance RNN-T performance for Mandarin speech recognition, this study introduces a novel transformer transducer architecture that integrates self-attention transformers with RNNs. We also investigate the selection of different modeling units for the transformer transducer. Furthermore, a new mixed-bandwidth training approach is proposed to develop a unified model capable of accurately recognizing Mandarin speech across multiple sampling rates.  

All experiments were conducted on approximately 12,000 hours of Mandarin speech data with sampling rates of 8kHz and 16kHz. Results demonstrate that the transformer transducer using tonal syllables achieves the highest performance, delivering an average relative improvement of 14.4% and 44.1% in Word Error Rate (WER) compared to models using tonal syllable initial/final units and Chinese characters, respectively. Additionally, it outperforms tonal syllable initial/final-based models with an average 13.5% reduction in Character Error Rate (CER).

Patent records offer detailed insights into technological innovations but lack information on inventors’ ethnic backgrounds. This study employs supervised learning methods to estimate ethnic origins from inventor names. Using a labeled dataset of 95,202 names, I develop a long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network model to classify names across 17 ethnic categories, achieving 91% accuracy. Applying this model to 2.68 million inventor records yields new descriptive findings on ethnic origin distribution patterns across time periods, countries, and technology sectors. The analysis reveals growing global ethnic diversity in recent decades, primarily driven by rising representation of inventors of Asian origin. While foreign-origin inventors remain most concentrated in the United States, their presence has expanded across other high-income economies. Notably, U.S. growth stems from increasing non-Western inventors in cutting-edge technology fields—a pattern not observed in other developed nations.

In the universal hypothesis testing framework, which involves distinguishing a known null hypothesis distribution from an unknown alternative, Hoeffding introduced a universal test in the 1960s. His test statistic is expressed in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (K-L) divergence between the empirical distribution of observations and the null distribution. This paper explores a modified version of Hoeffding's test, substituting the K-L divergence with a relaxed version known as the mismatched divergence.  

The mismatched test is demonstrated to be a generalized likelihood-ratio test (GLRT) for scenarios where the alternative distribution belongs to a finite-dimensional parametric family—effectively solving the associated composite hypothesis testing problem. Under certain conditions, both Hoeffding's test and the mismatched test exhibit identical asymptotic performance in terms of error exponents. This finding implies that the GLRT is optimal for distinguishing a specific distribution from others within an exponential family. Furthermore, the mismatched test offers notable advantages over Hoeffding's test in finite-sample settings.

Dual decomposition offers a practical approach for developing algorithms to identify the most probable (MAP) configuration in graphical models. However, in many real-world inference tasks, the standard decomposition suffers from a large integrality gap caused by frustrated cycles. Tightening this relaxation can be achieved by incorporating additional constraints that enforce cycle consistency. Previous research demonstrated that cluster-pursuit algorithms—which iteratively introduce cycle and higher-order consistency constraints—can accurately solve numerous challenging inference problems. However, these methods rely on explicitly enumerating candidate clusters, restricting their application to triplets or other short cycles.  

We address the cycle constraint search problem by introducing a nearly linear-time algorithm capable of identifying the most frustrated cycle of any length. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this search algorithm integrates with dual decomposition and cluster-pursuit techniques. The resulting method successfully solves MAP inference problems in relational classification and stereo vision with exact results.

In the supervised training framework, we focus on acquiring task-specific word embeddings. The process begins with initial embeddings derived from unlabeled data, which are then refined to generate embeddings tailored to the supervised training dataset. A challenge arises with words in the test set that were not present during training—these must rely on either their initial embeddings or a generic unknown embedding, frequently resulting in inaccuracies. To mitigate this, we propose a neural network trained to transform initial embeddings into the task-specific embedding space using a multi-loss objective function. While this approach is broadly applicable, we specifically illustrate its effectiveness in enhancing dependency parsing, particularly for sentences containing out-of-vocabulary terms, as well as achieving better performance in sentiment analysis tasks.

The National Football League partnered with Amazon Web Services to create an advanced sports injury monitoring and prevention program through a Kaggle competition. The initiative aims to accurately link each helmet to specific players, enabling precise tracking of their impact exposures during gameplay. Our project involves developing computer vision-based machine learning algorithms that assign helmet collisions to the correct players using tracking data. This paper outlines our method for automating helmet detection, tracking, and impact analysis. The system will also enable retrospective play reviews and long-term exposure trend analysis.

This study presents DiCOVA-Net, a deep residual network approach for detecting COVID-19 infection through cough sound analysis. The classification task presents data imbalance challenges, with significantly fewer infected cases than healthy samples. To enhance minority class recognition, we implement both data augmentation and cost-sensitive learning strategies. We further adapt the pre-trained ResNet50 architecture through specialized fine-tuning techniques tailored to this application. For improved generalization, our framework employs ensemble learning to combine predictions from multiple base classifiers trained with varying random seeds. Experimental evaluation on the DiCOVA benchmark dataset demonstrates the method's effectiveness, achieving competitive performance with an 85.43% AUC score that ranks among the top results in the challenge.

Phase retrieval involves recovering images using only intensity measurements. In practical scenarios, this problem is often underconstrained. Recent approaches employ generative models trained on available datasets to narrow down possible solutions. Yet, these models cannot perfectly represent all potential solutions, introducing approximation errors.  

To address this representation error in phase retrieval, we propose two key improvements. First, we adapt intermediate layer optimization (ILO) in a novel way to expand the generator’s capacity while maintaining output consistency with training data. Second, we develop new initialization strategies that enhance reconstruction quality. Through extensive testing on Fourier and Gaussian phase retrieval tasks, along with detailed ablation studies, we demonstrate the advantages of our modified ILO and initialization techniques.

The surge in smartphone adoption has brought with it a parallel escalation in mobile malware, both in volume and sophistication. Android, now the dominant mobile platform, has faced a particularly sharp rise in malicious software targeting its ecosystem. Alarmingly, modern Android malware exhibits increasingly advanced techniques to bypass conventional signature-based detection systems. This leaves app marketplaces vulnerable to hosting harmful applications that may go undetected until downloaded by unsuspecting users. To address this critical issue, this paper proposes a robust solution utilizing Bayesian classification models derived from static code analysis. These models leverage various code and application attributes that serve as markers for potentially malicious behavior. The effectiveness of the approach is validated through testing with real-world malware samples, with experimental results illustrating its detection capabilities.

Kernel ridge regression (KRR) is a widely used approach for non-linear, non-parametric learning. However, current KRR implementations demand that all data be stored in main memory, significantly restricting its applicability when datasets surpass available memory capacity—a common scenario in data mining, bioinformatics, and control applications.  

To address this limitation, the streaming computational model offers an efficient solution by processing data sequentially, handling one sample at a time and discarding it before proceeding to the next. In this work, we introduce **StreaMRAK**, a streaming adaptation of KRR. StreaMRAK advances conventional KRR by structuring the problem into multiple resolution levels, enabling continuous prediction refinement. By incrementally incorporating new samples, the algorithm optimizes memory efficiency while maintaining model accuracy.  

Additionally, StreaMRAK employs an innovative sub-sampling strategy that minimizes both memory and computational costs by generating a concise data sketch. This technique dynamically adjusts sub-sampling density based on kernel bandwidth and local data dimensionality. We validate our approach through experimental evaluations on two synthetic benchmarks and a real-world trajectory prediction task.

We introduce a novel estimation approach for topic models that differs fundamentally from existing simplex-based methods and automatically determines the number of topics K from the data. Our work establishes both finite-sample minimax lower bounds for estimating A and corresponding upper bounds for our proposed estimator, identifying conditions under which our method achieves minimax adaptivity. The analysis remains valid across all ranges of documents (n), document lengths (N_i), dictionary sizes (p), and topic counts (K), accommodating scenarios where both p and K grow with n—a challenging case inadequately addressed by prior work. Extensive simulations demonstrate our algorithm's superior speed and accuracy compared to existing methods, despite operating at an initial disadvantage: unlike the comparison methods that receive the true K value in our experiments, our approach must estimate this parameter. The simulations validate both our theoretical findings and the practical advantages of our method.

Even in worst-case situations, the junction tree algorithm continues to be the most broadly applicable exact MAP inference method with guaranteed polynomial runtime. However, its key feasibility constraint—requiring bounded treewidth in the corresponding MRF—severely restricts its practical applicability. Many real-world structured prediction tasks demand the modeling of global dependencies, whether through introducing global factors or imposing global constraints on prediction variables. Such constraints inevitably produce fully connected graphs, rendering exact inference via this algorithm infeasible.  

Earlier studies [1]–[4] addressing loss-augmented inference have shown how models with specialized global factors—representing non-decomposable loss functions in SSVM training—can enable efficient inference. In this work, we generalize the efficient exact inference framework introduced in [3], permitting richer interactions between the core model’s energy and the sufficient statistics of global terms without added computational overhead. We validate our method across multiple applications, including one beyond the scope of prior approaches. Precise electricity demand predictions are vital for sustainable energy systems. To enhance decision-making, particularly for end-user demand flexibility, forecasts must not only be accurate but also clear and practical. While traditional univariate forecasting methods have limitations, Global Forecasting Models (GFMs)—trained across multiple time series—have demonstrated superior performance in recent demand forecasting competitions and real-world applications.  

To bridge the gap between accuracy and interpretability in global forecasting, we introduce **Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Rule-based Explanations for Forecasting (LIMREF)**. This framework generates **k-optimal impact rules** for individual forecasts, treating the GFM as a black box in a model-agnostic manner. LIMREF produces two key types of explanations:  
- **Forecast interpretation rules**—clarifying how the model arrives at its predictions.  
- **Counterfactual rules**—providing actionable insights on input adjustments to alter forecasted outcomes.  

We validate LIMREF using a large-scale electricity demand dataset, incorporating external factors like temperature and calendar effects. Our evaluation assesses the framework’s explanatory power through both qualitative and quantitative metrics, ensuring meaningful and reliable insights for energy system operators.

This paper investigates multi-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) enabled mobile edge computing (MEC), referred to as UAVE, where multiple UAVs serve as aerial computing platforms to provide computational resources to ground-based user equipment (UEs). Unlike traditional fixed-location MEC systems, UAVE offers distinct advantages for temporary events, emergency scenarios, and on-demand services due to its flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and rapid deployment capability.  

Nevertheless, UAVE operations present several challenges, particularly in optimizing: 1) the association between multiple UEs and UAVs, and 2) the allocation of UAV resources to UEs while minimizing overall UE energy consumption. To address these challenges, we formulate the problem as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, which is computationally complex, especially in large-scale scenarios. To solve it efficiently, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based User Association and Resource Allocation (RLAA) algorithm.  

Simulation results demonstrate that RLAA achieves near-optimal performance when compared to exhaustive search in small-scale scenarios, while outperforming other benchmark algorithms in large-scale implementations.

Effective product question answering (PQA) is critical for e-commerce platforms, as timely and precise responses enhance user experience. While manual responses on community Q&A platforms are slow and difficult to scale, recent research demonstrates that product reviews can serve as a valuable resource for real-time automated PQA.  

Existing literature approaches PQA as a retrieval task, where the objective is to identify the most relevant reviews in response to a given product question. However, this paper addresses two key challenges: answerability and answer reliability. We recognize that many questions may lack answers within a finite set of available reviews. In such cases, returning irrelevant reviews—rather than a nil response—can significantly degrade user satisfaction.  

Furthermore, for answerable questions, only the most pertinent reviews should be included in the response. To enhance reliability, we introduce a conformal prediction-based framework that filters out unreliable answers, ensuring results are both precise and concise. This framework also identifies unanswerable queries, allowing the system to return nil answers when appropriate. Experimental results validate our approach.

We introduce a new neural topic model built within the Wasserstein autoencoder (WAE) framework. In contrast to current variational autoencoder-based approaches, we directly impose a Dirichlet prior on latent document-topic vectors. By leveraging the latent space structure and employing an appropriate kernel for minimizing Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), we achieve effective distribution matching. Our findings reveal that MMD substantially outperforms Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in aligning high-dimensional Dirichlet distributions. Additionally, we demonstrate that introducing randomness in the encoder output during training yields notably more coherent topics. To assess topic diversity, we present a straightforward topic uniqueness metric. Combined with the established NPMI coherence measure, this provides a more comprehensive evaluation of topic quality. Experimental results across multiple real-world datasets confirm that our model generates topics of significantly higher quality than existing methods.

Variational approximations for Gaussian processes (GPs) commonly employ a limited set of inducing points to construct a low-rank covariance matrix approximation. In contrast, this work leverages a sparse precision matrix approximation. We introduce the variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process (VNNGP), which incorporates a prior preserving correlations only among K nearest-neighbor observations—resulting in a sparse precision structure.  

Within the variational framework, VNNGP’s objective factorizes efficiently across both observations and inducing points, allowing for stochastic optimization with O($K^3$) time complexity. This makes it possible to scale the number of inducing points arbitrarily, including placing them at every observed location.  

Through extensive experiments, we compare VNNGP with other scalable GP methods, showing that it (1) significantly outperforms low-rank approximations and (2) exhibits greater resistance to overfitting compared to alternative nearest-neighbor approaches.

Online meta-learning is becoming a key technology for enabling edge intelligence within IoT systems. However, a major challenge—known as the "cold-start" problem—arises when a single agent must learn from numerous tasks to develop an effective meta-model for rapid within-task adaptation. Recognizing that learning tasks across multiple agents in a network often exhibit model similarities, we explore a fundamental question: *"Can limited communication accelerate online meta-learning among agents, and if so, to what extent?"*  

To address this, we introduce a multi-agent online meta-learning framework formulated as a two-level nested online convex optimization (OCO) problem. By analyzing the upper bound of the agent-task-averaged regret, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of multi-agent online meta-learning hinges on the extent to which an agent can improve its meta-model through distributed network-level OCO with constrained communication—an aspect that remains poorly understood.  

To overcome this challenge, we propose a distributed online gradient descent algorithm with gradient tracking. This method allows each agent to estimate the global gradient efficiently, requiring just one communication step with neighboring agents per iteration. The approach achieves an average regret of \( O(\sqrt{T/N}) \) per agent, highlighting—
