Answer-agnostic question generation presents a challenging yet important task, focusing on automatically creating questions from a given sentence without relying on predefined answers. This paper introduces two novel approaches to address this problem: question type prediction and an enhanced copy loss mechanism. The question type prediction module enables our model to identify appropriate question formats, allowing diverse question generation for a single input sentence. Meanwhile, the improved copy loss mechanism strengthens the original copy technique by ensuring all key words from the source text are effectively incorporated during question formulation. Our combined model achieves superior performance compared to existing methods in answer-agnostic question generation, reaching a BLEU-4 score of 13.9 on the SQuAD dataset. Human assessments confirm the quality of the generated questions. The implementation code will be made publicly available to support future research efforts.

Langevin diffusion is an effective technique for nonconvex optimization that helps escape local minima through gradient noise injection. The noise level, controlled by a temperature parameter, creates a tradeoff between high-temperature "global exploration" and low-temperature "local exploitation." To combine the benefits of both regimes, we introduce replica exchange—swapping between two Langevin diffusions at distinct temperatures. We analyze the acceleration effect of this method theoretically from two angles: (i) χ²-divergence convergence and (ii) the large deviation principle. This acceleration enables faster convergence toward global minima. Additionally, discretizing the replica exchange Langevin diffusion yields a practical algorithm. We provide theoretical bounds on its discretization error and validate its accelerated performance empirically.

Researchers often analyze complex time-varying systems by focusing on population-level dynamics rather than the behavior of individual components. While this approach simplifies modeling, it risks overlooking how each element contributes to the broader system. In this work, we introduce an innovative transformer architecture designed to learn from time-varying data while capturing both individual trajectories and collective dynamics. Instead of aggregating data upfront, our separable architecture processes individual time-series sequentially before integrating them—ensuring permutation invariance and enabling adaptability across systems of varying sizes. After validating our model's ability to uncover intricate interactions in many-body systems, we test it on neural populations within the nervous system. Our multi-scale transformer not only achieves strong neural decoding accuracy but also excels in cross-system generalization. The findings demonstrate that knowledge acquired from one animal’s neural activity can be effectively transferred to model neurons in another.

Recent studies have revealed that deep learning models trained through full supervision tend to depend on "shortcut" features—input patterns correlated with target outcomes in training data but unreliable or absent during testing or real-world deployment. Our experimental findings demonstrate that modern self-supervised models, particularly those trained on both images and text, yield more robust image representations while decreasing dependence on visual shortcut features in a practical medical imaging scenario. We also observe that these self-supervised models abandon shortcut features more rapidly than their fully supervised counterparts when fine-tuned on labeled datasets. While not a perfect remedy, our results strongly suggest that image-text self-supervised learning offers partial protection against the pitfalls of visual shortcut features.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning frequently faces challenges due to the exponentially growing action space resulting from numerous agents. This paper introduces HAVEN, a novel hierarchical reinforcement learning-based value decomposition framework designed for fully cooperative multi-agent tasks. To mitigate instability caused by simultaneously optimizing high-level and low-level policies—along with inter-agent coordination—we propose a dual coordination mechanism that aligns strategies across layers and agents. HAVEN eliminates the need for domain-specific knowledge or pretraining and is compatible with any value decomposition approach. The method demonstrates strong performance across various decentralized partially observable Markov decision process domains while providing an effective way to implicitly partition the decision space.

This study focuses specifically on evaluating the performance of AIS-INMACA. The model has demonstrated significant effectiveness in addressing key bioinformatics challenges, such as protein region identification and promoter region prediction, while reducing computational time (Pokkuluri Kiran Sree, 2014). Since its introduction, AIS-INMACA has undergone multiple adaptations (Pokkuluri Kiran Sree, 2014) to establish itself as a versatile bioinformatics tool capable of solving diverse problems in the field. Consequently, this research will prove highly valuable for researchers working at the intersection of bioinformatics and cellular automata.

In many academic programs, medical students begin their scientific training early in their studies. At our institution, for example, they frequently collaborate in interdisciplinary teams alongside researchers at various career stages—from postgraduate scientists in pharmaceutical or natural sciences to biostatisticians. Ensuring these students learn strong research practices, particularly in statistical analysis, is crucial to their education. A key component of this training is reproducibility, a cornerstone of modern scientific inquiry.  

Recognizing that even instructors may lack familiarity with fully reproducible workflows, I took on the task of developing a lecture series on reproducible research (RR) aimed at medical students and postgraduate pharmacists engaged in clinical research. The pilot series covered fundamental topics such as the definition of RR, its importance, benefits, and practical implementation.  

During an attempt to reproduce a published analysis, I encountered numerous challenges. Here, I use this experience to explore the complexities of RR, propose explanations and solutions, and advocate for standardized RR instruction in clinical research curricula. By sharing these insights, I hope to encourage greater awareness among both educators and learners about the necessity of adopting reproducible research practices.

Robust reinforcement learning (RL) aims to identify a policy that maximizes the worst-case performance across an uncertainty set of Markov decision processes (MDPs). This paper investigates model-free robust RL, where the uncertainty set is centered around a misspecified MDP generating a single sequential sample trajectory—assumed to be unknown. We introduce a sample-based method to estimate this uncertainty set and propose two algorithms: robust Q-learning for the tabular case and robust TDC for function approximation, both designed for online and incremental implementation.  

We establish theoretical guarantees for these algorithms: robust Q-learning converges to the optimal robust Q-function, while robust TDC converges asymptotically to stationary points. Unlike prior work [Roy et al., 2017], our convergence results hold without imposing additional conditions on the discount factor. Additionally, we derive finite-time error bounds, showing that both algorithms achieve convergence speeds comparable to their non-robust counterparts (within a constant factor). Empirical results further validate the robustness of our methods.  

Our framework is flexible and can be easily adapted to robustify a wide range of other reinforcement learning algorithms.

Contextual bandit algorithms—a specialized subset of multi-armed bandit methods that leverage contextual data—have proven successful in addressing sequential decision-making challenges in uncertain environments. Existing research often assumes that the true reward for a chosen action is freely observable by the learner, an assumption that fails in many real-world settings where obtaining accurate reward feedback incurs costs.  

A critical challenge arises when acquiring ground truth rewards is expensive: the learner must strategically determine when to gather this information, balancing the trade-off between learning efficiency and associated costs. From an information-theoretic standpoint, an even more compelling question is quantifying the potential efficiency loss due to these acquisition costs.  

In this work, we introduce a novel contextual bandit algorithm enhanced with active learning capabilities. A key innovation of our approach is that each query to an annotator for ground truth is accompanied by the learner’s prior knowledge about the reward, effectively reducing query expenses. By optimizing algorithm parameters, we demonstrate that our method achieves a bounded learning regret.

To establish baseline performance benchmarks and identify the most suitable image classification algorithm for mission-critical satellite imaging systems, twenty-three machine learning models were trained and evaluated. Using the Overhead-MNIST dataset—a satellite imagery counterpart to the standard MNIST handwritten digit dataset—initial assessments through PyCaret revealed that CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost classifiers achieved the highest accuracy, AUC, and F1 scores. Further analysis determined that a deep convolutional architecture demonstrated superior potential. The optimal solution, a convolutional neural network (CNN), achieved a 0.965 categorical accuracy on held-out test data, setting a performance benchmark for edge deployment and future model enhancements.

Forecasting the completion time of business process instances is invaluable for managing processes under service-level agreements. By anticipating the progression of active process instances, business managers can proactively address potential delays or unfavorable outcomes. However, achieving precise predictions is challenging due to the numerous factors influencing process duration. This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach using Recurrent Neural Networks, particularly LSTMs, which leverages event-specific data to generate highly accurate completion time estimates for ongoing instances. Real-world dataset evaluations validate the effectiveness of our method.

The extensive data requirements of DNNs often lead practitioners to gather large datasets from the Internet without thorough verification, given the prohibitive cost of manual curation. This practice, however, introduces potential vulnerabilities to backdoor attacks. A backdoored model is designed to output a specific target class whenever it encounters a predefined trigger pattern—an attack that can be executed by poisoning only a small portion of the training data.  

While adversarial training is widely considered a potential defense against backdoor threats, as it enhances model stability against input perturbations (within certain bounds), existing research has shown limited success in achieving this. To investigate the effectiveness of adversarial training in mitigating backdoor attacks, we perform comprehensive experiments across various threat models and perturbation budgets, revealing that the choice of threat model significantly impacts defensive performance. For example, adversarial training using spatial adversarial perturbations demonstrates strong resilience against typical patch-based backdoor attacks. Building on these insights, we introduce a hybrid defense strategy that achieves reliable robustness across diverse backdoor attack scenarios.

Detecting groups of similar objects within datasets is crucial across various applications. A key model for this task is the densest k-disjoint-clique problem, which aims to find k separate cliques in a weighted complete graph that collectively maximize the sum of their subgraph densities. This paper demonstrates specific conditions under which the optimal solution of a semidefinite program precisely identifies the densest k cliques in a given graph. The semidefinite relaxation proves particularly effective for datasets containing k well-separated, prominent clusters alongside a smaller number of outliers.  

The same methodology extends to biclustering, offering analogous recovery guarantees. Biclustering simultaneously groups both objects and their features based on expression levels—essentially partitioning the nodes of a weighted bipartite complete graph to maximize the sum of the induced bipartite subgraph densities. Mirroring the approach for the densest k-disjoint-clique problem, we establish that the correct partitioning can be reliably recovered under the specified conditions.

Clustering plays a fundamental role in data analysis, particularly in time series analysis. Due to its subjective nature, different users may favor distinct clusterings for the same dataset. Semi-supervised clustering resolves this ambiguity by incorporating user-provided guidance on instances that should (or should not) be grouped together. This paper explores semi-supervised clustering specifically for time series data. We demonstrate how COBRAS, a leading semi-supervised clustering technique, can be effectively adapted to this domain, introducing COBRAS-TS. Our comprehensive experimental analysis establishes several key findings: (1) COBRAS-TS significantly surpasses existing semi-supervised clustering methods for time series, setting a new benchmark for the field; (2) it can detect clusters containing distinct, separated components; (3) it recognizes clusters defined by localized patterns; (4) even minimal semi-supervision substantially enhances clustering accuracy for time series; (5) the selection of the clustering algorithm critically impacts results—contradicting prior assumptions in the literature.

The growing adoption of machine learning has made reusable model design increasingly valuable. This study investigates the reuse potential of pre-trained deep convolutional models, moving beyond their conventional role as feature extractors. We uncover hidden capabilities within convolutional layers, demonstrating that convolutional activations can effectively serve as detectors for identifying common objects in image co-localization tasks. Our proposed Deep Descriptor Transforming (DDT) method offers a straightforward yet powerful approach for analyzing descriptor correlations to pinpoint category-consistent regions, enabling precise common object localization across image sets. Experimental results confirm DDT's superior performance, significantly outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques on standard co-localization benchmarks. Additionally, DDT exhibits strong generalization to unseen categories and maintains robust performance when handling noisy data.

Crypto-ransomware inflicts irreversible damage by encrypting data, leading to significant losses. This paper presents a machine learning (ML) classifier designed for early detection of cryptographic ransomware based on program behavior. When signature-based detection fails, behavior-based analysis serves as a critical last line of defense to mitigate harm. Our findings indicate that ransomware exhibits distinct input/output patterns and file-content entropy, enabling reliable identification. A deep learning (DL) classifier achieves high detection accuracy with minimal false positives.  

We also conduct adversarial testing against our models using simulated ransomware in a gray-box analysis to identify vulnerabilities and enhance robustness. Beyond accuracy and resilience, trustworthiness is essential for an effective security solution. Ensuring correct inference data is critical, so we employ the Integrated Gradient method to interpret the DL model and analyze false negatives. The study demonstrates practical methods for developing and evaluating a real-world ransomware detector.

To optimize performance when users and data stores are spread across different regions, strategically placing distributed cache points is crucial for reducing unnecessary data transfers. In response, we’re creating a dynamic distributed caching framework that intelligently selects and relocates data segments across a network of shared cache locations.

Bibliographic reference parsers automatically retrieve structured metadata—including authors, titles, journals, and publication years—from reference strings. These parsers rely on either heuristic rules or machine learning techniques. However, no single parser or algorithm performs optimally in all cases. For example, a tool may excel at extracting titles in ACM citation style but rank lower when processing APA format. Similarly, one parser might be better suited for English author names, while another performs best with noisy or inconsistent citation data.  

This paper, an extended version of our recent RecSys poster, approaches reference parsing through recommender systems and meta-learning. We introduce **ParsRec**, a meta-learning-based recommender system that selects the most effective parser for a given reference string. ParsRec evaluates and recommends from ten open-source parsers: Anystyle-Parser, Biblio, CERMINE, Citation, Citation-Parser, GROBID, ParsCit, PDFSSA4MET, Reference Tagger, and Science Parse.  

Our evaluation spans **105,000 chemistry references**, testing two meta-learning strategies:  
1. **Global recommendation**—selecting the best parser for an entire reference.  
2. **Local recommendation**—choosing the best parser for each metadata field within a reference.  

The second approach, fine-tuned for individual metadata types, demonstrated superior performance.

Recommendation systems handling vast arrays of discrete items—like products, webpages, or videos—are commonplace across the tech sector. Deep neural networks have gained prominence in addressing these recommendation challenges. These models employ embeddings to convert discrete items into continuous vector representations, with vocabulary sizes and embedding dimensions significantly impacting model accuracy. However, these parameters are often chosen manually based on heuristic approaches.  

We introduce Neural Input Search (NIS), a method designed to optimize vocabulary sizes and embedding dimensions for categorical features while maximizing prediction accuracy under a fixed memory constraint for embeddings. Additionally, we highlight a limitation of conventional Single-size Embedding (SE)—where uniform embedding dimensions are applied to all feature values—resulting in inefficient model capacity and training data utilization.  

To address this, we propose Multi-size Embedding (ME), a novel approach that dynamically adjusts embedding dimensions based on feature values. Using reinforcement learning during training, NIS autonomously determines the optimal vocabulary size per feature and embedding dimension per feature value. In experiments across two large-scale recommendation scenarios—retrieval and ranking—NIS successfully identified...

Demand for training DNN models on end-user devices like smartphones is growing due to rising privacy concerns and the need to minimize communication costs. While datacenter servers rely on high-performance CPUs and GPUs, modern smartphones employ a heterogeneous array of specialized cores in a system-on-a-chip (SoC) design to handle diverse workloads. Our analysis reveals that inefficient smartphone SoC utilization during DNN training not only results in poor performance but also severely impacts user experience. This paper introduces Swan, a neural engine designed to accelerate DNN training on smartphone SoCs while maintaining seamless user experience. Large-scale evaluations demonstrate that Swan delivers 1.2 - 23.3x performance gains compared to current leading methods.

This study proposes stochastic hard thresholding algorithms to address AUC maximization in imbalanced classification. The key difficulty lies in handling pairwise losses inherent to AUC objectives. Our approach transforms the U-statistics formulation into an empirical risk minimization (ERM) framework, enabling the development of a computationally efficient stochastic hard thresholding method (\texttt{SHT-AUC}). Notably, this work presents the first stochastic hard thresholding solution for AUC optimization with a per-iteration complexity of $\O(b d)$, where $d$ denotes data dimensionality and $b$ represents minibatch size. Theoretical analysis demonstrates linear convergence within a tolerance error bound, with Gaussian-distributed data exhibiting slower convergence under increasing class imbalance. Comprehensive empirical evaluations validate both the computational efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

Adaptive control problems remain notoriously challenging to solve, even with plant-specific controllers. To circumvent the computational complexity of finding an optimal policy, one approach is to reformulate adaptive control as minimizing the relative entropy between a controller that disregards the true plant dynamics and an informed one. This yields the Bayesian control rule—a set of equations defining a stochastic adaptive controller for a range of possible plant dynamics.  

In this work, we apply the Bayesian control rule to derive BCR-MDP, a controller designed for undiscounted Markov decision processes with finite state and action spaces and unknown dynamics. Specifically, we develop a non-parametric conjugate prior distribution over the policy space that compresses the agent's entire relevant history. Additionally, we introduce a Gibbs sampler to generate random policies from this distribution.  

Early results demonstrate that BCR-MDP effectively prevents sub-optimal limit cycles by inherently balancing exploration and exploitation.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful machine learning techniques with diverse and groundbreaking applications. Within imaging science, they excel at producing synthetic datasets, generating realistic human faces, captioning images and videos, transforming images from one domain to another, converting text to images, forecasting video sequences, and creating 3D objects, among other uses. This paper explores the role of GANs in constructing artificial environments. We specifically examine their ability to describe visual content through captioning techniques and their capacity to modify images according to a desired theme using translation frameworks. Furthermore, we analyze how GANs contribute to building personalized, customizable worlds.

**Motivation:** Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) play a vital role in protein function across both healthy and diseased cells, with many essential biological processes dependent on these interactions. Understanding the nature of PPIs is key for building biological networks to analyze complex datasets. Despite their significance, functional annotations for PPIs remain scarce—for instance, only 4% of interactions in the IntAct database are functionally characterized. To address this gap, we propose labeling PPI functions by extracting relevant relationships from PubMed abstracts.  

**Method:** We constructed a weakly supervised dataset using the IntAct PPI database, comprising interacting protein pairs linked to PubMed abstracts with annotated functions. Using BioBERT, a leading deep learning model for biomedical NLP, we developed PPI-BioBERT to classify PPI functions. To enhance accuracy and scalability, we employed an ensemble of PPI-BioBERT models for robust uncertainty estimation and introduced interaction type-specific thresholds to mitigate class imbalance.  

**Results:** By analyzing 18 million PubMed abstracts, we automatically identified 3,253 new functionally annotated PPIs.

The degree to which neural networks memorize training data remains a compelling research question with both practical and theoretical significance. Here, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, substantial portions of training data can be recovered from the parameters of a trained neural network classifier. Our work introduces a new reconstruction approach based on recent theoretical insights into the implicit bias of gradient-based neural network training. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evidence showing that extracting significant portions of original training samples from a trained classifier is broadly feasible. These findings raise serious privacy concerns, as the technique could potentially expose sensitive training data through model inversion. We validate our approach using binary MLP classifiers across several standard computer vision datasets.

In complex networks, nodes with similar structural properties often play comparable roles (e.g., user types in social networks or hierarchical employee positions in organizations). To capitalize on this connection, recent research has introduced latent representations designed to detect structurally equivalent nodes. Yet, most existing methods suffer from high computational and memory demands.  

We present *VNEstruct*, a streamlined method for generating low-dimensional structural node embeddings that is both computationally efficient and resilient to changes in graph structure. Our approach examines the local neighborhood of each node and uses Von Neumann entropy—an information-theoretic measure—to extract topological features from the node's immediate surroundings.  

Additionally, for graph classification tasks, we propose enhancing node attributes by incorporating these structural embeddings, effectively transforming an attributed graph into a set of enriched node features. Empirical results demonstrate that *VNEstruct* delivers robustness in structural role identification, achieves state-of-the-art performance in graph classification, and maintains exceptional computational efficiency.

We address the challenge of approximating the optimal policy of a Markov decision process (MDP) through sampled state transitions. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches that rely on successive approximations to the nonlinear Bellman equation, we introduce a Primal-Dual $\pi$ Learning method, leveraging the linear duality between value and policy. This model-free method dynamically updates the policy and value vectors in a primal-dual framework as new data becomes available.

For infinite-horizon undiscounted MDPs with finite state space $S$ and finite action space $A$, the $\pi$ learning method achieves an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with a sample complexity of  
$$
\tilde{O}\left( \frac{(\tau \cdot t^*_{mix})^2 |S| |A|}{\epsilon^2} \right),
$$
where $t^*_{mix}$ is an upper bound on the mixing times for all policies, and $\tau$ quantifies the range of stationary distributions across policies.  

The method also extends to solving MDPs with explicitly given transition probabilities and rewards. When each state transition can be sampled in $\tilde{O}(1)$ time, $\pi$ learning yields a sublinear-time algorithm for averaged-reward MDPs.

The last ten years have witnessed a dramatic surge in digital health data stored within electronic health records (EHRs). Although these systems were originally created to manage patient medical histories and healthcare administration, researchers have increasingly repurposed them for diverse clinical informatics applications. Concurrently, the field of machine learning has experienced significant progress in deep learning methods, which have proven highly effective when applied to EHR datasets. This paper provides an overview of deep learning approaches for EHR analysis, exploring model architectures, technical considerations, and healthcare use cases. Additionally, we highlight limitations in existing methodologies and outline potential directions for future research in EHR-based deep learning.

Numerous open-domain conversational applications in real-world scenarios are designed with specific objectives during free-flowing dialogues, such as recommendation, therapy, or education. We investigate the challenge of incorporating these conversational goals into open-domain chat agents. Specifically, our aim is to develop a system that engages in natural dialogue while seamlessly steering the conversation toward a predefined topic. This task presents significant difficulties due to the lack of publicly available training data for such goal-oriented strategies.  

To address this, we introduce a structured methodology that employs coarse-grained keywords to guide the system’s responses. By using turn-level supervised learning, we ensure smooth transitions between dialogue turns, while discourse-level constraints help direct the conversation toward the intended target. Additionally, we curate a keyword-enhanced conversation dataset to support this research. Both quantitative assessments and human evaluations demonstrate that our system generates coherent and purposeful conversations, outperforming alternative approaches significantly.

Automated algorithm selection helps users choose the most appropriate algorithm for a specific problem by leveraging machine learning techniques. A key element of these methods involves regression models that estimate how well an algorithm will perform on new, unseen problem instances. For numerical black-box optimization, these models often rely on exploratory landscape analysis (ELA)—a method that evaluates various problem characteristics. These ELA metrics then train supervised regression models to predict algorithm performance.  

Initial research in this area focused on performance predictions for fixed-target scenarios. However, many real-world applications require selecting an algorithm that delivers the best results within a limited function evaluation budget. Addressing this fixed-budget scenario, we show that high-quality predictions can be achieved using standard supervised learning techniques by effectively combining two differently trained regression models.  

To validate our approach, we test it on a particularly difficult challenge: selecting the optimal algorithm from a set of highly similar options, specifically from the modular CMA-ES algorithm family.

The information bottleneck (IB) approach optimizes the balance between data compression and prediction accuracy in learned representations, proving effective in both supervised and unsupervised representation learning. Despite its success, IB has notable drawbacks. First, optimization is inherently difficult—the IB Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{IB} := I(X;Z) - \beta I(Y;Z)$ is non-convex, leading to solutions that depend on initialization and only guarantee local convergence. Second, evaluating solutions is non-trivial, often requiring analysis of the information plane by plotting $I(Y;Z)$ against $I(X;Z)$ across multiple initializations. 

Additionally, the IB Lagrangian exhibits phase transitions as the multiplier $\beta$ varies, where $I(X;Z)$ and $I(Y;Z)$ experience sudden jumps, severely slowing convergence. While recent work has introduced variational surrogate bounds to approximate the IB Lagrangian, their fidelity to the original objective remains uncertain. Here, we address the IB Lagrangian directly using augmented Lagrangian methods. By incorporating auxiliary variables, we reformulate the IB objective so that it can be efficiently optimized via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), offering a distinct alternative to prior approaches.

The growing reliance on machine learning (ML) systems for high-stakes applications has heightened the demand for innovative verification and validation methods that align with established assurance principles. In conventional system development, model-based approaches have proven effective by using abstract system models as a reliable foundation for evaluating implementations. Similarly, we propose an ML-based method that extracts a low-dimensional structure—called a manifold—from high-dimensional training data, which implicitly defines the intended system behavior. This manifold is then leveraged for various quality assurance processes, including test coverage evaluation, test case generation, and real-time performance monitoring of ML systems.  

Our approach employs variational autoencoders, an unsupervised learning technique that maps high-dimensional data to a lower-dimensional latent space while maintaining near-invertibility between the two representations. Initial experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this manifold-based framework: it enhances test diversity when measuring adequacy, produces realistic yet fault-detecting test inputs during generation, and offers an independent metric for assessing output reliability during runtime monitoring.

Recent studies on adversarial attacks and defenses indicate that PGD serves as a universal first-order $l_\infty$ attack, while PGD adversarial training effectively enhances model robustness against various first-order $l_\infty$-bounded attacks, establishing it as a leading defense strategy. However, a notable limitation of PGD adversarial training is its high computational overhead in generating adversarial examples, rendering it impractical for large-scale, high-resolution datasets like ImageNet. Furthermore, recent research has demonstrated that a simplified "closed-form" solution can achieve robustness on MNIST. This raises a critical question: Is PGD adversarial training truly essential for robust defense?  

In this work, we challenge this necessity by introducing an efficient training paradigm that achieves performance comparable to PGD adversarial training on standard datasets—using only noisy-natural samples. Our approach reformulates the min-max objective of PGD adversarial training into an optimization problem that minimizes the original network loss plus the $l_1$ norms of its input gradients. To address the computational complexity of the $l_1$-norm loss, we propose a practical solution by integrating a differentiable soft-quantization layer after the input layer. We formally demonstrate that training this soft-quantization layer with noisy-natural samples serves as an efficient alternative to minimizing $l_1$-gradient norms.

Adversarial imitation learning has emerged as a widely used approach for imitation in continuous control tasks. Numerous adaptations of its core components have been developed to improve both policy performance and algorithmic sample efficiency. However, these modifications are seldom evaluated comprehensively in controlled empirical studies, making it challenging to determine which high-level algorithmic decisions—or even low-level implementation specifics—yield meaningful improvements. To address this gap, we integrate over 50 of these variations into a flexible adversarial imitation learning framework and conduct an extensive evaluation (training more than 500k agents) using both synthetic and human-generated demonstrations. While many of our results align with established practices, some findings are unexpected or even contradict prior research. Notably, our analysis reveals that synthetic demonstrations fail to accurately represent human-provided data, and relying solely on artificial demonstrations for algorithm evaluation may produce methods that underperform in real-world scenarios involving human demonstrators.

Federated learning (FL) offers a secure approach for training AI models by leveraging decentralized datasets without requiring clients to share their raw data. In this framework, distributed clients collaborate through a central server to train a global model while preserving data privacy. However, FL faces significant communication challenges, particularly the overhead caused by transmitting model updates from multiple clients to the server during each training round. To address this bottleneck, over-the-air computation (AirComp) has emerged as a potential solution, enabling simultaneous transmission of model updates over a shared channel.  

Despite its efficiency, AirComp introduces vulnerabilities, as averaging model updates in this manner can be compromised by malicious or unreliable clients—known as Byzantine adversaries—that manipulate their local updates. To mitigate such risks while retaining the advantages of AirComp, we introduce a robust transmission and aggregation framework. Our approach involves randomly grouping participating clients and assigning each group a dedicated transmission time slot. The aggregated updates from these groups are then processed using a resilient aggregation technique to minimize the impact of adversarial inputs.  

Furthermore, we extend our solution to accommodate scenarios involving non-independent and identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) data, ensuring robustness across diverse and heterogeneous data distributions.

This study examines stochastic optimization problems for a broad range of objective functions, encompassing convex and continuous submodular cases. While stochastic proximal gradient methods are commonly employed for such problems, their efficiency diminishes in high-dimensional scenarios where projection onto convex sets is computationally expensive. To address this, we propose stochastic conditional gradient methods as an alternative, leveraging two key strategies: (i) Gradient approximation through an efficient averaging technique requiring only one stochastic gradient evaluation per iteration, and (ii) Computation of descent/ascent directions via linear programming. The averaging approach progressively reduces gradient approximation noise, while the substitution of projection steps with linear programming significantly decreases per-iteration computational demands.  

Under convexity and smoothness assumptions, we establish that our method achieves sublinear convergence at a rate of \( O(1/t^{1/3}) \) to the optimal objective value. Furthermore, for monotone continuous DR-submodular functions constrained by a general convex set, our method attains a \(((1-1/e)\text{OPT} - \eps)\) approximation guarantee with \( O(1/\eps^3) \) stochastic gradient evaluations. This result matches existing hardness bounds and bridges the gap between deterministic and stochastic continuous submodular maximization. Prescriptive process monitoring techniques utilize past data to recommend real-time interventions aimed at preventing unfavorable case outcomes or enhancing process efficiency. At the core of these methods is the intervention policy—a decision-making function that determines whether and when to act on an ongoing case. Existing approaches rely on policies that assess only the present state of a case, overlooking two critical factors: the balance between immediate intervention (given predictive model uncertainty) versus deferred action, and the assumption of unlimited intervention resources.  

This paper introduces an advanced prescriptive process monitoring approach that prioritizes ongoing cases by evaluating prediction confidence, uncertainty, and intervention impact. It allocates limited resources strategically to maximize overall benefits. The method is tested on real-world event logs, demonstrating superior performance compared to baseline methods in terms of achieved gains.

Recognizing offline handwritten mathematical expressions presents significant challenges due to two main issues: accurately identifying diverse mathematical symbols and correctly interpreting the two-dimensional structure of these expressions. Drawing on advancements in deep learning, this study introduces a novel neural network architecture integrating a Multi-Scale convolutional neural network (CNN) with an Attention-based recurrent neural network (RNN) to convert two-dimensional handwritten mathematical expressions into one-dimensional LaTeX sequences. The proposed model demonstrates strong performance, achieving a WER (Word Error Rate) of 25.715% and an ExpRate (Expression Recognition Rate) of 28.216%.

Co-evolving time series are prevalent across diverse domains, including environmental monitoring, financial markets, and intelligent transportation systems. This study focuses on overcoming two key challenges: (C1) effectively integrating known relationship networks among time series, and (C2) accurately representing hidden temporal dynamics relationships. We introduce a groundbreaking framework called the Network of Tensor Time Series, featuring two innovative components – the Tensor Graph Convolutional Network (TGCN) and Tensor Recurrent Neural Network (TRNN). TGCN addresses the first challenge by extending traditional Graph Convolutional Networks to handle tensor-based graph structures, enabling the modeling of complex interactions across multiple tensor-associated graphs. TRNN employs tensor decomposition techniques to uncover latent relationships within co-evolving time series data. Comprehensive evaluations on five real-world datasets validate the superior performance of our proposed approach.

Crowd-sourcing has emerged as a widely adopted method for obtaining labeled data in tasks where human judgment outperforms automated systems—such as image annotation, object matching, or sentiment analysis. However, depending entirely on human contributors is frequently infeasible, even for datasets containing thousands of entries, due to the time and expense involved (with each label costing both minutes and cents to produce). This paper introduces machine learning algorithms designed to enhance crowd-sourced databases, enabling scalable solutions that manage larger datasets at reduced costs. Our approach leverages the complementary strengths of humans and algorithms: while humans tend to be more precise, they are slower and costlier, whereas algorithms, though less accurate, are faster and more economical. Building on this insight, we propose two novel active learning techniques that integrate human and algorithmic contributions within a crowd-sourced framework. These algorithms draw on non-parametric bootstrap theory, ensuring compatibility with a wide range of machine learning models. Our findings, validated across three real-world datasets from Amazon Mechanical Turk and 15 benchmark UCI datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods.
